### Section 5 evidence: IK limbs bend as hinges and keep their side (2026-11-27)

`@margoengine/rigging/ik` (`solvePoseIK`, `solveSkeletonIK`, `addIKChain`) turned each bone by the shortest arc from its
old direction to its new one, which leaves the twist about the bone to chance: when a pole swung the bend plane, the
forearm's local rotation picked up swing about its other two axes and folded sideways or backward in the skin (the
planner demo's workers, KB-RIG-IKHINGE1). Each bone now also twists about its new direction so its old bend axis lands
on the new one (`keepHinge`), so the joint between two bones changes only by a rotation about one axis fixed in the
upper bone, and `keepBend` (default true) stops a pole folding an already bent elbow or knee to its far side.
Evidence: `packages/rigging/tests/ik.test.js`, 5 targets by 3 poles on a bent arm, keeps the forearm's change about
its own x axis to under 0.001 degrees with zero y and z parts (the old solve left 0.15 and 0.68 in them), and the
keepBend test folds the forearm backward with `keepBend: false` only. Missing: joint limits in FABRIK itself, which
stay with `addCCDChain` and `solveContactIK`.

### Section 5 evidence: friction through a bounce in the rigid kernel, against measured material pairs (2026-11-27)

The rigid kernel's strike (`physics/kernel/src/solver.rs`, `solve_impacts` and `collide_pairwise`) now solves friction in the cone
of the whole impulse, restitution included (KB-PHYS-BOUNCEFRICTION1). Evidence: `packages/physics/tests/rigid-materials.test.js`
holds seven oblique tennis-ball bounces to the rigid ball's exact solution at both solver tiers and six to Cross's measurements
(American Journal of Physics 70, 482, 2002) on three named surfaces, nothing fitted. Missing: tangential compliance (spin after a
gripping bounce runs up to 41 percent under the measured), recorded in `docs/limits.md`.

### Section 5 evidence: transmission proof through the default screen-transmission pass (2026-11-27)

`loadGLTF` and the parse, worker and progressive loaders attach `screenTransmission` (`@margoengine/gltf/transmission`) to a file with KHR_materials_transmission, KHR_materials_volume included since 2026-11-27 (KB-VOL-TINT-DISPLAY1: the tint's multiply blend on display-encoded light was up to 22 levels off Beer-Lambert; the pass is exact to 1 level on the slab case, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). The pass's volume path is the refracted chord through the slab, thickness x det(M) / |cof(M) r . n| in world units, the tint's estimate (it beat the plain thickness and the back-face depth d_V of Wyman 2005 against Cycles on every row). ### Section 5 evidence: quality gates list the whole tree past 1 MiB (2026-11-27)

The tracked file list passed 1 MiB (1,048,627 B), the default output buffer of `execFileSync` and `spawnSync`, so
`node scripts/quality-gate.mjs` (all gates), `scripts/hygiene.js` and `scripts/check-fixture-skips.mjs` failed with
ENOBUFS before checking anything (KB-GIT-LISTBUF1). Every `git ls-files` call in scripts and tests now states
`maxBuffer: 2 ** 28`, and `tests/git-list-buffer.test.js` fails on any call without one. Evidence: the sizes gate runs
to its report again on main.

### Section 5 evidence: dual-source blending of transmission, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-27)

With the `dual-source-blending` feature (requested through `EngineOptions.features`, no core change) gltf/pbr draws a
transmissive surface's tinted blend in one draw: entry `margoDual` returns the lit colour and the tint as
`@blend_src(0)` and `@blend_src(1)` of location 0, blended as colour `one` + `src1` and alpha `one` +
`one-minus-src-alpha` (`renderState.transmissionBlend`, materials `transmissionBlend`, default 'auto'). The WebGL2
layer offers the feature where the context has `WEBGL_blend_func_extended`: `@blend_src(1)` is GLSL ES 3.00
`layout(location = 0, index = 1)` under `GL_EXT_blend_func_extended`, and the four src1 factors map to the extension's
enums; without the feature, a module that enables it or a src1 factor is a validation error, as on WebGPU. Evidence:
`packages/materials/test/dual-source-browser.mjs` under Tonemap (rgba16float) reads the same centre texel with one
draw as with two, for one pane and for two panes, one draw saved per pane, and the coded refusal of 'dual-source'
without the feature, on WebGPU (RTX A6000, Edge 158) and on the WebGL2 layer (ANGLE D3D11, which has the extension);
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/dual-source.test.js` and `packages/gltf/test/render-state.test.js` pin the translation,
the feature, the validation and the pipeline. Missing: a WebGL2 context without the extension on real hardware (the
refusal is checked on a stand-in context only).

### Section 5 evidence: multi-draw ranges of one merged geometry, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-27)

Core draws a redirected batch's `draws` indirect argument sets (20 bytes each, WebGPU drawIndexedIndirect layout) in
order, or in one `multiDrawIndexedIndirect` call with `multi` in a render pass (never in a bundle).
`@margoengine/culling/multidraw` keeps one argument set per range, its instance count the batch's while shown and 0
while hidden, written only when one changes. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/multidraw-check.mjs` hides and shows
parts of three merged meshes and matches nine separate-part meshes pixel for pixel, with three indirect draws a frame,
one multi-draw call through a shim of the call, and no new snapshot recording when a range is hidden, on WebGPU (RTX
A6000, Edge 158) and on the WebGL2 layer. Missing: a run on a browser that exposes multi-draw-indirect natively.

### Section 5 evidence: snapshot rendering, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-27)

Core's `DrawOptions.snapshot` encodes the main draw's batch loop into a `GPURenderBundleEncoder` (WebGPU, "Bundles")
and replays it with `executeBundles` while the draw's bind group, which names its pipeline, is the recorded one; the
replay still walks the batches to upload changed rows and write indirect counts. `@margoengine/culling/snapshot`
keeps one recording per view and compares, before each main draw, what a recording bakes in (batch, its three
buffers, index count, back-cull choice, redirect buffers, count unless indirect). Evidence:
`packages/culling/test/gpu/snapshot-check.mjs` draws 16 steps (moves, recolours, hides, a new geometry, a batch that
stops drawing, a reset, a shader variant and its removal, direct counts) with snapshots on and off: identical pixels,
recordings only where expected, and no core draw encoded into the pass on a replayed frame, on WebGPU (RTX A6000,
Edge) and on the WebGL2 layer. Missing: a CPU-time measurement of the encode saved (speed phase deferred).

### Section 5 evidence: finite flood geometry at inland boundaries (2026-11-27)

The Water shader uses Flood's sea-edge mask when blending the solved field into the ocean. A lake behind a wall or
draining out of an open inland edge retains the finite-volume elevation through the boundary. WaveQuery evaluates
the shared mesh function. The focused regression `packages/water/test/flood-edge.browser.mjs` compares the captured
draw mesh with the solver at each edge and checks that a mixed map retains its west-sea transition.

Only Water's native coastal flow creates the ray field for breaking ocean surf. Flood surfaces disable those vertex
and fragment branches at shader creation, while keeping the solver's own surface and foam. The boundary regression
checks the selected shader branches and that detaching Flood restores coastal surf. Pipeline initialization and
constant expressions follow the [WebGPU and WGSL specifications](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/) (W3C GPU for the Web
Working Group, 2026).

The hydrostatic height follows the bed plus depth in Emmanuel Audusse, François Bouchut, Marie-Odile Bristeau,
Rupert Klein and Benoît Perthame's [well-balanced finite-volume scheme](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/bouchut.francois/publications/hydroproj_published.pdf)
(2004). Wet/dry reconstruction remains as described in Scott C. Medeiros and Scott C. Hagen's
[review of wetting and drying algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1002/fld.3668) (2013).

### Section 5 evidence: core's own clear colour is linear light in a linear capture (2026-11-26)

GPU maths and both backends (KB-CLEAR-DEFAULT1): with no `background` set, core's clear colour (display 0.018, 0.023,
0.035, drawn 5,6,9) was written with the same numbers to every target, so a float capture held about thirteen times
the light the canvas shows and a tone map drew 7,20,38. `captureClearColor` now decodes it with the sRGB transfer
function (IEC 61966-2-1) for a capture that holds linear light (a float format or an `-srgb` one), exactly as it does
a `background`, on both clear paths and in post's material clear; the frame's own target and display-encoded captures
keep the numbers, so a frame with no capture is unchanged. Evidence: `tests/clear-capture.test.js` (CPU) and
`packages/post/test/scene-background-browser.mjs` on native WebGPU and on the WebGL2 layer, Intel Arc 140V: with no
background, 5,6,9 with no effect, 0,1,4 under Tonemap and PostStack and 0,2,5 under Bloom, each within one step of a
`#050609` background under the same effect, in an empty scene, beside a mesh and in a half-canvas view (84 cases a
backend with the background cases). The package GPU checks that draw through a capture were run again over the new
backdrop (docs/known-bugs.md, KB-CLEAR-DEFAULT1). Missing: other GPUs and browsers; a real XR device (the simulated
stereo check only).

### Section 5 evidence: an `-srgb` view target is encoded once (2026-11-26)

Every pass of a frame writes display colour (core's shader, its clear colour, each package's display transform), and
an `-srgb` attachment encodes what it is given, so a view drawn into an `-srgb` texture stored its colour encoded
twice (KB-VIEW-SRGB1: #808080 as 188). GPU maths and both backends: core now draws such a target through a view in its
non-srgb twin format (WebGPU `createView()`, a format of the texture's `viewFormats`); the pass context's `format`,
core's pipeline and its 4x colour are the twin's, so the texture stores the bytes its twin would and a sampler reads
them as linear light. The caller names the twin in `viewFormats`; native WebGPU reports a validation error for the
view otherwise, and the WebGL2 layer, which keeps a twin-format copy of such a texture and copies raw bytes between
the two, makes the view either way. Evidence: `packages/core/tests/view-srgb.test.js` (CPU) and
`packages/core/tests/view-srgb.browser.mjs` on native WebGPU and on the WebGL2 layer, Intel Arc 140V: a `rgba8unorm`
and a `rgba8unorm-srgb` target read back equal byte for byte in 11 cases a backend (4x MSAA and 1 sample; a whole
view, core's own clear colour, two half views, a package pipeline, an HDR capture, a device restore). Missing: other
GPUs and browsers; `bgra8unorm-srgb` on a real GPU (the CPU test covers its view and format); the cost on the WebGL2
layer of sampling such a target each frame (its raw copy into an sRGB texture goes through client memory).

### Section 5 evidence: a scene's background is linear light in a linear capture (2026-11-26)

Core's clear colour follows a capture's format (KB-CLEAR-CAPTURE1): when a pass has redirected the draw into a float
target (every HDR capture, rgba16float on WebGPU and rg11b10ufloat on the WebGL2 layer) or an `-srgb` one,
`scene.background` and a view's `clear.color` are decoded with the sRGB transfer function (IEC 61966-2-1) on both
clear paths, so the display transform encodes them once. The frame's own target (the canvas, a view's `target` of any
format) and display-encoded captures keep the bytes, so a frame with no capture is unchanged.
Evidence: `tests/clear-capture.test.js` (CPU) and `packages/post/test/scene-background-browser.mjs` on native WebGPU
and on the WebGL2 layer, Intel Arc 140V: #808080 draws 116 under Tonemap and PostStack and 117 under Bloom
(181 and 182 before), as ColorBackground does, and 128 with no effect, in an empty scene, beside a mesh and in a
half-canvas view. Missing: other GPUs and browsers. Core's own clear colour (no background set) takes the same path
since KB-CLEAR-DEFAULT1 (the section above).

### Section 5 evidence: whole migration scenes in a browser (2026-11-26)

A new root browser suite (the migration examples in the `ROOT` list of `scripts/gpu-package-tests.mjs`) composes glTF
PBR, an HDR environment, sun shadows, an action mixer, orbit controls, SSAO, bloom, tone mapping, FXAA, GPU picking and
outline selection in one scene, beside four smaller ones, and checks pixels and behaviour. Evidence: passed on native
WebGPU and on the WebGL2 layer (ANGLE Direct3D 11), Intel Arc 140V. Missing: other GPUs and browsers not run; the
defect it found (KB-CLEAR-CAPTURE1) is fixed in core (the section above).

### Section 5 evidence: texture units counted before linking, glTF base maps packed by the limit (2026-11-26)

The WebGL2 layer counts a render pipeline's texture units per stage from its GLSL before linking (render.ts
`programUnits`: texture and sampler pairs a stage reads, a pair both stages read counted once in the combined count,
plus storage data textures; a texture that is only size-queried takes none) against MAX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS,
MAX_VERTEX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS and MAX_COMBINED_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS, and `createRenderPipeline` refuses past a limit
with code `unsupported` (errors#texture-units) instead of a link failure. `device.textureUnits(descriptor)` returns the
same count and keeps the translation for the next pipeline from that descriptor. gltf marks a material on a device
when its composed shader passes WebGPU's per-stage counts or the layer's count, and composes it with its five base
maps in one array (four units fewer); materials that fit are unchanged. Evidence: CPU checks (glsl.test.js
`stageUnits`; device.test.js refusal before link per stage; materials-ext.test.js no pack at 16, pack at a 12 limit)
and scripts/compat-units-gpu-check.js on native WebGPU and ANGLE Direct3D 11 (all 13 maps, the peak and shared maps),
RTX A6000. Missing: a GPU scene that needs packing on a real 16-unit device (the check's scenes fit after the shared
bindings); other GPUs not run.

### Section 5 evidence: shadow map viewer, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-25)

`ShadowMapViewer` (`@margoengine/shadows/viewer`) is a debug overlay: it loads the chosen depth layer with `textureLoad`
(the WebGL2 layer turns a load-only depth binding into a float one, `floatDepthLoads`), mirrors reversed depth and
linearises perspective depth with the map's near and far. A one-layer texture is bound as a '2d' view unless it was made
for '2d-array' (the compatibility level binds only the dimension a texture was made for). Evidence:
`packages/shadows/test/viewer-browser.mjs` reads the grey at a spot map's and a point light's -y face's centre, the floor
4 from the light, as round(255 (4 - near) / (far - near)) = 127 within 2, an empty face as 255 and a `bounds` cascade at
the middle of its box, on WebGPU and with `--compat`. Missing: no check yet over `ShadowAtlas` tiles or an area light face.

### Section 5 evidence: shader resources on the WebGL2 layer over ANGLE Direct3D 11 (2026-11-25)

The WebGL2 layer's GLSL back end now counts a stage's texture units and uniform blocks together: ANGLE's Direct3D 11
back end turns a uniform block of 50 or more rows into a shader resource after the textures, and past 16 the browser's
GPU process crashed at the first draw (KB-BOUNCE-COMPATUNITS1). Past the stage's texture unit limit the blocks are
declared inside a struct of the same std140 layout (glsl/emit.ts `fitShaderResources`); stages within it are byte for
byte unchanged. A lost WebGL2 context now loses the device instead of surfacing as a layer bug or a validation error.
Evidence: a raw WebGL2 repro with no Margo code (packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-srv-crash-repro.mjs: the crash
needs 17 resources and a 50-row block, ANGLE Vulkan draws every case), CPU checks of the GLSL per stage
(glsl.test.js), a lost-context browser check, and a real scene (scripts/compat-units-gpu-check.js: gltf physical with
13 maps, image light, both shadow kinds and LightBounce) on native WebGPU, ANGLE Direct3D 11 and ANGLE Vulkan, RTX
A6000. Missing: other Direct3D 11 GPUs (Intel Arc, Radeon) not run; the 50-row threshold is measured, not documented
by ANGLE, so the layer switches on the count of all blocks, not only large ones.
Step 1 of the unit plan (2026-11-25): gltf's sparse physical shader binds a glTF texture that several extension slots
share once, by colour space (shader.ts `shareOwner`), so the KHR_materials layouts that pack two maps in one texture
need 5 extension units, not 8. Evidence: CPU checks of the WGSL and bind entries (physical-map-renderer.test.js,
materials-ext.test.js) and the `shared` variant of compat-units-gpu-check.js on native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer.

### Section 5 evidence: the screen-space march on streets (2026-11-27, KB-POST-SSRSTREET1)

The Hi-Z march shared by SSR, its rough trace and SSGI (packages/post/src/hiz.ts) no longer re-tests a cell that sent
the ray down while the ray is inside it and its depth falls (one bit per level, cleared for the cells a step leaves),
which gives the same hits with fewer iterations, and it counts hits only on surfaces facing the ray. SSR's default
`steps` went from 64 to 128. Evidence: real frames of The Night City's avenue (streaks gone at 96 steps or more; the
demo's own 56 still leaves speckled misses near the frame's bottom) and `packages/post/test/ssr-street-browser.mjs`
on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (28 steps: 3.1 luminance steps from the 256-step frame before, 1.2 after). Missing:
GPU time not measured (build phase); a ray that runs out of steps is still a hard miss, with no fade by budget.

### Section 5 evidence: rough reflections with contact hardening (2026-11-25)

Planar reflectors (environment's Reflector, Refractor and PBRReflector with `contactHardening`), water's planar
reflection (`contactHardening`) and post's SSR now pick the blur mip from one reflection cone
(packages/shared/reflection-cone.js): GGX alpha = roughness^2 as a Phong exponent, the cone holding 3/4 of the lobe,
doubled for the reflected ray, its footprint at the world distance along the ray to what the pixel shows. Planar
surfaces find that distance from the capture depth and the capture matrix alone (any projection, the oblique near plane
included); SSR from the hit point, replacing its on-screen ray length, which left rays running away from the camera
nearly sharp. Evidence: CPU checks against the closed form, and real frames on WebGPU and the WebGL2 compatibility layer
(posts on a glossy floor, in calm water and under SSR: the foot's reflection keeps its contrast and the top's falls).
Missing: no anisotropic stretch at grazing angles, the box mip chain caps the footprint (8 planar, 5 SSR levels), and
no comparison against a path-traced reference. No benchmark claim is made. See the
[clean-room record](../clean-room.md#reflection-cone-rough-planar-and-screen-space-reflections-with-contact-hardening-2026-11-25).

### Section 5 evidence: shadows from the environment map (shadows/ibl, 2026-11-25)

`@margoengine/shadows/ibl` is a PostStack HDR stage: directions importance sampled from the equirect's luminance
times sin(theta) are traced per pixel against a BVH in the fragment shader, kept as the ratio estimator (cos-weighted
visible over cos-weighted total) with reverse-reprojected, decayed sums, and filtered with a distance edge stop. Ray
starts add half a pixel's step to `bias`: the 1x depth holds one MSAA sample, the nearest on WebGPU and sample 0 on
the WebGL2 layer, and without it the layer's floor sat 1 to 2 cm under its own surface and shadowed itself. Evidence:
`packages/shadows/test/ibl.test.js` (texel shares within 2% of luminance x solid angle at three rotations; the
estimator within 0.01 of a brute-force integral) and `ibl-browser.mjs` on both backends (mean visibility error 0.003
to 0.006 against a Node reference, still, rotated and after a refit). Missing: timing, and a comparison against a
path-traced frame of a real model.

### Section 5 evidence: short wind waves and sky reflection (2026-11-24)

Water now filters each ripple against its rotated pixel footprint. The old common six-metre
cutoff removed the longest wind ripple while that band still had visible energy. Nonzero chop
also shades two short gravity-wave bands whose curved crests vary across a moving wind field.
The normal and the roughness derived from it are shared by the beauty and SSR paths.

The procedural sky callback now samples the same two angular axes as HDR reflection. Its
real GPU witness changes roughness over a blue horizon with red above it and checks the
red contribution. The previous shader leaves that contribution at zero. Coarse surface
depth, authored swell, and water-query geometry follow their existing paths. No benchmark
claim is made. See the [clean-room record](../clean-room.md#short-wind-waves-and-open-water-reflection-2026-11-24).

### Section 5 evidence: discoloured water behind a ship (2026-11-23)

`ShipWakes` has a per-ship linear RGB tint for the turbulent stern trail. It shades the part of the water body
and foam that the stern has passed over, with the existing turbulence envelope. The uniform holds one extra vector
per vessel. The same fragment and buffer layout run on WebGPU and WebGL2. Core stays unchanged.

The browser witness changes and clears the tint with the wake time held still. It checks the RGB near the stern,
the pixels ahead and outside of the trail, and the unchanged foam-density values. The CPU fixture checks input
validation and the unchanged height and foam query. See the [clean-room record](../clean-room.md#colour-in-the-stern-wake-2026-11-23).

### Section 5 evidence: Kelvin wake crest phase (2026-11-23)

`ShipWakes` now uses the correct sign for the lateral part of the phase when distance along the trail is measured aft.
The positive stationary roots were previously evaluated with the opposite projection, which pitched the crests into
strong, linear breaks in a view down a long hull. The CPU test checks the closed-form cusp on both sides of a 128 m ship.
The water GPU fixture compares sampled heights to the CPU law over a grid on open and flooded water, on WebGPU and WebGL2.
The hull and foam terms are independent of the phase change. See the
[clean-room record](../clean-room.md#kelvin-wake-crest-phase-2026-11-23).

### Section 5 evidence: finite-quay draw and wet queries (SEA-12)

`WaterWake` accepts the finite receiver's fixed wet-cell and open-face bits. The vertex shader follows the
same connected bilinear stencil and one-sided slopes as the CPU receiver. Fragment clipping keeps the
shared water-body marker and leaves the scene's ordinary sea beyond the finite grid. The existing quay
browser chain compares the live solver at 4,225 drawn vertices on each backend. Height and normal residuals
stay below 1.11×10⁻⁷, and the dry patch matches the no-water background exactly. The geometric WaveQuery
samples the displaced vertices. Per-fragment clipping is a render effect.

### Section 5 evidence: open-ocean horizon depth (2026-11-23)

Water keeps its original homogeneous depth on the displaced grid. A separate flat quad fills the remaining ocean
beyond the camera's far plane at reversed-Z zero. The previous vertex clamp changed the depth plane of triangles
straddling the far clip and hid dry land in regional aerial shots. The existing Water pass draws both parts with
the same bindings, depth test and surface shader. Core and the public API stay unchanged.

The GPU regression in `packages/water/test/horizon.browser.mjs` puts a 1 km high plateau about 155 km ahead of a
26 km high camera. Its central RGBA pixel matches the dry reference exactly. The same fixture compares the near
field of bounded and camera-following grids and measures coverage at the horizon. It makes no speed claim.

The implementation follows James F. Blinn and Martin E. Newell, [Clipping Using Homogeneous Coordinates](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/c543j-0mg40) (1978), the W3C GPU for the Web Working Group's [WebGPU primitive clipping](https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#primitive-clipping), and the separation of resolved waves and distant surface appearance in Eric Bruneton, Fabrice Neyret and Nicolas Holzschuch, [Real-time Realistic Ocean Lighting using Seamless Transitions from Geometry to BRDF](https://diglib.eg.org/items/fb727c69-2be2-4edd-833e-f7a9baea9b63) (2010).

### Section 5 evidence: ink hatching over shadowed meshes (2026-11-22)

`@margoengine/toon/hatch` now wraps the light expression after the shadow and clustered-lighting passes. Applying
ink earlier removed the shader anchor used by Shadows and caused the frame to fail. The CPU fixture exercises the
pass order and verifies that ink wraps the shadow term. The browser fixture draws a board with both packages
attached. The core shader and exported APIs stay unchanged.

### Section 5 evidence: quay reflection and visible overtopping (SEA-12, 2026-11-27)

A mirrored finite-depth potential keeps flow on the wet side of a straight impermeable quay. The loads tests
check the incident and reflected complex phase, pressure and displaced volume from a real hull, and rejection
before either output changes. Water’s browser test checks the same solved wet surface on WebGPU and WebGL2,
with a 2.47×10⁻⁸ m maximum draw error. It clips the mirrored region in the fragment pass, retains the slopes,
and issues visual spray only for a rising crest above the sill. Both backends replay to hash `9a02347ea18709e6`.

### Section 5 evidence: ship wakes at harbor speed (2026-11-21)

At 1.5 m/s the 68 m test hull's analytic crest is about 0.23 m aft of the stem. The CPU and WGSL profiles broaden the
support around that crest and widen the side section as the crest scale shrinks. The crest height and centre remain those
of `bowWave`. The stern foam ramps in at harbor speeds and its density still decays using `foamLife`. The fragment shader
modulates that density with slow spatial noise so thinning foam breaks into patches. See the
[clean-room record](../clean-room.md#ship-wakes-at-harbor-speed-2026-11-21).

The WebGPU and WebGL2 readbacks measured 0.103 m at the bow witness and 0.011 m at each side witness at 1.5 m/s, with
zero outside the band. The new slow stern case reads 0.290 and 0.278 coverage in two lit patches 0.9 and 15 m behind a
separate hull, with zero forward and off the trail. The CPU decay test checks the underlying density, independently of the
patch locations. Existing 3 m/s height and foam bounds on both backends still pass. The profile continues to use the hull's
parametric waterplane. Grid resolution and lighting still affect how much detail resolves in a wide shot.

### Section 5 evidence: water displacement alongside a ship (2026-11-21)

`ShipWakes` models the surface outside the current hull as a smooth lift and drawdown behind the bow crest. The added
section has zero signed integral across the water on each side. It is evaluated in the existing CPU and WGSL height paths,
so the drawn surface, normals and queries agree. The speed-dependent bow height scales both effects. The new term uses the
existing hull dimensions, uniforms and draw. See the [clean-room record](../clean-room.md#ship-side-wash-in-water-2026-11-21).

At 18 m aft of the stem on a 68 m hull moving at 3 m/s, both backends read 0.101 m of rise on each side, −0.051 m in the
drawdown, and zero farther out. The CPU test also checks that the lift weakens at half speed and vanishes at rest. The new
shape is a heightfield approximation. It needs Water grid cells small enough to resolve the near-hull band.

### Section 5 evidence: bow wave planform (2026-11-21)

The near-field bow crest and its breaking foam use current hull coordinates. The existing bow contact profile sweeps aft and fades as the distance from the hull increases. The compact support ends the near-field crest before it carries on across open water. Kelvin height still uses the recorded bow trajectory.

WebGPU and WebGL2 height readbacks for a 68 m hull at 3 m/s measured 0.458 m at the bow shoulder and 0.344 m at the swept crest. Both measured zero on the old transverse line at that outboard station and zero farther out. See the [clean-room record](../clean-room.md#swept-bow-crest-in-water-2026-11-21).

### Section 5 evidence: ship wake foam history (2026-11-21)

Water's ships entry reads each turbulent foam sample from the stern's nearest historical segment. Kelvin waves still use the bow track. The two positions and arc lengths share the existing eight-float station layout. Vertex shading continues to evaluate only wave height and slope. The fragment shader uses the stern's time and speed, and rejects samples before the track begins or ahead of the stern. Zero-speed samples on a path retain the nearest newer moving heading so a stationary ship does not leave a false turn at the dock.

The CPU regression compares two hull lengths at the same speed. The WebGPU and WebGL2 tests read four GPU foam samples with a 72 m ship at 3 m/s. Their values were 0.553 near the stern, 0.192 farther astern, and zero ahead and outside the trail on both backends. See the [clean-room research](../clean-room.md#stern-foam-history-in-water-2026-11-21).

### Section 5 evidence: short-crested surf (2026-11-26)
The surf's breaker index swings along each crest in sections scaled by the
swell's deep directional spread, so breaking starts and stops along a crest
and the roller has a ragged toe and holes (KB-WATER-SURFBANDS1). On a 1:50
beach under the dune coast's swell the longest breaking section along 240 m
fell from 73 to 114 m to 37.5 to 46 m (packages/water/test/surf-crests.browser.mjs,
RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). TerrainColors' wind ripples now fade
with the wetness record's moisture, so the sea floor is smooth (KB-TERRAIN-SANDWET1).
See the [clean-room research](../clean-room.md#short-crested-surf-and-dry-sand-ripples-2026-11-26-kb-water-surfbands1-kb-terrain-sandwet1).

### Section 5 evidence: white water lit as a bubble layer (2026-11-26)
Water's foam is lit as a multiple-scattering layer from above: the sky's
cosine-weighted radiance (foamSky or the HDR irradiance) for every kind of
foam, a two-stream layer reflectance up to a deep layer's 0.84 to 0.87, and a
lumpy normal with hollows (KB-WATER-WHITEWATERLIGHT1). Under a uniform grey
sky of radiance L, dense whitecap foam went from one tone at 0.725 L to
0.86 L with a variation of 0.061, and surf foam on a sea without whitecaps
from black to 0.36 (packages/water/test/whitewater-light.browser.mjs,
RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). See the
[clean-room research](../clean-room.md#white-water-as-a-lit-bubble-layer-2026-11-26-kb-water-whitewaterlight1).

### Section 5 evidence: near sea detail and the reactive mask (2026-11-26)
Water's shading normal gains five gravity-capillary octaves (25 cm to 1.8 cm)
at Elfouhaily et al.'s short-wave spectrum for the chop's wind, the resolved
share leaving the glint lobe's Cox and Munk remainder
(KB-WATER-NEARDETAIL1), and Water writes TAA's reactive mask
(`reactiveTexture`) where its waves move a pixel a frame
(KB-WATER-TAASMEAR1), published on the pass context
(`packages/shared/reactive-mask.js`) so TAA reads it with no wiring and
takes the maximum of several masks in one r8unorm pass. In a 960 x 540 view 3.6 m over a 12 m/s sea, the near
water's 2 to 5 cm relief went from 1.8 to 13.7 luma levels, and TAA keeps
all of it with the mask against 0.34 without
(packages/water/test/near-detail.browser.mjs, RTX A6000, WebGPU and the
WebGL2 layer). See the
[clean-room research](../clean-room.md#gravity-capillary-detail-and-the-seas-reactive-mask-2026-11-26-kb-water-neardetail1-kb-water-taasmear1).
Weather's rain and snow and VFX's billboards reach the same registry with no
scene code (KB-TAA-PARTICLEMASK1): TAA's read counts as demand, so their mask
draws run only while TAA does; VFX effects share one r8unorm particle mask.
Evidence: `packages/sky/test/features-check.mjs` weather and
`packages/vfx/test/reactive-check.mjs` (86% against 48% of the no-TAA
brightness), RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. Ribbons, mesh particles,
`Flame`, splats and blended glTF still write no mask.

### Section 5 evidence: grazing refraction onto a shallow bed (2026-11-26)
The texel reprojection above diverges on a bed seen at a grazing angle, and
the crossing search used to hand its bracket back to it: 36% of the Kitty Hawk
s18 water drew the flat fallback bottom, in contour rings (KB-WATER-SEABEDMAZE1).
A bisected crossing within 5 cm or 2% of the ray's depth is now the hit, and a
ray that leaves the viewport takes its crossing before the edge or the last
on-screen texel. packages/water/test/refraction-grazing.browser.mjs paints the
bed two colours under a rippled sea seen from 6 m: 61.1% of the water missed it
before, 0.00% after, on the RTX A6000 in WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer.
See the [clean-room research](../clean-room.md#grazing-refraction-onto-a-shallow-bed-2026-11-26-kb-water-seabedmaze1).

### Section 5 evidence: above-water refraction depth (2026-11-21)
Water uses the existing opaque color and reversed depth snapshots. It solves
the intersection of a Snell-bent ray with a sampled texel's depth plane in
homogeneous clip space. A hit must reproject to the same texel. When the
initial estimate cannot converge, bounded depth probes bracket a crossing
and validate it with the same intersection. Optical attenuation uses the
hit distance. Shore foam keeps its separate straight depth comparison. The
active viewport occupies one four-float row in the Water uniform.
The GPU regression puts a submerged slab in front of the straight ray,
outside the bent ray, then removes it. The mean RGB in the 7 × 7 witness
region is identical in both frames on the RTX A6000 in WebGPU and the
WebGL2 layer. A dark seabed changes the bent-ray sample on both backends.
See the [clean-room research](../clean-room.md#above-water-refraction-depth-2026-11-21).

### Section 5 evidence: HDR ocean reflection and the camera waterline (2026-11-21)

Water and Underwater borrow an HDR Environment through `reflectionEnvironment` and `skyEnvironment`. They use its azimuth convention, live rotation
and radiance scale, so the reflected and refracted sky match the camera's background. The callback used by procedural
Sky keeps its original orientation. Water smooths the rough HDR reflection over a tangent-plane footprint in both
angular axes. The local change in the rippled normal contributes to the specular lobe width shared by the sky and SSR. Underwater blends partial wet and dry coverage within one pixel of the near-plane intersection.

The HDR water body and seabed use eight stratified cosine-weighted sky samples relative to 18% grey. The estimate keeps cloud light in the troughs when their normals reflect away from the horizon. Foam reuses this estimate. The initial procedural sky and its low-light behaviour retain their ambient model.

Planar water applies the wave's change from the flat reflected ray in capture space, fades to the sky over the filter footprint at the capture boundary and far horizon, and keeps sky lighting independent of the captured geometry. The reflector fixture measures a red-channel change of 11.17 codes in the capture interior, 1 at its feathered edge and 0 outside.

The GPU sky witness compares the colour of the visible background with grazing water before and after a 90-degree
environment rotation. The underwater witness checks subpixel coverage, an unchanged dry region, and the scale of the
Snell-window radiance. The feature uses the existing water capture and does not change core.

- Eric Bruneton, Fabrice Neyret, and Nicolas Holzschuch, [Real-time Realistic Ocean Lighting using Seamless Transitions from Geometry to BRDF](https://www-evasion.imag.fr/Publications/2010/BNH10/), 2010. The reflection footprint grows with the unresolved roughness.
- Curtis D. Mobley, [Estimation of the remote-sensing reflectance from above-surface measurements](https://misclab.umeoce.maine.edu/ftp/classes/OO2015/Readings/Mobley1999.pdf), 1999. Above-water radiance includes light emerging from the water body and Fresnel-reflected sky.
- Charles Cox and Walter Munk, [Measurement of the Roughness of the Sea Surface from Photographs of the Sun’s Glitter](https://opg.optica.org/josa/abstract.cfm?URI=josa-44-11-838), 1954. Wind-driven surface slopes broaden reflected light.
- Yusuke Tokuyoshi and Anton S. Kaplanyan, [Improved Geometric Specular Antialiasing](https://doi.org/10.1145/3306131.3317026), 2019. The box-pixel variance supplements the intrinsic lobe width.
- W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, [WebGPU Shading Language, derivative built-in functions](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#derivative-builtin-functions). The waterline uses the local screen derivative for pixel coverage.

### Section 5 evidence: water contact foam at depth discontinuities (2026-11-21)

Shoreline filtering uses derivatives of the depth gap clipped to the contact
band. A local fragment quad that spans open water and a deeply submerged
surface therefore cannot widen the foam band. The GPU regression reads the
foam target directly. On the RTX A6000, a submerged block fell from 360 foam
pixels to zero while 4,289 pixels remained over a near-surface block. This
applies to the main Water WebGPU shader and its SSR variant.

- Yusuke Tokuyoshi and Anton S. Kaplanyan, [Improved Geometric Specular Antialiasing](https://doi.org/10.1145/3306131.3317026), 2019. The box-pixel variance supplements the intrinsic lobe width.
- W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, [WebGPU Shading Language, derivative built-in functions](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#derivative-builtin-functions).
- Charles Loop and Jim Blinn, [Resolution Independent Curve Rendering Using Programmable Graphics Hardware](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/resolution-independent-curve-rendering-using-programmable-graphics-hardware/), 2005. Local derivative-based filtering informs the contact edge.

### Section 5 evidence: scatter texture maps, cut-out shadows and the cotangent frame (KB-SCATTER-TEX1, 2026-11-17)

`ScatterOptions.textures` patches core's lit fragment stage (base colour, alpha MASK, occlusion-roughness-metal, a
normal map through a cotangent frame from screen derivatives) and scatter's depth-only shadow stage (a fragment stage
dropping cut texels). The frame is divided by the sign of its determinant: WebGPU's dpdy grows downward, the opposite of
the GLSL convention the source note assumes, and without the sign the map tilted normals the wrong way (found by the
check). Evidence: `packages/scatter/test/maps.browser.mjs` passes on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 layer (cut half not drawn
and casting no shadow, opaque half green and shadowing, a (1, 0, 0) normal darkening a sunlit card), for `Scatter` and
`ScatterTiles`; `packages/scatter/test/maps.test.js` (32-byte vertices, mip chains with kept alpha coverage). Missing:
no measured cost of the three texture reads a pixel on a forest scene (speed phase deferred).

### Section 5 evidence: the flood solver on the GPU, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (water/flood push 3, 2026-11-17)

`@margoengine/water/flood` (`packages/water/src/flood.ts`, `flood-shaders.ts`) runs the reference's scheme as one WGSL
compute kernel per SSP Runge-Kutta stage. Each invocation reads a cross of cells two out along each axis and writes only
its own texel of two rgba32float targets, state (h, bed, foam, breaker) and momentum (0, hu, 0, hv), the layout Water's
spray and queries already read, so the WebGL2 layer runs it on its Fragment tier (3.3; a two-target rgba32float gather
was proven there first). Three state and three momentum textures (0 and 1 between steps, 2 for U1) and two r32float inputs (obstacles, fill), 27 MB at 512 x 512;
the first state is one more gather pass. The flood runs in place of Water's coastal flow through the solver bridge
(`waterSolvers`, query-state.ts). Walls raise the bed of every cell their segment touches (a slab test of the segment
against the cell square grown by half the wall's width, Kay and Kajiya 1986, SIGGRAPH, https://doi.org/10.1145/15886.15916),
a 4-connected line with no gap at a diagonal; a breach lowers the crest to the ground; buildings stand on the ground as
blocks read once from `obstacles(x, z)` (Schubert and Sanders 2012, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.advwatres.2012.02.012).
The step is fixed, 1 / (120 m) s with m from Courant 0.25 at `maxDepth` and `maxSpeed`.

How the GPU is compared with the reference, and the root cause of the gap push 2 left: the kernel matched the reference
to f32 rounding for 10 steps, then the gap grew to 1.5e-3 m by step 200 against the plan's 1e-4. It was not float32
sensitivity: one f32 ulp on every wet cell of the reference stays under 5e-7 m over 200 steps. A one-step check (each
GPU step taken again by the reference from the GPU's own state) found a 2.5% momentum gap in the two cells next to a
wall, and a plain JavaScript port of the kernel matched the GPU there to 7e-7. The reference was wrong: at the second
Runge-Kutta stage its wall ghost mirrored the state at the step's start instead of U1, so the edge cell's limited slopes
were taken against a stale neighbour. Fixed in the reference; regression `a wall is the mirror of the flow beside it at
both Runge-Kutta stages` (flood-bounds.test.js: a walled half equals its mirrored whole; fails on the old ghost at the
east wall). After it, GPU against reference after 200 steps: 1.7e-6 m and 9.0e-6 m^2/s on WebGPU, 1.8e-6 and 9.5e-6 on
the WebGL2 layer, and 2.1e-5 m and 4.6e-5 m^2/s after 1,000 steps, inside 1e-4 with no bound widened. The plan's bounds
on the GPU itself, both back ends (`packages/water/test/flood.browser.mjs`): Ritter at 400 cells (dam depth and speed
within 3%, front behind 2 sqrt(g h0) t, L1 0.22% of h0), walls at exactly 0 straight and diagonal and a breach that lets
water through, lake at rest over steps and an island under 5e-6 m/s after 10,000 steps, a closed town 1.7e-6 volume
drift over 20,000 steps with no water in a block, Courant 0.021 and 0 capped cells, inflow volume within 1e-5.
Push 4 (below) added the film clock and the sea; missing still: foam and spray from the flood (push 7), a wave maker for
swell and a swell on the open sea inside the map.

### Section 5 evidence: the flood's white water, current and wetting record (water/flood push 7, 2026-11-17)

GPU maths change in `packages/water/src/flood-shaders.ts`, both backends from one WGSL source. The stage carries foam x
depth as a fourth conserved quantity on each face's mass flux, upwind, with a 3 s e-folding loss (Callaghan et al. 2012),
and writes the breaker (Ihmsen et al. 2012 ramps on Froude, speed and a front, Chentanez and Muller 2010) into the
state's fourth channel; foam is never under it. A new gather pass a tick (`floodRecord`) writes the current (u, v, speed,
depth) and the wetting record (deepest depth, seconds since wet, ever wet) into two rgba32float ping-pong pairs, so the
WebGL2 layer runs it on its Fragment tier like the stage. Depth and momentum are unchanged: `test/flood.browser.mjs`
still meets the reference within 1e-4 and `test/flood-film.browser.mjs` stays bit for bit across 30 and 60 fps, seeks and
restores. Evidence: `test/flood-foam.browser.mjs` (RTX A6000, WebGPU and `MARGO_COMPAT=1` agree): foam and breaker 0
on a lake at rest, a dam-break front (Froude 1.6) white with 25 m^2 of foam falling under 0.03 after 60 s, the current
texture equal to the reading within 2.4e-7, and a bore run-up of 0.89 m under Shen and Meyer's U0^2 / 2g = 1.02 m. Cost:
one more dispatch a tick and 32 B a cell; Water's spray now spawns from the breaker at any depth (the coast flow's breaker
is 0 past 1.8 m, so its spray is unchanged).

### Section 5 evidence: film sub-frame accumulation (post/accumulate and headless/accumulate, FG-17 piece 1, 2026-11-25)

Two new optional entries; core, stage and the PostStack are unchanged. `@margoengine/post/accumulate` (`Accumulate`) is
an HDR PostStack stage: one fullscreen pass with two targets adds the frame times its weight into one of two
ping-pong `rgba32float` sums (float32 is not blendable, so the previous sum is read with `textureLoad`) and writes sum
times the float64 inverse of the total weight to an `rgba16float` mean that Tonemap and the display curve read, so the
tone curve is applied once to the linear average (Haeberli and Akeley 1990). `@margoengine/headless/accumulate`
(`subFrames`, `renderAccumulated`) schedules `samples` renders a frame at the middles of equal slices of the open
shutter (Cook, Porter and Carpenter 1984), with sub-pixel offsets from Owen-scrambled 2D Sobol points (Burley 2020)
mapped through the pixel filter's inverse CDF (Ernst, Stamminger and Greiner 2006), shuffled against time order; the
offset is a clip-space shift of a copy of the camera, so the caller's camera and the culling planes are untouched.
Evidence: `packages/headless/tests/accumulate-gpu.mjs` (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, identical figures): 64 box
samples of an orthographic edge at 20.3 px read 0.297 coverage in linear light; at radiance 4 the edge pixel is the
tone curve of the linear mean (244 against a still lit to that share, 244), not the mean of display values (76); two
runs bit-identical; an 8 px strip at 32 px a frame and a 180 degree shutter spreads over 24 px with energy 1.000 and
centroid 44.03 px (44 expected); abort rejects with its reason. CPU: `packages/headless/tests/accumulate.test.js`
(times, telescoping deltas, `samples: 1` equal to `renderFrames`, stratified box offsets, filters, seeds, range errors)
and `packages/post/test/accumulate.test.js` (uniforms, targets, resets, lifecycle). Missing: GPU cost per sub-frame.
Piece 2 (same day): `renderFrames` takes `samples` and `shutter` and runs `renderAccumulated` (loaded by package name,
so the video entry stays inside its budget); `renderCutscene` passes them on and calls `apply` and the player at each
render's time. Clocks start at 0 and each delta is kept as a (frame, seconds into it) pair, so one sample with shutter
0 still steps exactly `1 / fps`; `subFrameSteps` lists the deltas before a `startFrame`, and `seek` takes them as
`steps`, so a span equals the whole film's renders bit for bit (`packages/headless/tests/accumulate.test.js` compares
the span with the whole film's slice for three framings; `packages/cutscene/tests/render.test.js` checks the seek
of a sub-framed span; the GPU check adds `renderFrames` with samples equal to `renderAccumulated`, byte for byte).
Piece 3 (same day): `@margoengine/voxel-pathtracer/sequence` `traceFrames` traces one `renderImage` a frame, setting the tracer's `shutter` and `previousCamera` from last frame's camera pose and filling a moved instance's `previousMatrix` from last frame's matrix (Cook, Porter and Carpenter 1984, distributed ray tracing over the shutter); seeds are `frameSeed(seed, i)` per frame or fixed. The display mapping moved to `src/display.ts`, shared by `capture` and `pixels()` (tracer root unchanged). Evidence: `packages/voxel-pathtracer/tests/sequence.test.js` (call order, timing, seeds, motion fill, restore, abort) and `tests/sequence-browser.mjs` (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, the same figures): fixed noise bit-identical frames; a bar panned 16 px a frame with shutter 0.5 widens 7 px (8 expected, within 1), centroid 3.98 px (4 expected), energy within 1% of the mid-shutter still; `pixels()` equals the decoded `capture` PNG exactly. Missing: triangle-mesh instance motion (piece 4).
Piece 5a (same day): `@margoengine/voxel-pathtracer/from-engine` `traceSceneFromEngine` turns core meshes into a `PBRMeshTraceScene` (one trace mesh per geometry and material, one placement per visible mesh at its world matrix, materials from `PbrMaterial.data`; arrays cached per `Geometry`, so BVHs are reused). Evidence: `packages/voxel-pathtracer/tests/from-engine.test.js` and `tests/from-engine-browser.mjs` (raster against traced silhouette, IoU 1.000 over 3,037 px on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). Missing: terrain (5b), scatter (5c), engine lighting.
Piece 4a (same day): `@margoengine/voxel-pathtracer/mesh` mesh instances take `previousTransform` and
`motionInterpolation`; the Rust kernel takes a moving instance's world box over its whole interval as its TLAS leaf
(metadata bit 2), record word 31 points at a 32-word interval (shutter-open rows, TRS packet) and header word 11 counts
moving instances so the tracer samples a time per path only then. The triangle walk builds an instance's model
transform at the path's time once and the hit keeps it, so shading copies no motion rotation (the surface program stays
at 3; each triangle walk holds one, as the compatibility-route program counts in `tests/compat-staged.test.js` now
assert). Evidence: `tests/mesh-motion-browser.mjs` (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Vulkan, both tracer
entries): a translating quad and a turning, growing quad, each pixel within 5 binomial sigma of the closed-form time
coverage (worst 3.8 sigma), energy within 0.07 %; shutter 0 and equal transforms render the still bit for bit; a
singular interval is refused only while the shutter is open. CPU: `tests/mesh-motion.test.js` (swept root bounds,
interval words, TRS packet, a moving emitter left out of the light table, refusals, the sequence fill) and the
`moving_instance_keeps_its_interval_bounds_and_inverse` kernel test. Missing: a cost figure for long sweeps.
Piece 4b (same day): meshes take `previousPositions`. The Rust kernel builds one BVH over boxes holding both shutter
ends (SAH on the union), keeps each node's box at each end and appends a section of shutter-open node boxes (8 words a
node) and vertices (12 words a triangle); mesh-instances writes that section's offset into record word 27 and counts
deforming placements in header word 11. meshBlas blends node boxes and corners with one meshBlend at the path's time
(Woop, Afra and Benthin 2017), so a blended box holds the blended vertices and shared edges stay watertight; the hit
keeps its object-space geometric normal (Hit.ng), so normal readers need no vertex reads, and triangleHit takes its
three corners from its one call site (the compatibility-route counts in `tests/compat-staged.test.js` hold). A lone

a quad sheared across its shared diagonal and a growing quad on a moving instance, each pixel within 5 binomial sigma of
the closed-form time coverage (worst 3.5 sigma), energy within 0.04 %; shutter 0 and equal positions render the still
bit for bit. CPU: `tests/mesh-deform.test.js` and the `deforming_mesh_blends_boxes_that_hold_its_blended_vertices`
kernel test (blended vertices inside blended boxes at 17 times). Missing: blended shading normals and a cost figure for
large deformations.
FG-17-EMITTERS (2026-11-26): moving and deforming mesh emitters are sampled by next-event estimation. The Rust light
packet gives moving (record word 31) and deforming (word 27) instances close-pose records and lookup tables like still
ones; a face with zero area at close and some at open is picked by its open-pose area and stores area and normal 0.
sampleMeshEmitter(o) takes the light point at the path's own time (no new random number, Cook, Porter and Carpenter
1984): the blended object corners through meshLocal at that time (its one new call site), the area by the cofactor
identity 0.5 |L^T c| / |det L|, pdf pmf / area(t); meshEmitterWeight uses the same area and the hit's normal, so the
power-heuristic weights sum to 1 (Veach 1997). The proposal resolves its radiance itself, which removed two private
words (the staged compose route dropped from 9 to 8 pages); a moving point's shadow ray stops 8 Float32 ulps short
(a still point 1). At motion 1 the still branch runs the same statements, so shutter 0 and every scene without a moving
emitter render as before. Evidence: `tests/mesh-emitters-browser.mjs` (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer on ANGLE
Vulkan, MeshPathTracer and composed): for 'matrix', 'trs', deforming and deforming on a moving instance, image means
within 1.8 standard errors of a float64 polygon-irradiance oracle over the shutter (Baum, Rushmeier and Winget 1989),
worst 4x4 block 2.98, block rms 1.17 at most; 1,000 units out with a 50:1 lamp within 1.8; shutter 0 and equal previous
fields bit for bit equal to the still scene, plain, composed and textured mesh-pbr; energy within 1.1 standard errors
of a path-only reference, whose per-pixel variance NEE at 16 spp undercuts at 32 spp by 0.004 to 0.006 on a Lambert
floor and 0.84 to 0.89 on roughness-0.2 metal (a lobe narrower than the lamp). The still-emitter scenes of the baseline
page hash as on main, both routes (12 of 12). CPU: `tests/mesh-emitters.test.js` (the sampler run on the CPU against a
float64 mirror, 4 motion kinds x 3 entries x 3 times x 3 seeds, the hit weight on the same face) and the `light_tests`
kernel tests (a still packet pinned to its hash on main). Staged sample text: mesh 87,426 to 88,167 B, mesh-pbr
105,603 to 106,344 B, compose (every feature) 95,262 to 95,367 B (one more motionRotation copy, KB-L5a-10). Missing: a
position-aware pick (a light tree with swept bounds) for many small fast emitters.

Piece 6a (same day): `@margoengine/bvh/gpu-scene` (`GPUSceneBVH`, `sceneBvhWGSL`), the scene tree real-time ray
tracing builds on. Two levels (Wald, Benthin and Slusallek 2003): each distinct MeshBVH is one bottom tree in a shared
pool of nodes, triangle slots (three indices and the source face, 16 bytes) and positions; the top tree is built on the
CPU by 16-bin SAH over the instances' world boxes (Wald 2007), one instance a leaf, depth-first so a parent precedes its
children, and refitted bottom-up on `update()`, rebuilt past 1.5 times its built SAH cost. A ray enters an instance
through the world-to-object rows with its direction unnormalized, so the watertight test (Woop, Benthin and Wald 2013,
now one `triangleWGSL` shared with `bvhWGSL` in `src/gpu-pack.ts`) answers world distances and the face test follows
the transformed normal (mirrors included). Below depth 40 the top build splits by count, so no tree outgrows the
64-entry stack. Evidence: `packages/bvh/tests/gpu-scene-browser.js` in `test:browser` (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2
layer, identical figures): 20,000 of 20,000 rays match one float64 CPU tree of the 50 instances (3 meshes, 7 mirrored)
flattened into world space, any-hit agrees with closest on every ray, 20,000/20,000 after a refit and 3,999/4,000 after
a rebuild (one shared-edge tie), `sceneNormal` and `sceneMaterial` in a shader of our own give the CPU face normal and
material on 2,036 hits, front-only faces skip rays from inside a closed mesh, an empty scene misses. CPU:
`tests/gpu-scene.test.js` (every instance in one leaf, nested boxes, shared bottom trees, depth under 64 for boxes at
2^(i/4), refit and rebuild, record layout, input checks). Missing: bottom trees built on the GPU, instance add and
remove after create, and a stackless walk for the compatibility layer (not needed so far: the stack walk runs there).

Piece 6b (same day): `@margoengine/post/rt-reflections` (`RTReflections extends SSR`), hybrid reflections
(Barre-Brisebois et al. 2019; Stachowiak 2015). SSR gains one internal hook, `traced` (`SSRTrace`): while a subclass's
scene is live the mirror composite and the stochastic rough trace are patched by text (each patch throws when SSR's
shader changes shape, and the CPU test reads the patched code), and bind group 1 holds the scene's five buffers and a
64-byte light uniform. The screen's share of a ray is SSR's own fades (`cover`); the trace adds the rest, `rf - cover`
on the mirror path and `1 - cover` on rough rays, so no pixel the screen answers fully traces. Traced hits use core's
BRDF text with the engine sun, a `sceneAny` shadow ray, core's flat ambient and the instance emissive. Read-only storage
in a fragment shader runs on the WebGL2 layer through its data textures (M4), so no compute pass was needed. Evidence:
`packages/post/test/rt-reflections-browser.mjs` (in `test:gpu`, native and `--compat`; RTX A6000, identical figures):
a mirror floor under a box above the view shows the box's underside on 1,415 pixels, median 208 against the closed form
208.46; the sun behind a plate leaves it unlit, without the plate it reads 248, and `shadows: false` equals that frame
exactly; a rough floor with `stochastic` shows the box on 2,699 pixels; a disposed scene runs as plain SSR (dark).
CPU: `packages/post/test/rt-reflections.test.js` (option checks, the patched composite and rough trace, group 1 bound
once per pass, the light words, steady frames build nothing, no live GPU objects after dispose). SSR's own GPU tests
(ssr-rough, ssr-cone) pass unchanged. Missing: a GPU cost figure, the a-trous denoise of rough hits, quarter-resolution
tracing on the WebGL2 layer, and environment light at traced hits.

Piece 6c (same day): `@margoengine/post/rt-gi` (`RTGI extends SSGI`), hybrid diffuse bounce light (Barre-Brisebois
et al. 2019). SSGI gains one internal hook, `traced` (`SSGITrace`), the same shape as SSR's: while the scene is live
the one-bounce and multi-bounce trace shaders are patched by text (a patch that no longer applies throws) so a ray with
no Hi-Z hit traces the scene from the same start, and its hit adds into the same sum over rays. The traced-hit shading,
light uniform and bind group now live in one shared module, `src/rt-shade.ts`, used by `RTReflections` and `RTGI`.
Evidence: `packages/post/test/rt-gi-browser.mjs` (in `test:gpu`, native and `--compat`; RTX A6000, identical figures):
a white floor under an emissive ceiling that is never on screen, sun and ambient off, reads 181 against the closed form
180.54 with one bounce and with `multiBounce`; turned away it reads 0; a disposed scene gives plain SSGI's 0.
`rt-reflections-browser.mjs` gives the same figures after the shared-module move; SSGI's `ssgi-bounce-browser.mjs`
passes unchanged. CPU: `packages/post/test/rt-gi.test.js` (option checks, the patched trace for both bounce modes,
group 1 bound once, the light words, steady frames build nothing, a disposed scene rebuilds the plain trace, nothing
left live). Missing: ReSTIR GI reservoir reuse (Ouyang et al. 2021) and an SVGF denoise (Schied et al. 2017), a GPU
cost figure, and traced hits that carry the multi-bounce history (they are lit directly).

Piece 6d (2026-11-26): device fallback. The plan was to run both effects as SSR and SSGI below the WebGL2 layer's full
tier; measured, the half-float tier traces correctly (RTGI 181 against 180.54, RTReflections 208 against 208.46, the
full tier's figures) and the LDR tier already refuses every HDR PostStack, so neither tier falls back. The device that
cannot trace is one at WebGPU's compatibility feature level with too few storage buffers in a fragment shader
(`maxStorageBuffersInFragmentStage`; 4 by default at that level, and OpenGL ES 3.1 requires none): the traced passes
bind the scene's 4 (RTReflections) or those and SSGI's rays (RTGI, 5). `TracedLight.active` (`src/rt-shade.ts`) checks
the limit for both effects, warns once per device life with a linked `unsupported` error and runs the plain passes; it
never throws. A device that reports no such limit (a core device, the WebGL2 layer) traces. Bug found on the way and
fixed: plain SSR and SSGI failed every frame at the compatibility level, because each Hi-Z reduction read mip i-1 and
wrote mip i of one r32float texture in one dispatch, which that level forbids. `createHiZ` and `encodeHiZ`
(`src/hiz.ts`, shared by SSR and SSGI) now reduce each level into a texture of its own there and copy it into the
pyramid; at the full level the reduction is unchanged. Cost at the compatibility level: one texture copy per Hi-Z level
a frame (6 at most) and the levels' memory twice (an r32float half-resolution pyramid, about 2.8 MB at 1920 x 1080).
Evidence: `rt-gi-browser.mjs` and `rt-reflections-browser.mjs` in `test:gpu` with `--mode=half-float` and
`--mode=compatibility` (identical figures to native on the RTX A6000; the compatibility leg failed validation before the
Hi-Z fix), and `rt-gi-browser.mjs --mode=short`, a real compatibility-level device held to 4 fragment storage buffers:
one warning, every frame SSGI's 0. Chrome will not hold a device below 4, so the RTReflections short case is CPU only.
CPU: `packages/post/test/traced-fallback.test.js` (one short of the need: plain shaders, no group 1, no light uniform,
one warning over two frames; exactly the need or no limit: traced, no warning; a restore warns again) and
`hiz-compat-level.test.js` (at the compatibility level no SSR or SSGI bind group holds two views of one texture and one
copy per level runs in order; at the full level no copy). Missing: a run on a real OpenGL ES or Direct3D 11 class
device.

### Section 5 evidence: the blur reach follows a mover's whole screen motion and its sub-frames (headless look, KB-SCATTER-FRINGEVEL1, 2026-11-28)

The soft fringe of a near swaying leaf that held the sky's velocity was the leaf's own trail across the shutter: the
shot tool's geometry mask is the mean over 8 sub-frames (it steps in eighths there, 32 to 223), while depth and velocity
are the last sub-frame's, where the sky really is. TAA's velocity and `ScatterVelocity` were right. `shimmerMoving` now
sizes a mover's smear from its whole screen velocity (camera included) against pixels moving otherwise, runs it back
over the sub-frames' travel (`MovingFrames.subframes`, passed by `checkShot`), and applies the same reach to the next
frame (with `nextVelocity` and `back`). Evidence: `packages/headless/tests/look-clean.test.js` (FRINGEVEL1 test fails
on the old reach, 80 against 768 pixels). Blowup render (8 sub-frames, 180 degrees): shimmerMoving early 0.44 to 0.28,
mid 1.72 to 0.53; the leaf band at x 1680 to 1920 went from about 16,500 off pixels to about 1,700. Missing: mid's
residual 0.53 is one-pixel rims on near conifer sprays against the sky whose sway is under half a pixel past the camera
(v - f about 0.3 px), a separate cause under KB-LOOK-TV-SHIMMER2.

### Section 5 evidence: the moving-frame look checks know blur reach and stepped trails (headless look, KB-LOOK-TV-SHIMMER2, KB-LOOK-TV-SUBSTEP1, 2026-11-28)

`shimmerMoving` with the engine velocity leaves out the pixels a moving surface's own motion blur reaches: half its
motion past the camera's over the open shutter, at most `MotionBlur`'s `maxBlur` (McGuire, Hennessy, Bukowski and Osman
2012 tile-max and neighbour max, then a walk). `motionBlur` calls a staircase of sharp copies sharp (three or more
one-way jumps on a ramp of 8 px or more). Evidence: `packages/headless/tests/look-clean.test.js` (a flash on a still
edge 7 px from a branch swaying 8 px still fails, the reach follows `shutter` and `maxBlur`; 8-copy trails of a 24 px
and a 3 px bar fail, their smooth smears pass). Blowup render (8 sub-frames, 180 degrees): shimmerMoving early 0.48 to
0.44, mid 2.02 to 1.72; motionBlur early 0.00 and mid 0.88 unchanged by the stair test. Missing: the mid residual
(0.53 percent after lane C's KB-SCATTER-FRINGEVEL1 fix) is one-pixel rims on near conifer sprays against the sky.
motionBlur judges a mover narrower than its smear by its ramp plus the plateau it holds, which spans the smear, and
takes only the edge's own ramp round its crossing (KB-LOOK-TV-MBNARROW1, 2026-11-28; evidence: look-clean.test.js, a
smeared 12 px bar at 64 px passes, sharp, half smeared and 8-copy versions fail).

### Section 5 evidence: screen-space LOD rings in scatter (scatter, biomes, KB-BIOMES-SCREENLOD1, 2026-11-28)

Scatter's cull can end each of its first two rings where a mesh's finest feature (`lodSize`) projects under
`lodPixels` viewport pixels, from the camera's pixel footprint each frame with 5 percent hysteresis, as well as at the
ring's distance; without `lodSize` the WGSL is byte for byte the distance-only text. Evidence:
`packages/scatter/test/lod.browser.mjs` on WebGPU and the WebGL2 compatibility layer (switch distances at two
resolutions, two fields of view and two scales, within 2 percent; hysteresis). Biomes passes each tree's spray width
when `lodPixels` is set; it is off by default because the timber-valley blowup's speckle rose with it (KB-LOOK-TV-SPECKLE).
Missing: a default decided on frames from more than one shot.

`@margoengine/scenes/timber-valley` at `film` quality attaches `@margoengine/taa` with its defaults on the post stack's
