### Section 5 evidence: VolumetricFog's far air past range, clear air by default (KB-STORM-HORIZON1, 2026-11-16)

GPU maths. The froxel grid still integrates the near air out to `range` (shafts, noise, clustered lights, volumes).
Past it the composite adds the smooth medium in closed form along each opaque pixel's ray from the `range` plane to
the surface, or to infinity for the sky: the optical depth of sigma(y) = density exp(-falloff max(y - height, 0)) is the
exponential integral of Wenzel (2006) and Quilez (2010), split at `height` for the flat layer under it, with the
uniform case (falloff 0) as density times length. The tail's light is the medium's equilibrium radiance, the albedo
times the ambient plus the sun's Henyey-Greenstein phase (and the multiple-scattering series of Hillaire 2020 when
`multipleScattering` is set), and opacity is 1 - T_froxel T_tail, so the two parts join at `range` without a step.
`visibility` is Koschmieder's law, extinction 3.912 / V; with no density the default is clear air, 23 km at ground with
a 1.2 km scale height (LOWTRAN 7 "clear", Kneizys et al. 1988). With a Sky and no `ambient` the fog's ambient, near and
far, is the sky map's last row above the horizon in the view azimuth (Hillaire 2020; Bruneton and Neyret 2008), so a
fully fogged far sea is the fogged sky above it. Without a sky the froxel shader text is byte-identical to before.
Work count: one closed-form tail and one sky-map sample per composite pixel (per sample at 4x); no new pass, draw,
texture or buffer write; the uniform keeps its size (the composite WGSL hash and the two default-air floats are the
only GPU-tape changes, volumetric-workcount.test.js). Evidence (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer):
`npm run test:fog-far:browser` (every sea and sky pixel within 0.01 of exp(-optical depth) integrated on the CPU, in
uniform 1 km and 10 km fog and height fog with the camera above and inside the layer; Koschmieder 2.09% at V; the
sea 3 km out 0.3101 against 0.3092; the luma step at `range` -0.01 codes; the fully fogged far sea 0.00% from the
fogged sky above it and 10.8% from the unfogged dusk sky 0.3 to 0.7 degrees up; the old fog fails it at 0.1287).
Transparents added with `fog.add` take the same far air past `range` (KB-FOG-FAR-TRANSPARENT, fixed 2026-11-17: a
pane on the sea within 0.01 of the integral, and with a Sky within 1% of the fogged sea under it; the old shader is off
by 0.095). Missing: a run on a laptop iGPU and on Metal.

### Section 5 evidence: clustered lights integrated over each froxel slice (KB-FOG-BEAM1, 2026-11-15)

VolumetricFog took each clustered light at four points per slice on each froxel's centre ray, so a spot cone narrower
than their spacing in depth, or than a froxel row across, lit only the froxels whose points fell inside it: the Storm
Light beam drew as a row of separate blocks (temporal off, beam bearing 0.3, climb camera: 15 gaps along the right beam,
worst dip 0.98 of its level). Now each slice is split in four parts with a cluster lookup each; per light the part's
chord inside the range sphere and the outer cone is solved exactly (Eberly 2000), the inverse-square term is the
closed form (atan(b) - atan(a)) / h (Sun, Ramamoorthi, Narasimhan and Nayar 2005; Pegoraro and Parker 2009) and the
smooth rest is taken at 2 jittered equiangular points (Kulla and Fajardo 2012); a cone thinner than the froxel is
widened by the froxel's size seen from the light with its energy kept (footprint prefiltering after Toksvig 2005 and
Kaplanyan, Hill, Patney and Lefohn 2016). Work count: 8 light evaluations per froxel per light (4 parts x 2 points)
where it was 4; 8 points per part gave the same results within run noise at 32. Evidence (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the
WebGL2 layer): `npm run test:fog-beam-continuity:browser` (a beam 0.2 m across in froxels 0.4 m wide and 1.3 m tall:
each column 0.762 to 1.186 of its true light, L1 0.140; the old code 0 to 0.511), `npm run test:fog-beam:browser`
(reference now averaged over each froxel's area: beam L1 0.044, bulb 0.004, limit 0.05 unchanged),
`scripts/clustered-falloff-gpu-check.js` (14 lights, falloff and cone match the definition). Storm Light probe after
the fix, bearings 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9: 0 gaps, worst dip at most 0.205. Missing: a run on a laptop iGPU and on Metal.

### Section 5 evidence: the water surf field's sweeps on the WebGL2 layer's GPU (KB-WATER-SURFCPU1, 2026-11-18)

The surf field's build (water `SurfFieldBuilder`) kept its deepest-edge `atomicMax` and its relaxation sweeps in one
module over `array<atomic<u32>>`, and the layer sends any entry point that touches an atomic to its CPU tier: every one
of the width + height sweeps ran in JavaScript, 421 s for the first frame of a 512 x 82 coastal grid (RTX A6000, ANGLE
D3D11). The sweeps and the sources now read and write plain words in a second module over the same buffer (each
invocation its own cell, from one field to the other), which plans to the scatter tier; only the deepest edge stays on
the CPU. Work count: CPU-tier dispatches in that first frame from 596 (the 594 sweeps, the sources and the deepest edge,
by construction) to 3 (measured, layer counters); first frame 4.0 s on a loaded
machine; the surf check's breaking depths, heights and run-up read the same on both backends. Proof:
`MARGO_COMPAT=1 node packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs`. Missing: a run on a laptop iGPU and on Metal.

### Section 5 evidence: volumetric fog integration on the WebGL2 layer's GPU (bug sweep L6b, KB5663a, 2026-11-11)

The layer runs a compute entry point on the GPU only when every store writes the invocation's own texel; VolumetricFog's
column integration stores at each slice of a loop, so it ran on the layer's CPU tier (scattering volume read back,
14,400 columns of 64 steps in JavaScript, result uploaded), about 1 s a frame at the default 160 x 90 x 64 grid. On a
layer device the fog now integrates each froxel by itself (steps 0 to z in the column's order, one store), which plans
to the fragment tier; native WebGPU keeps the column kernel byte for byte. Work count: CPU-tier dispatches per fog
frame 1 to 0 (layer counters), GPU steps per column 64 to 2,080 ((n + 1) / 2 times, the fragment-era prefix cost of
Horn 2005 and Sengupta et al. 2007; a log-step scan would add in another order and round differently). Evidence:
`packages/environment/tests/volumetric-compat-route.test.js` (CPU: every fog stack plans to the fragment tier),
`npm run test:fog-route:browser` (A6000: the two kernels store the same 16 x 12 x 32 volume value for value on native
WebGPU; on the layer the GPU route and the CPU-tier column agree within one half-float step), and the quality features
check on the layer, which now ends with every knob restored (fog step saved 11.8 ms where it saved about 1,050 ms).
Missing: a run on a real laptop iGPU on the layer.

### Section 5 evidence: WebGL2 layer waits (KB-COMPAT-POSTTASK1, KB-COMPAT-GETERROR1, 2026-11-18)

The layer's fence polls (`onSubmittedWorkDone`, `mapAsync`) yield a port task and then a 1 ms timer set from it, never
`scheduler.postTask` with a delay, which Chrome on Windows runs on the 15.6 ms system timer tick (15.1 ms against 2.0 ms
a poll, Chrome 157). Allocation errors are read with one `getError` for every allocation since the last read, in a task
of its own or at an `out-of-memory` or `internal` scope boundary, with each error still in the scope it was raised in.
Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/task-polling.test.js` and `device.test.js`; water's owner/lifetime cases on the
layer made 13,255 `getError` calls in place of 61,489, and its check:owners took 344 s in place of 505 s (WebGL2 case
time 2.0 times native, was 2.9; RTX A6000, ANGLE Direct3D 11, loaded workstation). Measure page waits with GL call
counters and timer latencies, not under a CPU profile: the V8 sampler raises the Windows timer resolution and hid the
tick. Still missing: the same counts on Firefox and on ANGLE Metal; per-context program compiles remain (WebGL2 has no
program binaries).

Aborted maps (KB-SHOT-COMPATLOST1, 2026-11-26): a map the layer cuts off names its cause, the device loss ("The device
was lost before the buffer mapped") or the buffer's own destroy ("The buffer was destroyed before it mapped"), both
AbortError as WebGPU rejects them (W3C WebGPU, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/, `GPUBuffer.mapAsync` and `destroy()`).
Before, a destroy read as a loss. `LightProbes.bake()` reports any aborted readback map as its coded interruption.
Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/task-polling.test.js`, `packages/environment/tests/probes.test.js`. Missing: the
ANGLE Metal device loss behind the orrery shot is not reproduced on ANGLE Direct3D 11 or Vulkan (Intel Arc 140V).

check:owners CPU runs (2026-11-18): the CPU model runs one package per process, each under its own 120 s limit
(`cpuRuns` and `CPU_LIMIT_MS` in `scripts/support/owner-lifetime-registry.mjs`), and a timeout names the case still
running (`package/fixture/target/lifetime`). One process for all 75 fixtures summed about 160 s under one 120 s limit
(biomes alone about 90 s: each of its 52 cases attaches a BiomeView that builds its ground texture tiles on the CPU), so
a full run always timed out and read as a hang; there was no hang. Evidence: `tests/owner-lifetime.test.js` ("one
package per run", "names each case"); a full `check:owners -- --cpu-only` passes. Still missing: per-attach ground
tiles are rebuilt for every BiomeView (a speed item for the speed phase, not a correctness one).

### Section 5 evidence: WebGL2 layer resources in Firefox and in one draw (bug sweep L3a, 2026-11-11)

The layer writes zeros into every new texture level and layer at allocation (clears for renderable formats, whole-level
uploads from a zero-filled unpack buffer for the rest), so no browser initialises one lazily, and polls every fence
with `clientWaitSync(sync, SYNC_FLUSH_COMMANDS_BIT, 0)`. Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/zero-init.test.js`
(CPU, every level, layer, face and slice), and the Firefox 157 materials, lod and imposter checks on the layer with no
lazy-initialisation or flush warnings. A multisampled depth-stencil texture resolves a copy per sampled aspect, and a
block-compressed texture's sRGB twin view is filled from its kept blocks: `features.html` cases `msaaAspects` and
`compressedSrgbView` equal native WebGPU. Still missing: a run of these on a real OpenGL ES device.

### Section 5 evidence: height-correlated Smith in core's direct light (2026-11-11)

Core's WGSL direct light, its WebGL2 twin and gltf/pbr (base, coat lobe, extended isotropic path) use the
height-correlated Smith-GGX G2 = 1 / (1 + Lambda(v) + Lambda(l)) (Heitz 2014, JCGT 3(2), eq. 99; glTF 2.0 Appendix
B.3.2, current revision) in place of the separable G1 G1 (KB5875a). Evidence: `packages/core/tests/smith.test.js`,
`packages/gltf/test/smith.test.js` and `packages/webgl2-compat/test/smith.test.js` evaluate each shader's own
text against Heitz's Lambda over 150 (nl, nv, roughness) points (1e-12); G2 is never below G1 G1 and gains over 25
percent rough and grazing. gltf/pbr's naming proof fixture follows the same line (re-recorded). Since KB6016 every
other PBR direct light (clustered, materials, terrain, lod imposters, animation VAT, post material decals, voxel) takes
the same `smithGCorrelated`, and the separable `smithG` export is gone; `tests/smith-shaders.test.js` evaluates each
user and scans every package's source for a separable product. Its guard is max(den, 1e-30) (KB-G2guard, 2026-11-12):
the denominator is never below 2 nl nv, and the old 1e-4 floor cut G2 to 0.02 of 0.71 on smooth grazing surfaces; the
same test evaluates every G2 text down to nl = 1e-5, a2 = 1e-10. Core's copy takes the same 1e-30 floor since 2026-11-14 (`packages/core/tests/smith.test.js` checks its text at a2 = 1e-6, nl = nv = 0.001). Environment's split-sum DFG table
integrates G2 too since KB6016b (2026-11-24; the batch 160 IBL picture moved +1.4 % against Mitsuba principled's separable G, an accepted difference in docs/limits.md, and 484,953 -> 447,308 against the exact G2 split-sum model). Missing: no multiple-scattering compensation in direct light.
The GGX D is written |n x h|^2 + a2 nh^2 everywhere (KB6016c core and shared `ggxD`/`ggxDOf`; KB6016d,
2026-11-26, the last seven sites: shared `ggxDenominatorOf(n, h)` and `ggxNamed(..., n, h)` for environment's probe and
cube prefilters, voxel-pathtracer, materials' lobes and water's glints, ship lamps and FFT ocean), so float32 keeps D
near the peak of a narrow lobe. Evidence: `tests/smith-shaders.test.js` scans every package and shared source for the
cancelling nh^2 (a2 - 1) + 1, literal or templated, evaluates both forms in float32 at roughness 0.03 (scalar off by
over 10 %, vector within 1e-5) and the new texts against the textbook D; core's own GPU check is
`packages/core/tests/ggx-precision.browser.mjs`. Missing: no GPU-side precision readback for the seven sites.

### Section 5 evidence: dielectric Fresnel diffuse weight in core's direct light (2026-11-14)

Core's WGSL direct light weights its Lambert lobe by 1 minus the dielectric Fresnel (F0 0.04), as glTF 2.0 Appendix B
mixes a dielectric BRDF with a metal one: w = 1 - (1 - vh)^5, F = 1 - (1 - F0) w and the diffuse weight 0.96 w, in
place of 1 minus the Fresnel at the metal-mixed F0 (KB3240b, the packages outside core since 2026-11-12). Evidence:
`packages/core/tests/metal-mix.test.js` evaluates core's own shader text on the CPU against the specification's mix
(head on at base 0.5, metal 0.5: 0.0978817, against 0.0795775 before). Missing: part-metal visual baselines re-recorded
on the workstation (baselines are per machine).

### Section 5 evidence: allocation-free changed-row uploads (2026-11-11)

Core's `uploadRows` walks a batch's dirty-row words 16 bits at a time through a `Uint16Array` view, so no V8 tier boxes
a full 32-bit word (4294967295 is outside the 31-bit small integers). Evidence: `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` runs 10,000
changed rows at `--max-opt=1` and `--max-opt=2`: 15,024 B a call before, 0 after; the browser check's instanced scene
went from 4,048 B to 304 B a frame (RTX A6000, Edge 157); `tests/core-instance-cache.test.js` keeps the same
`writeBuffer` runs. Missing: the 680M machine rerun, and the 12 B the instanced scene still reads over its floor
(docs/known-bugs.md, open).

### Section 5 evidence: directional shadows at any model scale (2026-11-11)

`Shadows` no longer carries world-length defaults. Each receiver moves a quarter texel of its cascade along its normal
and compares one texel nearer the light, with the texel's world size read in WGSL from the cascade matrix
(`shadowPlace` in `packages/shadows/src/shader.ts`; normal offset after Holbert 2011, slope and texel scaled bias after
Dou, Yan, Kerzner, Dai and Wyman 2014, JCGT 3(4)). The light depth range reaches the farthest known caster instead of
100 m (Lauritzen, Salvi and Lefohn 2011, Sample Distribution Shadow Maps; Microsoft 2010, Common Techniques to Improve
Shadow Depth Maps), still models fit the cascades as core meshes do, and the default `distance` is 500 or 20 times the
camera's target distance. Evidence: `packages/shadows/test/scale-browser.mjs` renders one scene at 1 mm, 2 cm, 1 m,
100 m and 1 km plus the Khronos BoomBox, native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, RTX A6000 Edge 157, with the same umbra
and lit pixel counts at every scale (4,626 umbra, 335,079 lit, none darkened); every other shadows GPU test passes in
both modes. Steady-frame GPU calls and written bytes are unchanged in the deformed-shadows, quality-presets and
gltf-pbr-lighting-hooks proofs; only uniform values and shader text differ. `VirtualShadows` followed on 2026-11-11: receivers move a quarter
texel of the page they read along the normal, the depth bias is 2^-20 of a range that follows the reach (a whole
texel lifted deep shade off the coarsest level before feedback), and an unset reach scales with the camera's target distance in octaves
(`reachScale`); the same scene passes `scale-browser.mjs --virtual` at every scale in both modes, and
virtual-feedback-browser.mjs keeps its recorded pages per level (normal path: same pages, draws and uploads). Missing: other GPUs.

### Section 5 evidence: 100 device restores (2026-11-11)

`scripts/device-recreation-soak.mjs` (Rust engine port R20) forces 100 device losses in one page with core meshes,
`@margoengine/shadows` and `@margoengine/lod` attached; core restores each one and draws 120 frames before the next
(its budget gives up after four losses within 120 frames). It counts live buffers and textures on the current device
(created less destroyed) after the first and the hundredth restore and compares the two pictures. RTX A6000, Edge 157:
native WebGPU 12 buffers and 4 textures both times, the same picture; the WebGL2 layer 12 and 6, the extra two
being the canvas texture and the shadows route's nearest-depth level. That level went missing in about one restore in
seven until the route was kept once loaded (docs/known-bugs.md, fixed 2026-11-11); since then 400 restores kept 6.
The soak names each live texture by format and size when counts differ. Standalone, run by hand; no check
runs it yet. Missing: gltf/pbr models in the scene, other GPUs.

### Section 5 evidence: exact vector glyph coverage (lague plan 2, 2026-11-10)

`@margoengine/text/vector` computes glyph coverage per pixel from quadratic outlines (Lengyel, JCGT 6(2) 2017,
https://jcgt.org/published/0006/02/02/): roots along x and y rays chosen by control-point signs (constant 0x2E74), stable
root forms, exact nonzero window coverage for up to 4 crossings per ray, adaptive extra rays where a curve hull reaches the
pixel, and pixels per em from screen-space derivatives. Evidence: a TypeScript mirror of the shader equals an independent
winding test on 500 points x 200 glyphs (TrueType, CFF, CJK); cubic splits stay under 1/4096 em on every Source Sans 3 CFF
cubic (worst 2.41e-4 em); on the RTX A6000, native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, the mean coverage error against a 16 x 16
supersampled reference is under 1/64 from 4 to 400 px, rotated and zoomed (worst pixel 0.139), and the GPU matches the mirror
to a mean of about 0.001. Proof: `packages/text/tests/vector.test.js` and `packages/text/scripts/test-vector-browser.js`.
Missing: frame times (speed phase) and a run on a laptop iGPU.

### Section 5 evidence: one allocation failed per restore (2026-11-11)

`scripts/restore-fault-sweep.mjs` (Rust engine port R18) records every createBuffer, createTexture and mapAsync of a
device restore with core meshes, culling, lod, shadows and environment attached, then fails each one in turn with
`tests/support/gpu-faults.js` and follows it with a clean restore. RTX A6000, Edge 157: 40 calls on native WebGPU and
42 on the WebGL2 layer, each failure reported, and after the clean restore 28 buffers, 7 (native) or 9 (layer)
textures and the same picture every time. A failure in core, shadows or culling still stops the engine until that
restore (docs/known-bugs.md, open). Standalone, run by hand. Missing: gltf/pbr models, other GPUs.

### Section 5 evidence: alpha-tested mip coverage (2026-11-10)

`packages/shared/alpha-mips.js` builds the mips of `MASK` base colour maps (gltf/pbr, gltf/textured) on the GPU: an
area filter of the level above with alpha-weighted linear colour, then the alpha scale whose passing share is nearest
to level 0's (64-candidate bisection, exact 64-bit share comparisons, unscaled state fed to the next level). Evidence:
`packages/gltf/scripts/test-mask-mips-browser.mjs` on the RTX A6000, WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: every level's
passing texel count equals a float64 CPU reference, alpha within 0 bytes and colour within 1; the plain chain kept 40
of 1,024 texels at level 1 (259 expected) and none below. Missing: other GPU vendors, build time per map.

### Section 5 evidence: exact vertex alpha at an alpha cutoff (2026-11-10)

Perspective-correct interpolation of a constant stage output of 1 is not exact (0.99999994 in some pixels); a
constant 0 is. MASK colour pipelines in gltf/pbr (`exactAlphaShader`) and the `vertexAlpha: false` caster path
(`solidVertexDepth`, shared by shadows, selection, clustered, staging and taa) hand on 1 - alpha. Evidence:
`packages/gltf/scripts/test-mask-alpha-browser.mjs` on the RTX A6000, WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: alpha exactly at
the cutoff keeps all 77,822 grid pixels (40,257 cut before), 64 of 64 picks (56 before) and the same 7,974 shadow
texels as a 0.49 cutoff. Missing: other GPU vendors; instance tint alpha still interpolates in the plain path.

### Section 5 evidence: moving cut-outs in casters and picking (2026-11-11)

A MASK material whose UVs move (MToon UV animation) is cut in its casters and in picking at the same animated UV as
its colour pass: shared/caster.js `animatedDepth` carries the raw UVs to the fragment and evaluates the MToon motion
(rotation about 0.5, scroll, then the base map's affine rows, each motion phase x m + period x fract(k x m) with m the
mask's blue channel and the float64 phases and whole counts k of rigging's `uvAnimationPhases`, so it keeps its steps
after days of uptime; 2026-11-15, evidence packages/rigging/tests/mtoon.test.js) from an 80-byte uniform at bindings 7 to 9. Cascades, virtual shadows, clustered local and cube maps, staging contact shadows and
selection picking use it, and TAA object velocity reads the same function at bindings 9 to 11; such casters redraw
every frame. Evidence: `packages/rigging/tests/mtoon-uv-shadow.browser.mjs` on the RTX A6000,
WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: the shadow half and the picked half swap after half a texture of scroll, and stay put
without the fix. Missing: other GPU vendors.

On the WebGL2 layer the cascade caster first cast the whole quad: its alpha sample takes `margoAnimatedUV(...)` as its
coordinate, and that function samples the mask, so the layer's GLSL called its sampling helper inside its own
arguments. ANGLE's Direct3D 11 back end then reads the inner call's texture for the outer call (a raw WebGL2 shader
shows it; a renamed copy of the function reads right). The layer's translator (`packages/webgl2-compat/src/glsl/emit.ts`,
`nesting`) now gives each nesting depth its own copy of a sampling helper. Evidence: the `nestedSampling` case of
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/features.html` (five forms, layer against native, fails without the change) and
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/glsl.test.js`. Missing: ANGLE on other vendors (the change is the same text on all).

### Section 5 evidence: mip chains at odd sizes and for blended colour (2026-11-11)

`packages/shared/mipmaps.js` (gltf/pbr, gltf, materials, lines, points, rigging, sprites and ui mips) builds every level
with an area filter (every source texel weighted by its overlap, as `alpha-mips.js`): the 2x2 box at even sizes, and at
odd sizes, where the old single bilinear fetch at the centre of a 2.5-texel footprint skipped a texel, the full overlap.
One texel-load path for both sizes needs no sampler and keeps the shader smaller than two paths. `alpha: 'weighted'`
averages colour weighted by alpha and is used for gltf/pbr `BLEND` base colour maps. Evidence:
`packages/gltf/scripts/test-mipmaps-browser.mjs` on the RTX A6000, WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: every level of
plain, sRGB, weighted and gltf/pbr chains within 0.68 colour and 0.54 alpha codes of a float64 area filter of the level
above (38 and 95 codes before on odd sizes; the red last column of a 5 x 5 image now keeps 102 of 255 at level 1).

### Section 5 evidence: non-finite HDR input stays local in Bloom and Tonemap (2026-11-10)

Bloom's prefilter and composite, Tonemap's presentation shaders and LocalExposure's base read NaN and -Inf as 0 and
+Inf as 65504 (largest IEEE 754-2008 binary16). The test is on the bits (`bitcast<vec3u>`, exponent all ones), since
WGSL lets compilers assume finite floats; a prefilter tap whose bilinear result is non-finite is refetched as four
cleaned texels, finite taps keep the hardware filter, and the up chain is kept within 65504. Evidence on the RTX A6000,
WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: `packages/post/test/bloom-finite-browser.mjs` (64 x 64, +Inf, -Inf, NaN texels) gives every
texel 8 px from a bad one equal to the clean image (largest difference 10.2 before), and
`packages/tonemap/tests/finite-browser.mjs` gives frames identical to the clean source with and without
LocalExposure (3 bytes differed before). Missing: other GPU vendors. Core's lit shader is not clamped (core freeze).

### Section 5 evidence: bright environments fit half floats by a stored scale (2026-11-10)

`Environment` divides every RGB texel by `radianceScale` = peak / 60000 when the brightest finite texel is above
60,000, before the rgba16float (or rgba32float) upload; the equirect-to-cube resample, box mips, GGX prefilter and SH
projection are linear, so lighting multiplies the factor back through `paramsBuffer` w and every consumer of the stored
texels (background exposure, EnvironmentBlend weights, baked KTX2 metadata version 2, materials envMap) applies it.
Non-finite and negative texels are stored as 0. Evidence: `packages/environment/tests/bright-browser.js` on the RTX
A6000, WebGPU and WebGL2 compat: CubeFaces 1e6 sun SH within 3.6e-7 of an f64 projection (1.59 before), equirect sun
SH linear within 1.9e-4 on both upload paths (1.26 before on rgba32float), every texel finite. Missing: other GPU
vendors; a texel about 10^9 below the peak becomes a half subnormal.

### Section 5 evidence: stable GGX inverse CDF in the environment bakes (2026-11-10)

`importanceGGX` takes cosTheta and sinTheta from d = (1 - xi) + alpha^2 xi, so the f32 lobe no longer collapses onto
the normal below alpha^2 = 2^-24. Evidence: `packages/environment/tests/environment-browser.js` 4c compares all 16,384
cells of the default LUT with an f64 integration of the same Hammersley set (old shader 0.00117 at cell (0, 0), new
worst 4.9e-4, allowance f16 half step plus 3e-4), RTX A6000 WebGPU and WebGL2 compat. Missing: a prefilter check at a
collapsing roughness; with mips spaced roughness m / (mips - 1) no level falls below 0.0156, so it is not reachable
through `Environment`.

### Section 5 evidence: compat canvas present is a draw, not a blit (batch 166 job 2)

The WebGL2 layer's canvas present was a y-flipped `blitFramebuffer` plus a colour-masked clear. Under ANGLE D3D11
both run on ANGLE's own shaders, and afterwards a later draw that changed no uniform binding sometimes read zero from
its fragment uniform blocks (every instanced box black). A raw WebGL2 replay of the recorded calls, no Margo code,
reproduces it on ANGLE D3D11 and not on ANGLE Vulkan; an unflipped blit in the replay removes it. The present is now
the layer's own exact texel-fetch draw (`Replayer.presentTexture`). Evidence and counts: `docs/known-bugs.md`,
"ANGLE D3D11 flipped blit"; tests `packages/webgl2-compat/test/canvas-present.test.js` and
`present-uniforms-browser.mjs`. Missing: which of ANGLE or the NVIDIA driver loses the binding, and other GPUs.
No core, stage or public API change.

### Section 5 evidence: WGSL minus lookahead (batch 165)

The compatibility parser now distinguishes expression subtraction/negation from
statement decrement using WGSL's context-aware lookahead. The parent-failing
wgsl-minus CPU regression checks folded values, spans, chains and unchanged
decrement statements. The existing Tonemap custom-curve pixel oracle caught
the issue on ANGLE D3D11; its native shader and arithmetic are unchanged.
Sources, cause and exact reproduction context are in
[batch-165-workcounts.md](../whitepaper/batch-165-workcounts.md).
No GPU math, backend capability, public API, core or stage change is introduced.


### Section 5 evidence: optional Draco component widths

The optional Rust decoder's descriptor and all component-dependent quantization,
KD and predictor storage accept nonzero UI8 counts. Minima are budgeted vectors;
prediction scratch is allocated per attribute and reused across rows and faces.
The retained historical width17 stream fails with Invalid on the parent and
matches its frozen public output after repair. wide.rs adds independent authored
streams and strict malformed/budget checks through 255 components, while the
native quad tests every parallelogram predictor with full-width data. The new
draco-wide.test.js checks the shipped Wasm and typed TypeScript bridge. Existing
native/Wasm corpora remain unchanged. No core, default decoder, normal encoding,
prediction arithmetic or speed claim changes.

Clean-room sources compared: Frank Galligan / Google, *Draco Bitstream
Specification*, version 2,2, 2017, https://google.github.io/draco/spec/
(attribute UI8 component field, portable transforms and component-wise prediction);
Rust Project contributors, *Vec*, 2026,
https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html (bounded owned storage and slices);
WebAssembly Community Group, *WebAssembly Core Specification 3.0*, 2026,
https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/exec/instructions.html (linear-memory
bounds and loads/stores).
The existing batch-133 frozen public-API records supply the historical layout
observation. No foreign implementation or companion code was read or copied.

The dependent CPU gate exposed duplicate fileURLToPath declarations in navmesh's
border.test.js and wasm.test.js. Remove the two duplicate imports in each file;
the files could not parse on the parent, and all eight original cases pass after
repair. No navmesh implementation, assertion or test workload changes.

### Section 5 evidence: React Grid scene ownership

Grid uses the existing native-binding helpers to attach and detach its Lines

### Section 5 evidence: native display glass, fixes K2 job 1

The internal materials native-glass adapter owns the scene capture, snapshots and transfer-function shader. gltf/pbr acquires it for native transmissive models and copies the current scene before each primitive, after settling the renderer's deferred clear and closing the preceding draw pass. The shader decodes both stored light contributions, multiplies the linear transmission share (including the existing Fresnel, coat, sheen and Beer terms), adds, then encodes. Native HDR blending is unchanged. Shared capture ownership ends with the last model; resize and device restoration rebuild its resources. Core and stage are unchanged.

**Scene captures nest (GAP-FILM-LATE, 2026-11-15).** A pass that redirects `c.color` and later restores it is a capture, and captures nest: the one that begins first ends last. The HDR captures begin at -65 to -50 (PostStack -65, SSAO and Bloom -60, DOF -55, Tonemap -50) and end from 30; the native glass capture begins at -40 and presents at 29, inside every one of them, so under an HDR capture it sees the linear target and keeps the linear blend. At -64 it began outside SSAO, Bloom, DOF and Tonemap, presented its own colour at 29 before they wrote this frame into it, and every frame read the one before (a fresh engine's first frame black). The new begin stays below -25, where environment probes (`scenePasses`) skip captures. Still crossing: the shared scene depth capture (`acquireDepth`, -15 to 10000) and sciviz volume depth (-0.001 to 39) begin inside the glass capture and end after it by order; no picture fault is reproduced yet (the bug-sweep list, KB-FILM-NEST2). Evidence: `packages/materials/tests/native-glass-nesting.test.js` (Tonemap and Bloom fail on the old order, PostStack passes on both), `packages/materials/test/native-glass-browser.mjs` `hdrNesting` (native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 1x and 4x: one frame after a background change reads the new frame). Sources: W3C WebGPU, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/, section 3.4.1 (timelines: work submitted to a queue runs in submission order, and `mapAsync` maps only after the GPU's use of the buffer ends) and 17.1.1.3 (load and store operations), which rule out a readback ordering fault: the copy ran after the frame, the frame had drawn the wrong texture; O'Donnell 2017, "FrameGraph: Extensible Rendering Architecture in Frostbite", GDC (passes declared by order, resources by lifetime). A capture that begins inside the glass one may end after 29 (the shared scene depth, -15 to 10000; sciviz volume depth, -0.001 to 39): the glass then presents at 10000.5, once it owns the frame colour again (KB-FILM-NEST2, 2026-11-25). Evidence: `packages/materials/tests/native-glass-nesting.test.js` and `hdrNesting` in `native-glass-browser.mjs`; sciviz volume depth is covered on the CPU recorder only.

**Sky light follows this frame's camera (GAP-FILM-LATE, GAP-FILM-READY, 2026-11-15).** The sun's colour and strength (`sunlight`, the transmittance from the eye's altitude, Bruneton and Neyret 2008, "Precomputed Atmospheric Scattering", EGSR, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2008.01245.x) are set in `onPreUpdate` from the engine camera's altitude. They read the altitude the sky passes stored in the frame before, so a frame was lit by the previous camera (1 level on 0.06 % of a 2560x1440 film) and a fresh sky's first frame from sea level. Evidence: `packages/sky/test/eye-altitude.test.js`. With both fixes the Film Studio bench film draws its final pixels on the first `render()` of a fresh process; pipelines a package compiles asynchronously are warmed with `warmUp` from `@margoengine/quality`.

Evidence: packages/materials/tests/native-glass.test.js checks shared ownership, per-surface copies, attachment restoration, HDR bypass and the shader arithmetic. packages/materials/test/native-glass-browser.mjs compares one and two overlapping surfaces against an independent IEC transfer-function sum at 1x and 4x, on native WebGPU and compatibility. It fails on the old two-draw path. No wall-clock claim; other GPU vendors remain unmeasured.

Clean-room sources compared: W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, *WebGPU*, 2026, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ (plain UNORM has no automatic transfer conversion); Khronos Group, *Data Format Specification v1.4.0*, 2025, https://registry.khronos.org/DataFormat/specs/1.4/dataformat.1.4.inline.html (linear and sRGB transfer functions); Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li and Kenneth E. Torrance, *Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces*, 2007, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr07/195-206 (reflected and transmitted radiance shares). The standards determine the compositor; the paper supports retaining the existing energy split. No companion code was read.

K2 dependent CPU gate repair: OIT assertions retain every geometry/OIT pass and exact draw counts while identifying the native glass adapter's passes separately; scene color is the capture attachment and the original depth stays in place. The capture registers after its model joins the existing segment, preserving the single HDR model run; the new CPU pass-count regression guards MSAA stores/loads and the exact live-dispersion compatibility case passes.

### Section 5 evidence: native display glass in caller-owned passes (KB2281)

`PBRDeviceRenderer.draw(context, pass, view, options)` (gltf/pbr `createRenderer`) takes `options.snapshot(pass, target)`. On a display-encoded target the renderer installs an external native-glass source for the draw (materials `externalNativeGlass`, one context-sized single-sample snapshot texture per renderer, released with it), so the same native glass shader and binding apply. Before each glass surface the caller's hook ends the pass, writes the colour so far into the snapshot and returns the reopened pass, which `draw` hands back. `@margoengine/xr` lends the hook from its eye loop when a drawn model has a native glass material (`nativeGlassMaterial`, shared with gltf/pbr) on a display-encoded layer: the eye pass then stores its 4x samples, and the hook resolves them into the snapshot with a resolve-only pass (XR layer textures may lack COPY_SRC) and reopens the eye pass with `load` and the eye viewport (KB2281-xr, packages/xr/tests/xr.test.js). `rgba16float` targets and draws without the hook keep the native blend. Evidence: packages/gltf/test/external-glass.test.js (one snapshot per surface, pass ownership, HDR bypass, refusal of a hook that returns no pass); packages/materials/test/native-glass-browser.mjs `externalGlass` (rgba8unorm, 128 grey: 143, 155, 165 with the hook against the IEC sum 143, 154, 165; 197, 221, 239 without), native WebGPU and compatibility. Same sources as K2 job 1 above.

### Section 5 evidence: opt-in linear-light blending (KB3148b)

`blendSpace: 'linear'` (materials `Material.blendSpace`, gltf/pbr `PBRRenderState.blendSpace`) gives a plain BLEND material on a display-encoded target the native glass path: the draw ends the pass, the capture snapshots the colour so far, and `linearBlendShader` rewrites only the main fragment entry's return to encode(a * lin(src) + (1 - a) * lin(dst)) with alpha a + dst.a * (1 - a), pipeline blending off. The draw context (`DrawFrame.glass`) records whether a capture lends the snapshot, so a derivation made before the capture began is never reused after it; a model that first draws the option without a capture acquires one between frames (`wantGlass`, plugins cannot join a running frame graph), in the scene that drew. Linear-blend derivations are not batchable. Default 'display' unchanged, so no picture and no steady-frame work count moves unless the option is set. Evidence: packages/materials/test/native-glass-browser.mjs `linearBlend` (native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 1x and 4x, materials and glTF, set before and after the first frame), packages/materials/test/render-state.test.js. Source: IEC 61966-2-1 sRGB transfer; Porter and Duff 1984, "Compositing Digital Images" (SIGGRAPH), over operator in linear values.

### Section 5 evidence: linear-light layers in weighted OIT (KB3148d)

glTF PBR hands a BLEND material whose `renderState` holds only `blendSpace: 'linear'` to a transparency hook that declares `linearLayers` (`PBRTransparency`); on a display-encoded target its pipeline sets `margoLinear`, which clears a per-pixel mark (OIT's revealage `.g`, now `rg16float`, or an `r8unorm` fourth target with `blending`). Once per draw holding such a surface glTF PBR passes the hook a function that copies the colour so far into the native glass snapshot; OIT calls it after its accumulation pass, keeps its display composite unchanged, then draws the marked pixels again with blending off: encode(decode(average) * (1 - R) + decode(scene) * R), mixed with the display result by the mark at MSAA edges. No mark, copy or draw on an HDR target or when no linear layer drew; the display path's draws, bind groups and buffer writes are unchanged, its revealage target 2 bytes per pixel larger. KB3148e: the hook moved to the shared `TransparentPass`, so `ExactOIT`, `MomentOIT`, `PeelOIT` and `PreciseOIT` take linear layers too. The per-layer passes (`ExactOIT`, `PeelOIT`) store a linear layer's alpha negated and, only in a frame where one drew, resolve one layer index per render pass far to near: a snapshot copy, the display layers of that index with the hardware blend, then its linear ones with blending off, over(decode) per layer; frames without one keep the single instanced or looped resolve. `MomentOIT` marks in its optical target's free `.a` (additive, so a 4x edge mark is the mean count per sample), `PreciseOIT` in a revealage `.g` (`rg16float`), and both redraw the marked pixels after their composite as `OIT` does. `PeelOIT` now peels in the frame's own context with `depth` and `descriptor` swapped and restored, so per-context lookups (the native glass capture) see the frame. Evidence: the same linear-check.mjs, now over all six passes (100 cases native, 82 on the WebGL2 layer), and the KB3148e test in oit.test.js. Sources as above, plus Yang, Hensley, Grun and Thibieroz 2010 (per-pixel linked lists), Everitt 2001 (depth peeling), Muenstermann, Krumpen, Klein and Peters 2018 (moment-based OIT), Wyman 2016, "Exploring and Expanding the Continuum of OIT Algorithms", HPG, https://research.nvidia.com/publication/2016-06_exploring-and-expanding-continuum-oit-algorithms (collect, then resolve: a per-layer resolve composites layer by layer), Maule, Comba, Torchelsen and Bastos 2011, "A survey of raster-based transparency techniques", Computers and Graphics 35(6), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2011.07.006. Evidence: packages/oit/test/gpu/linear-check.mjs (native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 1x and 4x, plain and `blending`, materials and glTF, before and after the first frame: 137 and 165, display 94 and 141), packages/oit/test/oit.test.js (KB3148d tests). Sources: McGuire and Bavoil 2013, "Weighted Blended Order-Independent Transparency", JCGT 2(2), https://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/09/; Porter and Duff 1984, "Compositing Digital Images", SIGGRAPH; IEC 61966-2-1:1999 sRGB transfer; Gritz and d'Eon 2007, "The Importance of Being Linear", GPU Gems 3, chapter 24.

### Section 5 evidence: verify cache settlement

After the build prints sizes and the catalog, verify settles the shadow result
cache before launching its parallel checks. It merges recorded inputs, hashes
and packs package outputs, publishes passes and enforces the archive cap. This
is parent-process work, so an empty child-process list does not imply a hang.
Verify now names that work before it begins. Previously every newly packed
package synchronously statted and sorted the entire archive directory.

Windows directory enumeration already returns sizes and timestamps, which
Node's Dirent omits. `scripts/support/archive-metadata.ps1` reads those fields
through the system .NET runtime, avoiding a separate native metadata lookup per
archive. Every insertion still takes a fresh inventory and enforces the same
cap. Node's listing supplies tie order; links/directories and disappeared
entries retain the stat path, and other platforms use the original stat scan.
The helper has a hard 60-second limit and propagates errors. Sorting happens
only when deletion is necessary; archive writes, compression, keys, poisoning,
comparisons, retirement and checks are unchanged. No timestamps are memoized.

`tests/result-cache.test.js` compares the former full-stat path with enumeration:
128 existing archives plus 12 outputs require 1,614 versus zero per-archive
stats under cap, and 1,548 versus zero at cap, with identical retained names
and bytes and zero archive-content bytes read by eviction. Both paths perform
12 Node listings; Windows also performs 12 native metadata enumerations.
Further fixtures cover shared touches/additions/removals, backwards timestamps,
per-write eviction, ties and recreated keys. `tests/archive-metadata.test.js`
matches stat metadata, fractional/pre-epoch times, Unicode paths, directories,
disappearances and helper failures.
`tests/verify-cache-progress.test.js` requires the progress line before work.
These deterministic regressions run in verify, hence check:merge. No elapsed
speed result is claimed; every inventory still scales with archive count and
uses a short system helper process on Windows. Sources are in `docs/clean-room.md`.

Validation: the single full verify passes 14,233 tests with zero failures/skips
and no cache disagreements. The final expanded focused suite passes 42/42.
Lint and hygiene pass (the initial standalone hygiene required rebuilding stale
worktree declarations). A read-only inventory of the live shared store reports
59,914 archives and zero per-file stat calls on the native path. Cache counts
can change as other lanes write; deterministic fixtures supply the comparison.

## Owned Chromium process-list ordering (section 5 supplement, 2026-11-09)

Client close must follow the owned browser's bounded CDP process-list read.
Previously those operations raced, so a healthy session could be disconnected
before its reply and cleanup entered the helper fallback. The retained process
list is now passed to native termination; client cleanup and termination still
run concurrently after that read. Deterministic coverage in
`tests/browser-teardown.test.js` fails on the parent and checks one list request,
list-before-disconnect and native-end-before-driver-kill. All 56 scoped browser
selection, teardown and shutdown tests pass. All nine voxel GPU suites and the
decoder browser, decoder Node/glTF and glTF GPU gates pass after the repair.
The voxel README gate passes with its unchanged five known failures (18 of 23
examples successful). No shutdown deadline, rendering assertion or performance
budget was relaxed. The full verify run found only an excluded-workspace link
in a report removed on 2026-11-16 with the GPU scheduler (KB-GPULOCK-ALL); its existing regression guards that repair.

## Per-instance attributes by row index (section 3 supplement, 2026-11-26)

`@margoengine/materials/instance-attributes` reads a read-only storage buffer by `instance_index`: in the colour pass
through a vertex input (shared with a node graph's `instanceIndex`) and a flat varying (location 6 or 8), in depth passes
through a built-in added to the caster's vertex entry. Rules that follow: a pass that draws a materials caster must draw
a primitive's instances in row order from instance 0; a culler or sorter that reorders rows must skip a material whose
`shading.instanceRows` is true (`shared/instances.js` `readsRows`); the beauty shader names `f.model` so plain meshes are
never merged into one instanced draw whose batch position would read as a row. Evidence:
`packages/materials/test/instance-attributes-browser.mjs` (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). GPU picking draws gltf/pbr
instances through the same caster code (`instancedDepth` after the vertex move, one ID per row; evidence
`packages/selection/test/instanced-move.browser.mjs`, both back ends). Missing: adapters without
vertex-stage storage buffers (compatibility mode), instance velocity for TAA,
GPU runs of the shadow atlas and contact shadows.

## Caster records and live bindings (section 3 supplement, 2026-11-27)

A depth pass keeps the bind group of a moved caster while `material.displacement` returns the same record. Rule: a
material that makes such records returns a new one when what its entries bind changes (`reboundCaster`,
`packages/shared/displacement.js`), compared only after a pass has bound them so no GPU resource is made before one
draws. `@margoengine/materials/instanced-curve-flow` keeps every curve's frames in one texture and each instance's
choice in per-instance rows, so the rules above apply to it. Evidence: `packages/materials/test/curve-flow-browser.mjs`
and `packages/shader/test/deform-check.mjs` (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer; KB-SHADOW-STALEMOVE1). Missing: a swapped
plugin texture under clustered shadows and picking has no GPU run of its own.

## GPU work runs directly (Scott, 2026-11-16)

GPU work runs at once, as many jobs as are started, and every command keeps a hard timeout. `scripts/run-with-timeout.mjs` starts a command and ends its whole process tree after `--max` minutes (default 10), exiting 124. Nothing queues, nothing is refused and nothing records usage, and a shot does not pause: it renders from its first frame to its last. The one pause that remains is the heat pause of `scripts/gpu-package-tests.mjs`, which waits for the machine to cool. Proof: `tests/run-with-timeout.test.js` (2, 5 and 20 runs start together; a hung command ends at its timeout).

## The WGSL corpus draw runs in parts (2026-11-18, KB-COMPAT-CORPUSTIME1)

`webgl2-compat test:browser` drew every recorded corpus pipeline in one step and needed 487 to 510 s for the draw
alone, past the 10 minute GPU step limit once robot-planning's clearance kernels (90 s or more each in ANGLE's
Direct3D compiler) joined the corpus. The draw now runs as five package scripts, `test:browser` (render pipelines),
`test:browser:compute` and `test:browser:compute-robot-planning-1` to `-3` (one clearance kernel each, 90 to 200 s),
chosen by `--part` in
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/corpus-draw-parts.mjs`. Every pipeline still runs in full; the step limit is not raised.
`test/corpus-draw-parts.test.js` fails when a part drops a pipeline, holds one twice, is empty or has no script. A
package whose compute kernels take the compiler minutes goes in `OWN_COMPUTE_PART` with its kernel count, one part
per kernel; a kernel recorded beyond the count fails the test and the run.

## Corpus refusals are asserted, not skipped (2026-11-26, KB-COMPAT-CORPUSRED1)

The WGSL corpus holds what the packages built on real WebGPU devices, some of which the WebGL2 layer does not offer:
modules behind `enable subgroups;` and `enable clip_distances;` (the packages build them only when the device has the
feature), compute kernels sized past WebGPU's default 256 invocations, and pipelines recorded with more texture units
than WebGL2 has (gltf/pbr packs those materials on the layer). `packages/webgl2-compat/test/support/corpus-refusals.mjs`
holds the one rule the corpus checks assert: each such module is refused with its coded error (the enable named, the
device's own texture-units wording), counted against a recorded count with its cause, and a count above the recorded
one fails. The WGSL checker types the subgroup built-in functions behind `enable subgroups;`, so the layer's coded
refusal is what a page sees, not a type error. Evidence: compute.test.js, glsl-corpus-browser.mjs,
corpus-draw-browser.mjs; khronos-gallery's material on the layer: scripts/compat-units-gpu-check.js --compat.

Workgroup limits (2026-11-27, KB-COMPAT-WGSIZE1): the layer's createComputePipeline holds `@workgroup_size` (each axis
and the product, constants applied) and the workgroup variables' bytes to its device limits at creation, as WebGPU
does; before, only the lazy planner checked the product, at the first dispatch. Evidence: compute-limits.test.js;
compute.test.js and the browser corpus compute part hold the recorded oversize kernels to that refusal.

Loops end on any buffer contents (2026-11-27, KB-COMPAT-CORPUSFBO1): a dispatch that never ends resets the GPU, and
the loss is reported by whatever runs next (KB-COMPAT-LOSSREPORT1, fixed below). The morph weight kernel's key search now
bounds `keys-1u` and its midpoint. A recording that replaces a changed kernel names the old module with
`record-wgsl-corpus.mjs --add --drop=<key>`. Evidence: animation morph-gpu.test.js (CPU tier with a work budget),
scripts/animation-morph-gpu-tests.js native and forced compatibility, the browser corpus compute part (0 failures).

A texture made on a lost context is not refused (2026-11-27, KB-COMPAT-LOSTMSAA1): `getInternalformatParameter`
answers null there, so only a format with no renderbuffer reads null as unsupported (lost-report.test.js,
lost-context-browser.mjs). A frame lost with its device leaves the one before it on the page and prints nothing, so a
post check that reads one frame after another also reads the canvas in the render's task and the device's loss
(`scene-background-browser.mjs`; KB-POST-HALFVIEW-ONCE1, still open). `SceneFade` draws on canvas views only
(KB-FADE-TARGETVIEW1, `scene-fade-target-browser.mjs`, both backends).

XR on a transparent canvas, stand-in `navigator.xr` only (2026-11-27, RTX A6000): at 1 sample, with TransparentCanvas
attached, `immersive-ar` and `immersive-vr` eyes of WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer matched (Bloom within 1) for no effect,
Tonemap, PostStack, Bloom, FXAA, TAA and DOF; no eye held colour above its alpha; empty AR pixels were 0,0,0,0 except
under Bloom's glow; VR eyes were opaque. KB-XR-AREFFECTS1 and KB-XR-AR4XCOMPAT1, found there, are fixed above. Not covered: a headset, a
browser compositor, additive displays and composition layers.

A pass that redirects the scene's depth gives it back (2026-11-27, KB-XR-AREFFECTS1): `SceneTarget` in its final
resolve or restore at 1 and 4 samples, only between equal sizes, and `DepthCopy` for depth-only redirects
(`acquireDepth` at 1 sample, `StencilBuffer`). An XR eye's depth is its AR coverage and the compositor's depth layer.
A capture owner makes its final resolve at order 29.8 or later, so every draw below 30 reaches the picture
(KB-POST-LATEDRAW1, `late-draw-browser.mjs`). On the WebGL2 layer a 4x sample load returns the resolved texel; the AR
blit counts coverage by depth testing instead (KB-XR-AR4XCOMPAT1). Evidence, stand-in headset on an RTX A6000, both
backends: `ar-effects.browser.mjs`. Missing: a headset, an AR device, a browser compositor.

A GPU reset is the device's loss (2026-11-27, KB-COMPAT-LOSSREPORT1): Chrome answers the synchronous query that waited
for a reset (LINK_STATUS and COMPILE_STATUS false with empty logs, checkFramebufferStatus 0x8cdd, getError 0) before
isContextLost() turns true and CONTEXT_LOST_WEBGL is queued, one task later; no synchronous signal exists (measured, RTX
A6000, ANGLE Direct3D 11). So `CompatDevice` judges every error read from GL in a later task, in one place
(`reportable`): the uncaptured dispatch, `popErrorScope` (in order, null on a lost device, as WebGPU) and the async
pipeline rejections (`settlePipeline`). The layer's own helper program that does not link is an `internal` error
through that path, reported once, instead of a synchronous throw. A real link failure or incomplete framebuffer on a
live context is still reported. The adapter's capability probes (highp int, fresh clears, inverse trig) read GL status
on the adapter's own new context and decide only workarounds for it; the preview renderer and `webglPicking` keep
their contract (`failed` on a lost context). Evidence: lost-report.test.js (fails on the parent), lost-context-browser.mjs,
compute-browser.mjs, and two real resets: a link and a render pass right after the reset, with isContextLost() still
false, raised nothing and lost the device. lost-context-browser.mjs repeats that on every test:gpu without a driver
reset: it crashes the browser's own GPU process through CDP `Browser.crashGpuProcess` (Chrome, RTX A6000: the first
link after it fails with an empty log, a new framebuffer reads 0x8cdd and isContextLost() stays false for the whole
synchronous block).

## The fast gate checks changed files' format (2026-11-19)

`npm run lint` (scripts/lint.mjs) runs `biome lint` over the tree as before, then `biome check --error-on-warnings` on the files changed since the merge base with origin/main (committed, uncommitted and untracked; noExplicitAny stays with hygiene gate 3's allowlist). `biome lint` alone never checked formatting and passed on warnings, and hygiene scores format in warn mode over about 2,800 files Biome would reformat, so packages/netcode/tests/browser/signal.mjs and scripts/publish-rehearsal.mjs landed unformatted and tools/shot/cli.mjs with an unused import. The changed files only are held to the rule, so the step costs well under a second beyond the tree lint; a file touched by a change is formatted whole. tests/lint-changed.test.js checks the wiring and that an unformatted file and an unused import fail.

is the single checked-in default (`deferred`). No gate enables speed work.

Correctness GPU commands run directly. Classified timing
commands are refused before they start with `ERR_SPEED_PHASE_DEFERRED`.

`scripts/speed/budgets.mjs`, speed test registrations and standalone drivers,
listed in the release inventory. Mixed CPU files
still check values, geometry, errors, allocations and work counts. Pure speed
callbacks are registered only in the active speed phase, with explicit deferral
output rather than skipped tests or passing substitute numbers. Repeated EXR,
USDZ and polygon comparisons do no timing work in the build phase. The million-
voxel paste scene keeps its equality checks in correctness without best-of rounds.

The WebGL2 layer's pixel comparison (`visual:compat`) captures with Chromium's partial raster off, so the page's
own painting cannot make a still frame differ between two loads (KB-VC-SCIVIZ, 2026-11-27).

Biome flythrough and object-camera correctness run as ordinary GPU checks. Separate
`flythrough-speed.mjs` and `objects-frame-speed.mjs` retain the original speed
scenes, sampling, baselines and assertions. The
flythrough's worker scheduling, send/copy counts, clock monotonicity and GPU
validation stay in correctness. Visual compatibility's 50 ms timing-only step
defers while the pixel comparison still runs. Quickstart keeps all pixel and
interaction checks and moves its unchanged 300 s default speed assertion to the
named budget suite. Clock behavior, readiness deadlines, timeout/teardown safety,
deterministic byte/allocation/draw/triangle/pass counts, and local CI per-commit
duration history with its 1.5x jump flag are retained.

After Scott ends the build phase, set `MARGO_SPEED_PHASE=active` on a quiet
machine and run `npm run test:speed`. Commands run one at a time with hard
process-tree limits; direct benchmark and `--timing` entries read the same phase.
Every listed scene and budget must pass before release, as must busy-retests.
The phase is not permission to weaken a budget, change a scene or publish busy-
machine speed numbers. External rival fixtures remain outside this repository.

Evidence: `tests/speed-phase.test.js` uses fabricated readings to prove unchanged

or new speed claim is part of this change.

## Browser shutdown evidence (batch 160, section 5 supplement)

The Windows browser owner distinguishes native process exit from ChildProcess
close. After native termination succeeds, it releases stdout, stderr and both
CDP pipes and awaits a close event latched at launch before driver cleanup. The
four-pipe regression fails under the previous ordering. Native handle waits
check process creation time before polling, with a live replacement-process
regression for PID reuse. These repairs retain the 30,000 ms shutdown budget.
The root catalog and browser launcher tests exercise the shared owner; this
change adds no rendering capability and does not change core or stage.

### Owned Chromium ended without helper programs (section 5, 2026-11-09)

Symptom: GPU suites in five lanes passed every check, then failed with
`SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT`, "still open: browser", at the unchanged 30,000 ms budget
(for example sciviz: 30 checks, then 46.5 s in all). The pipe repair above did
not stop it.

Cause: the owned browser was ended by two programs started at close time.
`taskkill.exe` builds the tree from WMI (its binary holds the `Win32_Process`
and `ParentProcessId` queries; it takes 0.65 to 1.6 s per call on this PC when
idle), then a Windows PowerShell waits for the handles. Its result was read
from its output lines only, so a taskkill that did not start, ran out of time
or failed in WMI reported "no process ended", which read as "nothing left".
Nothing then ended the browser, and the close waited for an exit that only
Chromium's own starved shutdown could give (68 to 146 s under load, above).
The helper wait also had the whole 30 s budget, so its own "Chromium processes
did not exit" error could never be reported first. The failures clustered in
windows when helper programs were failing on this PC: Windows Error Reporting
holds powershell.exe console-host crashes (`ConsoleControl` static
constructor) in groups of four at the same seconds as GPU driver resets
(LiveKernelEvent 141, eight groups on 2026-11-09), and the WMI log holds
failed `Win32_Process` enumerations (0x80041032, 0x800706BE). No failing run
was traced phase by phase: eight traced sciviz runs and the CPU loops passed
(close 1.1 to 1.9 s), so the chain above is shown by these records and by the
deterministic regressions, not by a captured hang.

Fix (`scripts/lib/browser.mjs`, `stopOwned`): the browser process is ended
through the handle Node holds (`ChildProcess.kill`, TerminateProcess), and
each process Chromium lists for itself over CDP (`SystemInfo.getProcessInfo`)
by its pid, then the close waits for the listed processes to exit and for the
browser's `close` event. Process termination uses no helper program; the
Windows child-exit wait now uses the existing creation-time-aware native waiter. Measured on this PC: killing
only the browser process left two Edge utility processes
(`entity_extraction_service`, `edge_collections`) running past 10 s, so the
listed children are ended explicitly; with them, the whole tree, crashpad
included, was gone in 50 to 285 ms (with a live WebGPU device). Only a browser
that does not list its processes within 5,000 ms (`LIST_PROCESSES_MS`) takes
the old taskkill route, and its browser process is still ended through its
handle afterwards. `taskkillTree` now returns the root pid when taskkill could
not run, so `endTree` waits for and reports it instead of returning success.

Regressions (`tests/browser-teardown.test.js`): with the helper route reporting
nothing, as it did, a fake owned browser and a real child process with five
pipes both reach `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` "still open: browser" on the parent commit
and close at once with the fix; `stopOwned` ends listed children without a
helper and falls back only when the list never comes; the taskkill failure
modes return the root pid; the existing real-browser test checks every listed
process has exited after the close. The 30,000 ms budget is unchanged. Not
measured: a capture of the original hang, other Windows PCs, and GPU resets
during a close (a process held in the kernel by a reset still has to exit).

Sources: Microsoft, [TerminateProcess](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-terminateprocess)
(asynchronous; a process exits once pending I/O completes; wait on its handle);
Raymond Chen, [Why do some processes stay in Task Manager after they have been killed?](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/?p=102303)
and [Why can't I delete a file immediately after terminating the process?](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20120329-00/?p=7973);
Node.js [child_process](https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html) (`close`
after stdio ends, `exit` before it; `subprocess.kill`); Playwright
[BrowserServer](https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browserserver) and
[Browser.close](https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser) for a connected
client; issue reports of taskkill.exe exhausting WMI on Windows desktops
([openai/codex 34260](https://upd.dev/openai/codex/issues/34260)); libuv's
Windows grandchild pipe inheritance discussion ([libuv PR 343](https://github.com/joyent/libuv/pull/343)).
Only documentation and issue text were read, no other project's source.

## Purpose and authority

This document preserves the engine-specific technical design, validation model, measured limits, and known gaps that
were previously mixed with repository coordination instructions. It does not define task assignment, branches,
integration, publishing, or source-control operations. Those are external workspace responsibilities.

The implementation and focused tests are authoritative when this document disagrees with current code. Most detailed
measurements below were audited at commit `67ca53a5` on 2026-10-29. Later committed records supersede those snapshot
values. Status words mean:

- **Enforced**: executable code or a test rejects a violation.
- **Verified**: the cited implementation or test was inspected.
- **Measured**: a committed result records the value and conditions.
- **Documented**: the contract exists, but this document does not claim a live run.
- **Unverified**: a known evidence gap.

## 1. Deterministic transform kernel

### 1.1 Components and build

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/kernel/Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` | Rust crate `margoengine-kernel`, built as `cdylib` and `rlib`; release uses `opt-level = 3`, fat LTO, one codegen unit, aborting panics, no overflow checks, stripped symbols. |
| `rust-toolchain.toml` | Pinned minimal Rust toolchain and `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target. |
| `packages/kernel/src/lib.rs` | Layout, transform evaluation, constraints, bounds, culling, exports, and native unit tests. |
| `scripts/build-modern.js` | Cargo build, Binaryen optimization, validation, compression, and generated embedding. |
| `packages/core/src/wasm.ts` | Generated raw-deflate payload encoded as base64. Consumers need no Rust toolchain. |
| `packages/core/src/kernel.ts` | `TransformStore`: instantiate, bind typed-array views, grow, tick, and report errors. |
| `packages/core/src/engine.ts` | Slot allocation, public transform setters, per-frame tick, and instance updates. |
| `scripts/kernel-opt-experiment.js` | Historical optimization experiment. It is currently stale; see known gaps. |

The source build runs Cargo for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with SIMD enabled, then `wasm-opt` with `-Oz`,
`-ocimfs 300`, SIMD, bulk memory, non-trapping float-to-int support, stripped metadata, and convergence. The normal
package build can instead decode the checked-in payload. Both paths validate the module, enforce raw Wasm under
30 KiB, compress with raw deflate at level 9, and verify a lossless round trip. At the audit snapshot the payload was
9,011 bytes raw and 3,435 bytes before base64 after deflate.

`npm run modern:build` rebuilds from Rust (`scripts/build-core-kernel.mjs`). `npm run build:packages` uses the checked-in
payload and needs no Rust toolchain. `npm run test:kernel` runs `cargo test --locked`.

Every Rust crate that ships as Wasm follows this pattern (2026-11-10): its built module is committed (a `.wasm` beside
its entry, or a base64 `.ts` blueprint), `npm run build:packages` copies it and never runs cargo, and a record beside
it holds a hash of the crate's sources, its `path =` dependencies, `rust-toolchain.toml` and the build script that
sets its flags. `scripts/wasm-blueprints.mjs` lists all 23 shipped crates; `npm run hygiene` fails on a stale record
or an unlisted crate, and `npm run wasm:rebuild -- --compare` rebuilds every blueprint from source and fails on any
byte difference. Evidence: `tests/wasm-blueprints.test.js` (staleness rules); `packages/decoders/tests/build-without-rust.test.js`
builds the decoders with cargo removed from PATH (it failed with `spawn cargo ENOENT` before the decoders' Draco, HDR
and AVIF modules were committed). On 2026-11-10 two clean builds of every crate on one Windows PC (rustc 1.99.0) gave
identical bytes; four committed modules (biomes erosion, compute decomp, procedural buildings, sciviz flow) differed
from a fresh build of their current sources in 6 to 66 bytes near the end of the module and were rebuilt. Unmeasured: byte equality across
operating systems. The `rlib` target lets native tests execute the same algorithms with owned vector storage.

### 1.2 Linear-memory contract

One Wasm instance owns one fixed-capacity kernel. The kernel allocates a float region followed by a byte region at an
aligned `__heap_base`; tick performs no allocation. Capacity is limited to `2^23` so the layout remains below the
wasm32 4 GiB address space.

Constants at the audited layout:

- `TAIL = 24`, `DATA_LANES = 86`, `FLAG_LANES = 7`.
- Float lanes: translation 0-2, quaternion 3-6, scale 7-9, parent 10, world matrix 11-26, local sphere 27-30,
  world-sphere structure-of-arrays 31-34, planes and Euler storage 35-37, limits 38-49, scratch matrix 50-65,
  scratch sphere 66-69, and snapshot 70-85.
- Flag lanes: active 0, visible 1, constrained 2, hidden 3, hierarchy depth and inherited-hidden bit 4, tick state 5,
  changed 6.
- The constraint mask uses bits 0-2 for translation and bits 3-5 for Euler rotation (`ROTATION = 56`).

| Region | Indexing and shape | Producer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Translation, quaternion, scale | `lane * capacity + id`, one structure-of-arrays lane each | JS setters; rotation sync may rewrite quaternion |
| Parents | `10 * capacity + id`, parent id stored as f32, `-1` for none | JS hierarchy setter |
| World matrices | `11 * capacity + id * 16 + element`, column-major | Kernel publish pass |
| Local spheres | `27 * capacity + id * 4 + component` | Geometry-bound setup |
| World spheres | Four structure-of-arrays lanes at 31-34 | Kernel publish pass; suited to four-wide SIMD culling |
| Frustum planes | First 24 values of the lane-35 region | Camera update |
| Euler XYZ | After the 24 plane values, `id * 3 + axis` | JS rotation setter; constraints |
| Limits | After the same tail, 12 values per entity: min/max for translation and Euler axes | JS constraints |
| Scratch matrix and sphere | Per-entity blocks | Kernel staging only |
| Snapshots | 16 values per entity | Kernel bitwise change detection |

The layout costs 351 bytes per slot: 86 f32 lanes plus 7 flag bytes. A committed measurement recorded 352.1 bytes
per slot at 1,048,576 slots. Core adds approximately 5 bytes per slot for the host-side seen and slot arrays. The
mixed layout is deliberate: streamed values and culling spheres are structure-of-arrays, while records copied whole
are per-entity blocks.

`kernel_new` is the only allocator. On wasm32 it owns one static kernel per instance, grows linear memory by pages,
zeros storage, initializes parents to `-1`, and returns null on invalid capacity or allocation failure. `kernel_data`
and `kernel_flags` expose byte offsets; JS constructs all typed views from those offsets. Bounds checks are omitted
only where the layout proves safety. Value, hierarchy, capacity, and finiteness checks remain.

The numeric layout constants are duplicated in Rust and TypeScript. There is no direct generated or compile-time
comparison between those lists; behavioral tests are the current drift detector.

### 1.3 Slot allocation and growth

Removed ids enter a LIFO free list and are reused before the monotonic `next` id advances. A new slot resets
translation to zero, quaternion and scale to identity, parent to `-1`, constraints and hidden state to zero, and Euler
values to zero. Geometry later supplies bounds.

When an id reaches capacity, the store doubles up to `2^23`:

1. Copy every current view out of Wasm memory.
2. Drop the static kernel instance.
3. Bind a larger kernel at the same base address, growing linear memory if required.
4. Recreate every typed view and restore each old view as a prefix.
5. Rebind every live mesh matrix subarray.
6. If the larger bind fails, rebind the old capacity, restore all copies, and rethrow.
7. Mark the new kernel for one full recomputation.

Old views must never be retained across growth. A memory grow detaches their buffer; without a memory grow they still
alias a layout whose column offsets changed. Growth copies about 351 bytes per existing slot and has no isolated
committed timing.

### 1.4 Change detection, hierarchy, and atomic publication

There are no descendant dirty lists. Each entity has a 16-lane bit snapshot containing translation, quaternion,
scale, parent, local sphere, and hidden state. Comparing bits means signed zero and NaN payload changes are visible.
All four four-lane groups are visited even if an earlier group changed.

A tick proceeds as follows:

1. With culling enabled, validate all 24 frustum-plane floats.
2. Validate every constrained value and min/max pair; all must be finite and `min <= max`.
3. Clamp constrained axes. If an Euler axis changed, synchronize its quaternion through the kernel's one XYZ
   expansion.
4. Clear per-tick state.
5. Visit active ids in order. Resolve a parent recursively before its child, memoize completed work, reject cycles,
   reject invalid or inactive parents, and enforce depth at most 64.
6. Recompute when the snapshot changed, the full flag is set, or the parent was recomputed. Write only to scratch.
7. If every active hierarchy succeeds, copy changed scratch matrices and spheres to published regions and set sticky
   changed bytes. A failure publishes nothing and sets the next tick to full.
8. Set initial visibility from local and inherited hidden state, then optionally cull.

Parent composition uses the parent's scratch matrix, which always contains its last computed value. Local TRS is
validated for finite values and a nonzero quaternion; a zero scale is valid (glTF 2.0 section 3.5.3, KB-GLTFA B1)
and gives a zero matrix column, with shaders turning normals by the cofactor matrix and guarding a zero result. Quaternion normalization and affine composition
accumulate in f64 and publish f32. The final matrix and transformed sphere must be finite.

World-sphere centers are transformed normally. Radius uses `r * sqrt(norm1 * normInfinity)` of the world matrix's
3x3 part, a conservative spectral-norm bound under non-uniform scale and shear. Culling tests six planes and keeps a
sphere that touches a plane. SIMD handles groups of four, with a scalar remainder. The implementation remains linear
in active entity count; no spatial index is present.

Euler XYZ radians share the tail region after the planes. The kernel owns the single `qX * qY * qZ` expansion and a
deterministic sine approximation: range reduction by tau plus an 11-term f64 Taylor series. A direct Euler write and
a constraint clamp therefore produce the same quaternion bits. One unverified edge remains: native `f64::round`
and Wasm `nearest` differ at exact half-way turn reductions.

`kernel_tick` returns 0 on success, `id + 1` for an invalid entity, and `capacity + 1` for an invalid frustum. The
host converts these to coded range errors. Scratch-first publication and the full-after-failure flag make updates
atomic.

### 1.5 Host bridge and frame loop

Public transform setters validate before writing directly into Wasm-backed arrays. Translation, scale, quaternion,
parent, and visibility setters make no per-entity tick calls. Euler writes call `kernel_sync_rotation`; a multi-axis
`.set` synchronizes once. Quaternion writes normalize without array iteration or `map`, then update Euler lanes in JS.
`Engine.writePoses(ids, poses, count)` (extension surface) is the bulk form of `setPosition` plus `setQuaternion`: it
checks every row (a live slot by the `active` column, values finite as float32, a nonzero quaternion) before writing any,
then writes the same bits, as both go through one `storeQuaternion`. It looks no mesh up, so its callers drop ids of
disposed meshes. `@margoengine/physics` writes its awake root bodies through it, one call a sync.

Each rendered frame:

1. Runs plugin pre-update, resize, and camera update.
2. Copies 24 camera-plane floats into the store.
3. Calls `kernel_tick` once per drawn view, plus the main camera after a multi-view frame where required.
4. Performs a full instance collection after structural, scene, layer, or material changes (every row then counts as
   changed).
5. Otherwise scans one visibility byte per slot against the last frame's: a mesh shown takes its batch's next row, a mesh
   hidden gives its row to the batch's last row (24 floats moved, the moved mesh's slot updated from row float 23); then
   finds sticky changed bytes, clears them and copies only those matrices into their rows. Each changed row sets its bit
   in the batch's `rows` bitset and counts in `dirty`. The batch's `mask` counts its drawn rows that need back faces
   (double-sided or mirrored, read from the row itself), so hiding or unmirroring the last such row puts the batch back on
   the back-culled pipeline (`tests/core-material-setters.test.js`).
6. Uploads each batch's changed rows once (`uploadRows`: one `writeBuffer` for each run of neighbouring set bits, clamped
   to `count`, no sort and no allocation).

There is no per-entity Wasm call during a normal tick and no kernel allocation in tick. Host work still scans one
visibility byte per slot and copies each changed row. A culling flip costs 2 map lookups, 24 floats and 96 uploaded bytes;
at 50,000 boxes with 500 flips a frame that is 1,000 lookups and 48 KB instead of a full collection's 100,000 lookups and
4.8 MB (counted in `tests/core-instance-cache.test.js`, which also proves on 200 random frames of flips and moves that the
uploaded rows equal the instance rows and the drawn set is exact). Row order inside a batch therefore depends on the order
of flips, which changes draw order among one geometry's instances: identical opaque pixels except an exact depth tie. Several
cameras on one scene flip most rows and then cost what a full collection costs. The WebGL2 renderer still uploads
`[0, count * 24)` every frame. The cost of `kernel_sync_rotation` has not been isolated.

`@margoengine/stats/phases` times these steps from outside core: step 3 is its `tick`, steps 4 and 5 are its `cull`,
and it reads the frustum test as part of `tick`, because the test runs inside `kernel_tick`. It wraps `store.tick`,
`createCommandEncoder` and `queue.submit` and adds two frame graph passes, so a change to this frame order must keep
`packages/stats/test/phases.test.js` and `scripts/test-stats-browser.mjs` in step.

`@margoengine/scene` adds no kernel entry and no core bytes. `TransformWriter` (`/bulk`) writes the columns the setters write, from
typed arrays, with validation and column lookups once per call; Euler rows still go through the mesh's own `syncRotation`, so
`kernel_sync_rotation` runs once per row. A bad value or a disposed mesh changes nothing. The scene helpers read the store and
its parents, so a world value is right before any frame. A change to these columns or to the setters must keep the package in
step. Evidence: `packages/scene/tests/bulk.test.js` (bit for bit what the setters give, world matrices included) and
`packages/scene/tests/scene.test.js` (against the Wasm kernel's matrix, mirrors and uneven parents included). Measured,
diagnostic, Node, 10,000 meshes: positions 0.12 ms against 0.59 with setters (perf-history entry 70). Missing: a quiet run, and
the whole frame with thousands of moving meshes.

### 1.6 Kernel evidence and limits

The native and host suites cover:

- TRS, atomic failed updates, culling at plane contact, inactive slots, hierarchy composition, cycle rejection,
  depth, constraints, inherited hiding, exact changed sets, rotation synchronization, layout edges, signed zero, NaN
  payloads, all snapshot groups, and failed-tick recovery.
- An oracle in `tests/core-dirty-transforms.test.js`: incremental results match a fresh full recomputation bit for
  bit, including growth, 1% moving entities, 63-deep chains, removal, reuse, and one million entities.
- Growth preserves every value and replaces views; invalid capacities and failed growth leave state unchanged.
- `setQuaternion` creates no arrays across 1,000 calls.
- Build-time Wasm validation, compression round-trip, 30 KiB raw limit, and the combined core-stage size gate.

Recorded snapshot values: unchanged tick about 3.3 ms at 100,006 entities, 20.2 ms at 499,992, and 41.5 ms at
1,000,012, roughly 41 ns per entity per frame at the largest point. Above 1,048,576 slots was not measured. Initial
capacity is 1,024 and the enforced cap is 8,388,608.

Bit-for-bit claims are scoped. Incremental versus full recomputation is verified on the same Wasm. Cross-machine
kernel equality is expected by design but unverified. JavaScript's approximated `sin`, `cos`, `pow`, `hypot`, and
related functions are not promised to have the same final bits across JS engines.

Known kernel gaps:

- Closed 2026-11-10: `npm run hygiene` fails when `wasm.ts` was not rebuilt from current Rust source (`packages/kernel/wasm.json`, `scripts/wasm-blueprints.mjs`; see 1.1).
- Native Cargo tests do not execute the Wasm SIMD paths; JS tests execute the checked-in Wasm.
- No direct cross-machine kernel-bit test and no focused kernel fuzz target.
- `scripts/kernel-opt-experiment.js` expects the old compression and 70-float/5-flag layout; it must not be treated as
  runnable evidence until updated.
- The native/Wasm half-way turn-reduction rounding difference is untested.
- Growth and one rotation-sync bridge call lack isolated cost measurements.

### 1.7 Physics kernel
