The plain and shared SEA-06 kernels step candidate depth and discharge in solver-owned buffers.
The native corrector checks the state and volume products before publishing. A step that would take
more than 4,096 explicit CFL substeps returns an error before changing the world. The extreme-state
fixtures exercise both memory modes, the Coriolis half-turn limit, overflow rejection and exact replay
through repeated wetting and drying. Water's coastal renderer reads the accepted cells, with the same
dry-to-wet transition tested on WebGPU and WebGL2.
The optional single-period bed model damps the depth-integrated discharge. A separate column
eigenmode solution checks the thin, intermediate and deep cases and exact replay. With the
laboratory inputs fixed, the laminar term improves T20 run-up and leaves other camera bands open.
Shared-memory worker lanes split the native flux sweeps into disjoint lines, and the coordinator
folds boundary fluxes in serial face order. The physical state begins publishing only after each
phase completes. Plain, shared serial and threaded snapshots use the same state layouts. The
ordered sweep count is exposed as a deterministic work receipt.


Rigid axis locks project the angular impulse and held torque before applying the rotated inverse inertia and
then project the resulting velocity. This uses the same available degrees of freedom as the contact solve.
The `bodyMobility` port publishes the corresponding response at frame zero and at coupling ticks. The
rotated-body impulse regression checks every input axis and the surviving off-diagonal angular response.
The field registry reserves accumulator sums at first publication and rebases both retained field mirrors
with solver cells. The focused CPU and Flood browser regressions cover restored frame-zero loads and
equal and opposite accepted water impulses on both renderers.
[David Baraff, Linear-Time Dynamics Using Lagrange Multipliers (1996), §§2–3](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~baraff/papers/sig96.pdf)

`SchoolSolver` (LIFE-04) imports the world's WebAssembly.Memory. Its plain and shared Rust builds put
read-only linker data in slot 4. The host supplies each instance a separate stack and gives the existing
neighbour grid only its bounded world-allocated scratch. The blueprint build checks both variants
and verifies their placement and stack use on a pre-filled arena. Coupling tests exercise two instances, shared fields
after a memory grow, integer-cell coordinate shifts, 24/30/60 fps hashes and snapshot restore.
Analytic checks cover quadratic coasting and turn curvature. A crossing-predator fixture covers anticipation
and regrouping. The original film shots need wiring and review once the locomotion consumers adopt the intent field.

The drawn flock, `GPUFlock` in `@margoengine/vfx/flocking` (LIFE-04, parity bar P14), is not a world solver: it steps
Reynolds's rules for up to 262,144 boids in eight WebGPU compute passes over a spatial-hash grid and draws them in one
instanced draw. Its counting sort ends in a rank pass that lists each bucket by boid index, so the atomic scatter's
order never reaches the step: one GPU and driver give the same state every run, also after snapshot and restore, and
one 16,384-boid step matches the f64 CPU twin within 1e-6 m (`packages/vfx/test/flocking-check.mjs`, Intel Xe2). On the
WebGL2 layer the CPU twin steps the flock and the same instanced draw shows it. Evidence still missing: the rival-speed
comparison (speed phase) and a discrete or AMD GPU run.

The optional `CrushShellSolver` (BREAK-03) places its plain and shared Wasm kernels in the same
arena, with empty static data and a separate stack for each instance. Build-time placement and
prefilled-arena checks cover both variants. A failed force evaluation leaves the published
positions, velocities, material history, reactions and ledger at the previous tick. The world
test exercises analytic gravity, fixed reactions, live bending and plastic replay. Centred
rigid spheres exchange reciprocal contact load through the existing force and impulse
accumulators. Matching the reaction's impulse and its first time moment keeps both rigid
velocity and contact-induced travel consistent with the native sphere prediction. The proof
covers fixed support reactions and moving momentum, energy and replay. Optional Coulomb
friction uses node and rigid point mobility within each native half-kick. Its reciprocal tangential
impulse and angular impulse retain their first time moments. Energy loss is read from snapshot-owned
interval receipts. The fixed-sheet and live free-sheet checks cover slip, spin, energy and replay.
Authored cohesive
seams use two quadrature points and a snapshot-owned maximum-jump history. Their released
edges separate in the real mesh and expose four vertices and area in a versioned aperture
port. SEA-10 integrates the live triangles against the pressure head and carries the water on
the rigid hull. The coupled proof checks water flow and resulting motion across separate
origin cells. Optional Hill-48 yielding uses projected material axes in the native return.
The evidence compares three held-out measured equal-biaxial yields and verifies the native
world response under different triangle bases. Automatic crack paths and simultaneous
contact manifolds remain open.

A second Rust kernel, the own rigid-body solver, is the solver of `@margoengine/physics` since 2026-11-24: Rapier left every 3D package (the `./next` preview became the root entry, and ragdoll, react, game and the umbrella package run on it). Over the world the entry carries its user-level features in TypeScript: the character controller (shape casts: slide, climb, autostep, snap to ground, push), the ray-cast vehicle (a spring and damper per wheel, drive and brake force, friction circle), ropes, `addModel`, followed bodies and debug lines; these use `Math.sin` and `Math.cos` and so are outside the bit-equal replay, which holds for the world itself. Evidence: `packages/physics/tests/next-character.test.js`, `depth.test.js` (vehicle, rope), `physics.test.js`, ragdoll, react and game suites. Missing: Rapier's cone-joint motors in ragdoll (known-bugs KB-PHYS-SWITCH-CONE1), group-free queries (KB-PHYS-SWITCH-GROUPS1), contact-margin shape casts (KB-PHYS-SWITCH-CAST1). It shares the transform kernel's pattern, not its code. Its narrow phase runs once a step, before islands, over pairs with an awake body: manifolds of up to four points live in rows of the world, so a snapshot carries them, and hulls are rows too, held for the world's life. Boxes and hulls go by the separating axis test; anything with a ball or capsule goes by GJK distance and an expanding polytope. Two bodies count as touching, for islands and sleep, when their pair holds points, no longer when their fat boxes overlap. Evidence: both paths against brute force in doubles on random poses, native; Wasm through the replay. Each point keeps a normal impulse, a tangent impulse as a world vector and a friction drift from step to step, by feature id and then by place, in rows of the world, so a snapshot carries them. A clipped face of more than four points reduces to the four of largest area with the deepest always kept; last step's ids and feature win ties, so a resting pile does not swap points on noise. The solver is soft step: per substep, velocities, warm start, 2 biased passes, poses, the friction drift tallied from the speeds the poses moved with, as many relax passes as biased ones, restitution. Within a pair the normal rows of the manifold sweep to convergence each pass and friction takes one sweep; the relax pass solves the normal before friction, so friction's cone is the normal the relaxed contact holds (2026-11-07: a drift tallied inside the relax pass saw speeds the points before it had changed and left a resting block's anchors twisted, creeping 2.1e-6 m in 5 s; one relax pass left the anchors' push in a 14-row pyramid, which rocked; one normal sweep let the first point take a whole strike, so a cube dropped flat spun and slid; evidence `a_block_slides_at_its_rate_from_release`, `a_cube_dropped_flat_lands_flat`, the pyramid and dominance tests, native, Wasm through the replay). A four-point manifold ends each sweep with the exact step along the one impulse pattern that moves no body (its points' shares of one load), which Gauss-Seidel settled only by the leak, about 3 percent a sweep, so soft passes used to run out at 16 sweeps; they now settle in about 4 (2026-11-08, perf-history 80, counted with `--features counts`). A ball's or capsule's gap within a step is read from its core plus its radius along the normal, so a rolling ball's point stays on the floor (2026-11-08: fixed to the ball it rose r (1 - cos a) and the ball ran 0.33 percent fast; evidence `a_ball_rolls_from_rest_at_five_sevenths_of_g_sin_t_on_thirty_degrees`, native, Wasm through the replay), and a strike seen across an open gap notes gravity's gain over the gap (`a_ball_bounces_to_e_squared_at_four_substeps_of_one_pass`). Inside the slop a biased pass closes a point rigidly to the slop's depth, a speculative row of (gap + slop) / h as in Catto's Solver2D soft step, so a loaded point no longer sinks faster than a light one and a cube on a slope below tan t = mu holds from release (2026-11-08, `a_cube_released_on_a_slope_below_tan_t_equal_to_mu_holds_from_its_first_second`, native, Wasm through the replay). One pass a substep does not settle a deep pile at a quarter of the substep rate, so at one pass a contact between two dynamic bodies that neither dominates takes an eighth of the rate (Catto's Solver2D advice to keep the stiffness well below the step rate) while it carries under 50 times the lighter body's weight (`CHAIN_LOAD` in `solver.rs`); the ground, kinematic and dominant bodies and heavier loads keep the quarter, so a 1:1000 stack sags as before. The 20-row pyramid at 4 substeps of one pass sleeps at 2.28 s, 30 rows at 2.03 s; at two passes or more the code path is the old one, bit for bit (2026-11-08, `a_pyramid_settles_at_one_pass_a_substep`, native, and the harness in Node). Before that change: 8 substeps by default, one pass more than the plan and twice its substeps, because 4 substeps and 1 pass let a 20-row pyramid creep 20 cm and throw a 1:100 stack (build record, batch 124). Evidence: every proof native with sleeping on and off; Wasm through the replay. Missing: speed against Rapier, which batch 129 measures.

Joints are one six-axis row class: each axis along or about frame A is locked, limited, driven or free. A substep runs rows, warm start, settling passes, one pushing pass, poses, rows again, a relaxing pass. Locks along a path of joints are solved exactly by a Cholesky factor in doubles, from Householder QR of M^-1/2 J^T joint by joint; a path nothing leans on closes its whole error and relaxes on rows from the new pose, the two stages of RATTLE. Where a branch or a ring ends a path, paths meet by block Gauss-Seidel at a share of 0.2. Only the pushing pass carries a position bias, and the warm start does not remember it: remembering it makes every mode the passes have not settled a triple integrator with the error as its only feedback, which grew an 8 by 8 grid to 1.5 m of gap and 100 m/s (`docs/clean-room.md`, PK24). This is a rule of the step: a row with a rigid position bias keeps its bias out of its memory, or it has a gamma term of its own, as motors and contacts do. Evidence: closed forms for a swung bob and a parallelogram, energy of a double pendulum, a 50-link 1000:1 chain, grids to 30 by 30, native; Wasm through the replay, whose scene now holds joints of every locked kind. Missing: a lock's turning arm is read at the start of a substep, so a light link under a large pull is an explicit spring and a 50-link chain laid level under a 1000:1 end mass stretches 2 times its length by step 60 (`docs/known-bugs.md`; the fix needs the turning read implicitly), exact loops and branches (a 1000:1 load on a grid opens 7 cm), exact limits (one row at a time: twelve hinges on their stops droop 0.91 m), and speed against Rapier.

Rows that depend on each other are the solve's singular case, and four rules cover it (`docs/limits.md`, Own physics joints, gives what each costs). K = J M^-1 J^T is never formed: Householder QR with column pivoting of A = F^T J^T (F F^T = M^-1 per body) gives its Cholesky factor with complete pivoting (Higham 1990, section 5.2), one front of at most 12 rows a joint along the path, with a stop at n u of a row's size, n the path's rows and u f32's epsilon (his test 4.3). Eliminating K joint by joint carried W^T E W into each Schur complement (his Lemma 2.1) with no bound on W, and a 13-row path on 12 freedoms read 4e-7 where rationals give 0 (2026-11-08, `a_path_with_more_locks_than_freedoms_drops_the_row_that_depends`); a reflection rounds each row only by its own length, and that row reads 1e-32. A lock's bias is capped at `joint_max_push` plus what the turning carries its anchors. A pushing pass is cut when a body's turn would rise by more than 0.2 rad times N / M in a substep (Buss and Kim 2005, section 4), on the rise only, as a push that takes back a limit's kick slows its body. Only its position bias is cut: the pass first solves the speeds along a path's locks whole, then the bias on the same factors, capped from the speeds those leave (2026-11-08; one cut solve of both left a limit's kick of 7,500 rad/s in a joint web and handed a neighbour 457,390 rad/s, `a_cut_push_still_takes_back_the_speed_along_the_locks`). Cost: one more forward and back sweep of each path in the pushing pass. A warm start worth more than one push's energy is taken only to the minimum of the dual along it, our own rule. A body past 1e15 stops the world: `world_lost` names it and `KernelWorld.step` throws, as the state may hold no NaN. Before this the replay's own scene reached NaN on 27 of 40 seeds, and that was also the one mismatch between native and Wasm: every differing word of 652,560 bytes at step 174 was a NaN against a NaN of the other sign. Evidence: `kernel/tests/stability.rs`, each rule with a test seen failing without it; the rule counts on `kernel/tests/joints.rs` show the cut and the cap leave every figure there as it was. Missing: the rules are tuned on Windows x86-64 native and Wasm in Node only, and the search has no paper. Evidence for the factor: kernel pivots against exact rational elimination agree to 1e-13 on every path of two web seeds at their fastest steps, native only (a one-off check, not a test); Wasm through the replay. Open: near a toggle a path's row that does not yet depend is answered in full, so web seed 49 reaches 10,991 m/s and a joint 165.8 m open and the 60 webs have no gap bar (`docs/known-bugs.md`); the joint gap of a chain laid out level is held through its first swing only (`a_chain_laid_out_level_holds_its_first_swing_under_a_heavy_end`: 1e-4 of the length at 1000:1, 100:1 and 10:1 to step 160); over 20 s a joint opens 4.2 mm at 1000:1 and 6.1 mm at 1:1 (`docs/known-bugs.md`, KB2161). Evidence for the taut locks' inertia (2026-11-27, `taut_inertia` in `kernel/src/joints.rs`: the pull of a lock across its arm, h^2 F . r, in the inertia the joints' rows turn a body by): that test fails at step 32 without it; `a_chain_laid_out_level_stays_a_chain_as_it_snaps_taut` fails with the pull read before the relaxing pass; the pendulum period and double pendulum energy tests keep their bars (0.003 percent; +0.053 J and -0.074 J of 0.098 J), where the backward Euler form of the same term loses 11.1 J; the replay holds the Wasm build bit-equal to native. Missing: nothing rings a snap's turning down, shares of the term other than all of it come apart at a later snap for a reason not found, and sliding joints, ropes and turning locks carry no such term.

A joint's lever (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/tests/stability.rs`). A joint's linear rows turn about the point on body A where B may stand: the arm on A plus the gap along the axes the joint leaves free, a slider's place on its rail, and never the gap across a locked axis, which is drift. Run to the anchor on B, the relaxing pass's J v = 0 held B at its drift as A turned and gave it w x gap: a box on a spherical joint 4 m out on a kinematic body turning 1.287 rad in a step reached 712.6 m/s against its anchor's 308.9 with one substep. Now spherical, revolute and fixed joints give exactly w r at 1, 8, 32 and 128 substeps, and a slider gives a bead the true r0 w sqrt(cosh 2 w t) (`a_joint_does_not_turn_its_drift_into_speed`). Native builds count the work kinematic bodies do through joint and contact impulses (`solver::DRIVEN`, a joint's position bias left out; none of it is in the Wasm build), and the joint webs may not gain energy past it at any substep count (`a_web_of_joints_gains_no_more_than_its_kinematic_bodies_give_it`): seed 1's knot of two sliders and a spherical joint runs to 1.2 million m/s at 128 substeps on the work of the body that turns, the geometry of a point where two rails cross. The webs' joint gap is measured less what the joint's two bodies travelled in the step, as a flung body leaves the cube within it. Evidence: both tests, the first seen failing on the old lever. Missing: the ledger is loose (a kinematic body's catch is inelastic, and its work counts in full: three times the energy a caught box keeps), so it bounds gross gains only; the snapped-joint figures are the tight check, native and through the replay hashes.

Locks at the end pose (2026-11-28, KB2161, `packages/physics/kernel/src/joints.rs`, clean-room PK68). After the passes the poses move and every path's locks are closed at the pose reached, by Gauss-Newton on the path's Newton matrix J W G^T with G the locks' discrete gradient over the substep and a backtracking line search on the gap; a path with more locks than freedoms takes its rows by threshold partial pivoting (u = 0.1) and drops the dependent ones. The speeds follow the midpoint rule: twice the projection's shift over h, and the loads, a tree's implicit springs included, move the poses by h^2 a / 2. The locked part of that move's turn is taken back at once, before the poses move, by one exact linear step of each exact path on the substep's start rows (`take_back_locked`), and what the locks gave for it is solved at the pose reached on the projection's own matrix and counted as their impulse and shift (`credit_take_back`), so the projection closes only what the free motion and the centres' shift opened: a light bob turned by a torque on its hinge reads within 1e-4 of the closed form at 1, 2 and 8 substeps, where closing the turned-back pose left it 60 % short at 1 substep (KB-PHYS-LOCKTURN1). A taut three-axis lock damps the free motion only where its geometric stiffness passes h^2 k = 4 m, and an island's substep level counts the spin across its locks. All of it lives in the world's block, so a copy of the bytes is still the whole world and islands on threads share nothing: a joint's rows and poses at the substep's start and its line-search step in JOINT_SCRATCH (JOINT_LOCK_START, JOINT_STEP), each body's speeds at the substep's start and what a tree's springs changed of them in columns of their own, and each path's Newton solve in its own slice of NEWTON, a row class sized once a step in `prepare_joints` from the paths' lock rows (`newton_words`, cost in docs/limits.md). The discrete gradient's sinc and (1 - cos) / t^2 past their series come from the turn's quaternion (sin t = 2 s w, 1 - cos t = 2 s^2), as no trigonometry may reach the state. Evidence: the level chain of 50 links under a 1000:1, 100:1 or 10:1 end holds under 1e-4 of its length for 20 s through every snap taut (`a_level_chain_holds_a_heavy_end_through_every_snap`); the bob's period and the double pendulum's energy keep their bars; all 60 web seeds gain 0 J over the kinematic bodies' work within 1800 s each (`a_web_of_joints_stays_in_the_numbers`); a cantilever of implicit springs lands within 0.0008 % of its springs' balance at 8 to 64 links and 4 or 16 substeps. A path of 64 lock rows or more solves its Newton step on the band of its matrix (`newton_banded`, O(n w^2), partial pivoting inside the band on the unit-diagonal scaling, rounding stop at (w + 1) u), the same to the bit as the dense QR on hanging chains of 3 to 40 hinges (`a_long_path_s_banded_step_is_the_whole_matrix_s`). A tree's forward kinematics runs after the locks close, as the midpoint move opens a joint on purpose for the projection to close, and the start speeds the midpoint reads are the ones each rigid coupling holds (`hold_start_couplings`). Each iterate moves each body once by the sum of its joints' moves (`move_path`): 100 and 200 hinged links hold within 1.4e-6 m (`a_long_hinge_chain_holds_its_joints`, KB-PHYS-LONGCHAIN1). The paths of a tree meet at its branch bodies in one exact solve (`group_trees`), and a body's gain in the step's share is summed over every joint that holds it: a 1 g hub between three 15 g arms holds within 1.3e-6 m while it swings (`a_light_hub_between_heavy_arms_holds_its_joints`, KB-RAGDOLL-LIMPDRAW1). A loop (a ring, a grid) is not projected and its passes keep their share of the gap, as before the projection: projected, a 30 by 30 grid ran every iterate of both stages every substep, 58 times slower (KB-PHYS-LOCKGRIDSLOW1); a 12 by 12 grid now takes no projection iterate (`a_grid_s_loops_take_no_projection_iterate_and_a_chain_takes_a_few`, a work count under `--features counts`). Missing: the 100,000:1 chain; a loop's locks closed at the end pose (an exact solve of a loop's rows); and no browser scene measures the snaps yet beyond the replay goldens and the JS suite on the Wasm build.

Substep levels per island (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/tilt.rs`). Each island picks its own level k each step, world substeps times 2^k up to the 7,680 Hz tick of `@margoengine/math/clock`, from its own state alone: the least k at which no body in contact turns more than 2 asin(1 / 4) = 0.5054 rad a substep (the turn at which the relaxing pass could take back more than the push gave, derived from |dW| < |W|), and at which its standing structures get contacts stiff enough not to tip without going over a quarter of the substep rate (`tilt_gains`: a discrete Hardy inequality along each support path, every interface held at half the tipping bound, stiffness from masses and contact shape only). The rest of the world steps as before, to the bit (`tests/locality.rs`). Warm impulses are scaled down when the level goes finer and kept when it goes coarser. This closed KB-PHYS-PILECREEP1, KB-PHYS-BLOCK1 and KB-PHYS-SPINFRICTION1. Evidence: `kernel/tests/solver.rs`, 20- and 30-row piles at both g and the block solver's 30 rows, under 1 mm/s and flat from 30 to 90 s; `spin_energy.rs`, at most 1.000 of the start energy from 20 to 2,000 rad/s at frictions 0.1 to 1; the 50-row pile flat at 8.4e-4 to 9.6e-4 m/s from 15 to 75 s, measured once on the Mac (4 minutes a run, too long for the suite). An interface that needs more turning stiffness than the finest level gives asks for no level, derived: a level raises a patch's rate and not its moment arms, so a point or an edge, with none across it, never gains stiffness from substeps. Nor does a support on a convex curved feature (ball, capsule, cylinder or cone side): it rolls, and its stability is the rocking condition c < rho, in which the springs do not appear; it is classified from the features in contact and is not a patch (`rolls` in tilt.rs; before, a resting ragdoll's hips capsule held its island at level 3 and a joint 4.2 cm open). `adaptiveSubsteps` (default true) switches the levels; false is the fixed stepping of earlier releases, and only then does phase by phase (`islandMajor: false`, deprecated, removed in 2.0.0) give island by island's bits (`kernel/tests/replay.rs`). Cost, measured on the Mac in Wasm, 10,000 steps: the kernel replay scenes 0.4 s with and without levels; the Physics-API replay scene 3.2 s per 1,000 steps without and about 190 s with, as a 1 to 10 cm body the scene's torque impulses spin to 1,000 to 3,000 rad/s touches a 16-body cluster and keeps it at the finest level on about 35 percent of the steps (the level is right; a multirate solve that steps the fast body apart inside its island is a speed-phase item, recorded in docs/limits.md). The replay proof runs that scene's 10,000 steps with fixed substeps and 500 with levels, native, Wasm and browsers alike. Missing: a 100-row pile has not been run, and the speed figures are native Mac only, Wasm through the replay hashes.

A limit is rigid up to its edge and soft past it. Up to the edge its row closes any gap within the substep and no more, and it reads and moves through the Schur complement of the joint's own locks. Past the edge it pushes with the contact's soft constraint, so a limit and a floor that cannot both hold rest instead of trading rigid pushes, and being soft it remembers all it gives. A cone joint is two such rows: the twist about frame X, read as 2 atan2(q.x, q.w) of the swing and twist split (Dobrowolski 2015) with its rate along the bisector of the two X axes, and the first-order distance past an ellipse of the swing's rotation vector, along that ellipse's gradient. Evidence: a thrown rod stops at a cone of 0.5 rad and stays at 0.5000, ellipses of 0.3 and 0.8 hold each limit, a tilted twist stops at 0.3993 of 0.4, a limb a floor holds past its cones sleeps, a link of a hundredth of the mass carries a full one 0.008 rad past its cone, all native, and Wasm through the replay. Missing: the push past an edge scales with the mass the row sees, so a hand of a hundredth of the density rests 0.49 rad past its cone under its arm.

What a pair may do is settled in the narrow phase, the only place that looks at it each step: a pair of a disabled body or collider, groups that do not meet, a joint or a refusing filter has no contact; a sensor pair or one whose solver groups do not meet only finds out whether it overlaps, and takes no part in islands; every other pair gets its manifold. A step's last act compares what each active pair found with what it remembers and lists the changes, two words an event, for the entry to read and clear; a pair of sleepers, which no step looks at, keeps what it had. Dominance is a bit on the pair for the step, read where a pair's two bodies are fetched, and only between dynamic bodies, so it costs a solve nothing when unused. The contact filter is the kernel's one import, called only when set. Evidence: `packages/physics/kernel/tests/events.rs`, `packages/physics/tests/next-events.test.js`, each behaviour in `packages/physics/README.md`, native and through the entry; Wasm through the replay, whose scene holds sensors, groups, a filter, dominance and a disabled body. Missing: a sensor reads the pose a step starts from, so it reports up to a step late.

Four more header words (2026-11-24): the share of each joint impulse carried between steps, one world cap on linear speed, and a frequency and damping ratio for contacts with a body that does not move (held under a quarter of the substep rate like every contact); `next-world-settings.test.js`. Sleep reads the pose as well as the velocity (2026-11-24, KB-PHYS-SLEEP-PUSH1): the soft solver closes a joint's or a contact's error by moving the pose and leaves no velocity, so `begin_step` resets a dynamic body's sleep timer when the pose it moved through in the last step has kinetic energy per unit of mass above the body's sleep threshold, and a body asked to sleep is ready at once (`ASKED_TO_SLEEP`). A joint also has a `JOINT_DISABLED` flag (`joint.enabled = false`) that takes it out of the solve like a broken one, and `joint.force` and `joint.torque` read the impulses its rows carried over the last substep. Evidence: `next-sleep-pushed.test.js`, `next-joint-api.test.js`; the replay hashes on file were regenerated, since a body no longer sleeps early in the 10,000-step scenes.
Dynamics beyond the contact solver (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/README.md`, the parity table). Solver settings (contact stiffness and damping, maximum push, allowed penetration, joint shares, a contact warm start share) are header words with a checked setter, and part of a snapshot. Speed caps cut a dynamic body's twist twice a substep, before the poses move and after the relaxing passes. A joint breaks when the impulse its linear or angular rows carried over the last substep, over that substep's length, passes its limit; it then solves nothing and its bodies may collide. A cone's rotation motor is three motor rows along the target frame's axes, solved before the limits in the same pass, with its target in columns of its own. A multibody is a tree whose joints are the ordinary joints plus a velocity projection onto the joint space after each substep's solves (the normal equations H qd = J^T M v of Featherstone's joint-space inertia matrix, solved over the tree by articulated-body inertias in O(links) with 6 by 6 matrices kept in the scratch rows of each link's joint, so a tree has no size cap; a 200 link chain holds its length to 1 mm and replays bit for bit) and a forward-kinematics pass that puts a link back where its parent and joint place it once it is more than 1 mm or 1 mrad away, with the position correction fed back as a speed as in SHAKE with RATTLE. Evidence: a double pendulum at 8 substeps stays within the same 0.077 J of its energy as plain joints over 8 s and keeps its joints within 0.25 mm; a tree with 1000 kg ends that plain joints throw 42 m apart holds within 0.9 mm; hinge limits hold to 1e-7; a single pendulum matches the exact solution of the physical pendulum to 4 decimals at 1 s; Rapier's multibody pendulums agree within 5 cm over a second (`next-multibody-oracle.test.js`). Measured while building it: applying the position correction every substep without the deadband lost 0.5 percent of the energy a second, first order in the substep, because the velocity projection after a chord step removes a share (omega h)^2 / 4 of the kinetic energy each time; the deadband leaves that to the rows, which keep the energy. A motor joint (2026-11-26, `JOINT_MODE` column, `cap_motor_vectors` in `joints.rs`) cuts the sliding and turning motors' impulses back to their caps as vectors after the per-axis rows; an island's substeps are the world's plus the most its bodies ask (`EXTRA_SUBSTEPS`, the scratch `ISLAND_SUBSTEPS`, and the state `SUBSTEP_EXTRA` beside `SUBSTEP_LEVEL` for warm starts and break loads). Evidence: `tests/motor-joint.test.js` and `tests/additional-substeps.test.js` (an island with extra substeps equal bit for bit to a world at that count, adaptive levels on and off); worlds with neither step bit for bit as before (the same scene of a multibody chain, a stack and a joint after 400 steps), and the replay fixture's state lists moved only by the new zero columns. A joint's armature (2026-11-26, `JOINT_ARMATURE_*` and the scratch `JOINT_ROTOR_*` columns) adds its rotor inertia to the projection's joint block, D = S^T A S + a, and the rotor's momentum a times the speed it had when the step began to the right side, the cost 1/2 a (qd - rotor)^2 (Featherstone 2008, section 9.7); the speeds are read before the step lands its impulses and carried on by each projection. Evidence: a pendulum with a rotor as heavy as its bob swings at the period sqrt((I + a) / (m g L)) gives to 0.03 percent, a held torque and an impulse turn a hinge at tau / (I + a) to 1e-4, and a damped hinge loses what the augmented mass predicts to 0.1 percent (`tests/multibody-armature.test.js`). Worlds with no armature step bit for bit as before: every body's pose and speed in a scene of a multibody chain with a limit, damping and a ball link, a stack and a plain joint equal the old build's after 400 steps; the replay fixture's `kernel` and `kernelSweeps` state lists moved only by the six zero armature columns of their joints, and the `physics` lists, with no joints, are unchanged. Missing: speed, and joints with two free turning axes keep their rotation whole in the pose pass.

World parameters and readings (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/README.md`, `docs/rapier-parity.md` rows P-07, P-15 to P-33, V-01 to V-04). The kernel's imports are the contact filter, the contact modifier and a clock (`env.clock`, milliseconds, read at the phase boundaries of a step: begin, broad phase, narrow phase, islands, solver, CCD, events). The readings sit in the `World` struct, outside the arena, so a snapshot and `world_hash` never see a wall-clock value and the replay stays bit for bit; evidence `next-parameters.test.js` "the phases of a step are timed, add up to the step, and stay out of the hash". `max_ccd_substeps` is a header word (default 1) that gates the one CCD pass, so 0 turns CCD off for the world and any other value runs it; the pass resolves a body's whole sweep, so more passes find nothing more (evidence: 1,000 bullets at 300 m/s, none through a thin wall by default, some through at 0). The length unit is not a kernel word: it scales four tolerances of the solver and the sleep speed in the entry, and a world in centimetres plays out as the metre one to 1e-4 of a unit (the kernel's own constants, such as the CCD touch distance and the hull skin, stay in metres). The ray-cast vehicle (TypeScript over `raycast` and body impulses) was held to Rapier's controller on the same car for the first time: its four wheels each cancelled the whole sideways slide from the same chassis speed, so a parked car rocked and drove at 58 percent of its engine force, and its grip pushed at the ground and rolled a grippy car over in a bend; the wheels now share a slide and take a roll influence (0.1), after which ride height, spring lengths, speed after 3 s and the line of a bend agree with Rapier's to a few percent (`next-vehicle.test.js`). Missing: Rapier's finer solver and CCD timers, a separate static contact softness, joint warm-start switch, friction model choice, contact clustering and recycling (rows P-18, P-20, P-26 to P-29).

CCD and fast turning (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/tests/ccd.rs`). The CCD pass swept a body's turn as the angle between its poses at the ends of a step, a rotation vector of at most pi, so a body that turned 29 rad a step was swept as turning under 3, and one that turned exactly a circle as not turning (CCD did not even check it). Every substep's turn is now added into a body column, `TURNED` (written by `integrate_poses`, zero at the step's start), and the sweep takes the angle between the poses plus whole circles until it is the nearest to that sum; whole circles end at the same pose, so the sweep still ends where the step did. Evidence: `a_bar_turning_whole_circles_a_step_is_checked_by_ccd` (fails with the old sweep), and the 1,000 spinning bullets of `a_thousand_bullets_at_300_m_s_never_pass_a_thin_wall`, whose capsule number 180 leaves its first strike of a height field turning 1,750 rad/s (29 rad a step) and went through it in the second step once the solver's rows followed the turn (the next commit). Missing: the sweep still turns about one axis at a constant rate between the poses, as Mirtich's conservative advancement does; a body whose axis changes within the step is swept along the straight turn, not its own path.

Contact rows of a turning body (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/tests/spin_energy.rs`). A step's contact rows are made once from the pose it began with, and the world inverse inertia and the effective masses with them; a body that turns 6.7 rad a step (400 rad/s) was then solved with an inertia it no longer had. An impulse P at an arm r changes the angular velocity by W (r x P) with W the world inverse inertia, and the energy by P times the mean speed of the point only when W is the body's own: with the first pose's W the projection stops being dissipative. A 2 x 0.04 x 0.04 m bar (3.2 kg) turning in place with its tips through a wall 2 cm thick held 3.2 times its energy at 400 rad/s and 3.4 times at 2,000 with friction 0.5. After each substep's poses `refresh_turned_contacts` redoes `solver_mass` and the effective masses of the pairs of every body that has turned more than `STALE_TURN` (1e-3 rad) since the step began, with the arms as they were (Catto's Solver2D soft step holds anchors fixed across substeps; refreshing the arms as well took the 100 rad/s case from 1.0 to 1.64 times). Below a milliradian the inertia is off by under a part in a thousand and the rows are left as they were: refreshed at every grain of rounding, the 465-cube pile of `a_pyramid_of_thirty_rows_settles_at_one_pass_a_substep` crept at 4 mm/s (0.6 before, and 1.1 at 26 and 28 rows with no refresh at all: that test and the joint web of `a_path_with_more_locks_than_freedoms_drops_the_row_that_depends`, whose seed 1 opened a joint 72 m, are at the edge of chaos), so a body turning that slowly keeps its old bits. Result: 1.0 at 20, 100, 400 and 2,000 rad/s without friction and at 20, 100 and 2,000 with it, 1.031 at 400 with it (open: KB-PHYS-SPINFRICTION1, the relaxing pass gives back friction at a higher slide speed than the pushing pass took it at). Sources: Catto, "Solver2D", 2024 (box2d.org, soft step, relaxing and restitution); Macklin, Storey, Lu, Terdiman, Chentanez, Jeschke and Muller, "Small Steps in Physics Simulation", SCA 2019 (the substep and the relax); Box2D v3 and Rapier cap the angular speed per substep instead (Rapier's `allow_fast_rotation`), which loses spin. The two papers' text was not read in full this time; the energy argument above is the reasoning the change rests on.

Restitution from the pre-solve approach (2026-11-27, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `note_approach`, test `packages/physics/tests/rigid-validation.test.js`). A strike used to note its approach speed inside the pushing pass, after the pairs solved before it had pushed its bodies; a push one pair gave a ball was then the next pair's approach, and both bounced it: three balls 2 mm apart struck at 1 m/s left at -0.5, 0.5 and 1, with 1.5 times the energy (five balls, 4 times). Every point of a pair with restitution now notes its normal speed before the warm start, Müller et al.'s pre-solve v_n, and a strike bounces from that; pairs with no restitution are skipped, so a scene without bounce does the same work and gives the same bits. Result: a five-ball cradle spaced 2 mm, 5 mm or 2 cm passes the strike on exactly (the last ball leaves at 1 m/s, the rest stop, within 1e-3); a touching cradle still shares the strike out in one solve (docs/limits.md), with momentum kept and no energy made. Evidence: `a_strike_passes_down_a_spaced_row_of_balls_and_makes_no_energy` (native, `kernel/tests/solver.rs`) and the cradle test in Node through the Wasm kernel; the bounce tests `a_ball_bounces_to_e_squared_*` pass unchanged. Missing: a browser run.

Strikes one pair at a time (2026-11-27, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `collide_pairwise`, called by `run_substeps` before `note_approach`; test `packages/physics/tests/rigid-validation.test.js`). Solved with the contacts, a strike into a line of touching balls was shared along it: five touching balls left at about -0.19, 0.28, 0.30, 0.30 and 0.30. Each substep a point of a bouncy pair that carried no load, approaches faster than two substeps of gravity and touches or will within the substep now takes -(1 + e) v_n m_n, sweep after sweep until none approaches, before the contact solve (Guendelman, Bridson and Fedkiw 2003, section 6); a point still apart takes part only when one of its bodies touches a third (within the slop) through another bouncy pair or was moved by a strike of the pass, so a lone strike keeps the speculative row and its exact bounce. Each impulse takes energy out for e up to 1. Result: one or two balls struck into a touching cradle send as many off, at four strike phases and both tiers; towers of ten boxes at restitution 0, 0.5 and 1 stand and sleep. A loaded point is a resting one: the first build without that test let a tower at e = 1 rock down at the high tier. Cost: none for a scene with no restitution (one scan of the window's pairs); with one, a scan of the pairs a substep and, on a strike, up to one sweep a pair, each with an O(pairs) touching test. Missing: a browser run; a work count for the sweeps.

Held strikes, time of impact and the hung cradle (2026-11-28, `kernel/src/joints.rs` `held_response` and `apply_held`, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `collide_pairwise`, `solve_impacts`, `shift_poses`, `end_strikes`, `kernel/src/layout.rs` PAIR_STRIKE_LATER; tests: the three hung cradle tests in `packages/physics/tests/rigid-validation.test.js`, KB-PHYS-HUNGCRADLE1). A hung, touching cradle lost about 1 percent a strike and swung as one within 15 s. Four causes, all in the strike: a jointed body took the strike with its free mass, so its joints took the difference back inelastically; a strike across a gap was applied at the substep's start, so the striker stopped short and later pushed the line below any strike; any load at all on a point read as rest, and the micro-loads joint drift leaves between hung balls made the end pair a resting one; and a strike the pass saw end its substep short met the line in the contact solve's speculative row and relaxing pass, which shared it. Now a point of a body with a locking joint is struck with the response its joints give (the operational-space inverse inertia of Khatib 1987, Featherstone 2008 chapter 11; read as the difference of two exact path solves, with and without a probe impulse, over every joint path that holds the bodies, capped at 32 bodies and 16 paths, past which the free mass is used as before); its friction rubs through the same response; a strike across a gap moves each body it changed back by its time of impact once the substep has moved the poses (Mirtich and Canny 1995); a load is rest only when held for the step it would take out the strike; and a line strike that does not close this substep is kept open in both contact passes for the pass to make in the next. Result: a five-ball hung cradle at e = 1, friction 0, swings one in, one out for 60 s at both tiers (middle balls within 0.03 degrees), the end ball's turning height 99.85 percent of the release at `high` and 97.7 percent at `standard` after 60 s; the rest is second order, about g h^2 / l a strike (0.019, 0.0048 and 0.0012 percent at 8, 16 and 32 substeps), symplectic Euler's modified energy handed between balls. At e = 0.995 the first strike gives ((1 + e) / 2)^8 of the height to 3e-5; at friction 0.1 the end ball leaves at (1 - mu r / l)^4 of its speed, the rigid Coulomb answer to 0.15 percent at `standard` and 0.01 percent at `high`. Cost: none without joints or restitution; a held strike costs two path solves of up to eight sweeps over the paths that hold it, and a rub two more. Missing: a browser run; a strike on a reduced-coordinate multibody still takes its free mass; the second-order loss would need a collision step that keeps the discrete energy (Fetecau, Marsden, Ortiz and West 2003).

Friction that converges in a pair (2026-11-28, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `friction_rows`; test `kernel/tests/solver.rs` `a_plate_held_near_its_friction_rides_a_deck_pitching_far_from_it`, KB-PHYS-CONECUT1). In the relaxing pass, which decides the cuts, a pair's friction rows sweep its points until no impulse moves by more than rounding, as its normal rows do (projected Gauss-Seidel, Erleben 2013), and a point's anchor is cut to its cone only from the last sweep's answer; the pushing pass keeps one sweep, since swept to the end its anchors' pull did work no relaxing pass took back (a joint web gained 2e-3 of its drivers' work against the 1e-6 `a_web_of_joints_stays_in_the_numbers` allows). From one sweep the points' shares were uneven, a point reached its own cone while the patch held 30 percent inside its own, and its anchor was cut alone; anchors cut one point at a time no longer agreed with a rigid move, so the points pushed against each other at their cones and a plate 60 m from a pitching deck's axis slid 2.2 mm in 36 s at 1.3 times its friction demand. It holds within 0.03 mm now, and the storm deck's held plate moves 0.88 to 0.97 mm at every factor from 1.29 to 1.4, where it moved 1.5 to 3.9 mm. Several pairs on one body (a chair's legs) saturated one pair at a time until KB-PHYS-MULTIPAIRCREEP1 (next paragraph).

Friction patches across colliders (2026-11-28, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `group_patches`, `patch_friction`, `fit_patch_anchors`; tests `kernel/tests/solver.rs` `a_plate_cut_into_four_colliders_rides_the_storm_deck_as_one_collider_does`, `a_chair_rides_the_storm_deck_as_a_plate_does`, `a_chair_rests_on_a_floor_tilted_near_its_friction`, `kernel/tests/compound.rs` `compound_boxes_stack`, KB-PHYS-MULTIPAIRCREEP1). Once a step, from the canonical lists (so the same at any thread count), the listed pairs between the same two bodies whose normals agree to 1e-6 and whose surfaces move alike are linked into a patch, a ring in solve order inside one island; only islands with a body of several colliders or a part pair are sorted. In the relaxing pass the patch's last pair sweeps every point of the patch until it settles or 16 sweeps; the anchors are cut point by point from the last sweep and then all take the patch's shift, the mean of its anchors weighted by normal impulse, which never reaches past the anchors it is taken of; the same mean is taken when the patch is made, so a point new this step takes the patch's anchor. A shift and a turn fitted by least squares was tried and grew without bound in a stack of three two-box bodies (its turn extrapolated to lightly loaded points). The pushing pass and bodies of one collider are unchanged. Evidence: on the storm deck at 1.3 times the demand a plate of one, two and four colliders moves 0.85, 0.92 and 0.86 mm (two and four were 4.7 and 11.8 mm) and the chair 1.3 mm (2.9 cm); the chair on a floor tilted to tan 0.47 against friction 0.72 stays within 0.03 mm. Evidence missing: the joint sweep reaches 16 sweeps on nearly every patch (rigid patches have redundant rows), measured harmless here but not proven in general; the patch's anchors hold no twist of their own; a patch is per body pair, so a body resting across two others is two patches.

Strike pieces (2026-11-28, `kernel/src/strike.rs`, `narrow.rs` `refresh_pair`, `solver.rs` `prepare_rows`; tests `kernel/tests/strike.rs`, `kernel/tests/threads.rs`, KB-PHYS-CCDKNOCK1). Contacts are found once a step, so a body that turns more than a radian a substep meets corners no manifold holds, and more substeps cannot find them: a spinning steel bar striking a free plate at 300 m/s was knocked 44, 25, 11 and 18 m/s at 8 to 64 substeps where a fine step gives 63. Finding points again between substeps was measured worse (0.7 m/s at 8 substeps), as the strike is five impacts within 3 ms. Now an island with a dynamic CCD body advances conservatively: each piece is the least gap of its CCD pairs, at least 2 percent of the thinnest CCD piece, over the fastest they close (normal speed plus spin across the normal times reach; a ball about its centre and a revolved shape about its axis do not count), and from the first cut every piece finds the island's pairs again and remakes their rows, carried impulses scaled down to a shorter piece and kept whole going longer, as between levels. Up to 512 pieces an island a step. Evidence: four bars of the next-ccd scene within 5 percent of the fine step at 8 substeps, bullet 64 within 2 percent at 16 to 64; a rolling CCD cylinder bit for bit as one without CCD; the threads test with two struck plates the same bits on 1 to 8 threads; islands that do not cut run the old code path, so the replay hashes hold. Evidence missing: islands with joints, couplings, multibodies, kinematic bodies or mesh, compound, filtered or modified pairs take no pieces (KB-PHYS-CCDKNOCK2); the cost of the pieces on the 1,000-bullet scene is not measured (speed phase).

A resting depth continuous in the load (2026-11-28, `kernel/src/solver.rs` `normal_rows`; tests `kernel/tests/solver.rs` `a_resting_depth_is_continuous_in_the_load_inside_and_past_the_slop` and `packages/physics/tests/next-parameters.test.js`, KB-PHYS-RESTDEPTH1). Inside the slop a point is closed by a rigid speculative row, past it by the soft spring, whose rest under a weight is g / omega^2 past the slop (Catto, "Soft Constraints", GDC 2011; Catto, "Solver2D", 2024). The rigid row closes a point to the slop to within the gap's float32 rounding; closed a rounding short, it stayed in the rigid row with no give, so a 5 cm ball rested 6.9e-5 m higher at g 9.80665 than at 9.81. A point within two units of the last place of the gap's largest coordinate of the slop now counts as closed and is the spring's, and the ball rests within 1e-7 m of slop + g / omega^2 for g from 2 to 20, from above, inside and past the slop. Evidence missing: far from the origin the rounding band grows with the coordinates (64 micrometres at 270 m), KB-PHYS-POSEROUND1.

A pair tallies the normal impulse of a whole step: what each point holds after the relaxing pass is all it gave in that substep, its warm start included, and a bounce adds its own. `contactforce` reads the tally from the solve list, so it costs a listener only. Evidence: a resting stack reads its weights to 1e-5, the impulses of a landing add up to m g t to 1e-5, native; Wasm through the replay.

A rope and a spring are joints with no lock: their first axis is the line between the anchors, and what it reads is their distance. A rope is a limit on that row and a spring a motor in the force model, so both use the rows above and neither joins a path. Evidence: a slack rope lets a weight fall as free fall, a taut one swings with the elliptic period to 0.01 percent at 60 degrees and stretches 0.00007 m at the jolt; a spring keeps its period to 0.003 percent and the decay of implicit Euler to 0.2 percent, and settles at its static stretch to 1e-5 m, native; Wasm through the replay, whose scene holds both. Missing: a rope is one row at a time, so two ropes under a 1000:1 end mass rest 35 mm long; `Rope` on the own solver (batch 128) is spherical joints on a path, which do not have this limit.

A convex hull from points is built in the entry's TypeScript, on the add path, by Quickhull with fat planes, then merged into the large faces the clipper needs; the kernel only checks and stores it. A face holds up to 256 edges, so the clipper's buffers are left unwritten until used, rather than cleared on every face contact. The kernel refuses two neighbouring faces as one plane split in two only when they meet under 0.8 degrees and every corner of each lies within half of FLAT of the other's plane, as an angle alone refused real creases of random clouds. Evidence: 85 point sets hold every point within 2.0e-5 of their size and the kernel takes each, and a 256-sided cylinder stands on its cap, in Node; the replay holds four hull bodies bit-equal across Node, Chromium and Firefox. Missing: build cost against Rapier (batch 129).

A body's kind can change between steps. Two fixed bodies have no pair, so a body that stops being fixed walks the sorted ends once for the fixed colliders its boxes overlap, and one that becomes fixed drops its pairs with fixed bodies, which ends their touches; the body wakes and is listed again. A body's own solid (mass at a point, principal moments along a frame of its own) joins its colliders by the parallel axis theorem, and with no collider mass it is the body's figures exactly. An island may ask for extra solver passes: a substep runs `iterations` plus the most any awake island asks for, and a pair or joint path joins a pass only when its island's extra reaches it, so each island runs the last `iterations + e` passes and the pushing pass stays the last for all; `tests/next-bodies.test.js` holds such an island bit-equal to a world of that many passes and the others bit-equal to the plain world (LIM-433). With no island asking, the passes take no lookup.

A spherical motor is three motor rows, one a frame axis, on the rotation vector left between the joint's frame on body A and body B. Its target is that frame, moved onto the rotation asked for, so what is measured stays small and tells rotations apart near half a turn. The rows read the free body and not the Schur complement a limit uses: a motor is soft, the passes converge on its own fixed point, and a ball rod lands within 0.0006 rad of the implicit Euler closed form at every step measured. Tan, Liu and Turk 2011 is the same stable step in generalized coordinates; here it comes from the implicit form of the row (`docs/clean-room.md`, PK24). Evidence: critically damped closed form to 0.0006 rad, a slanted target to 1e-6 rad in a second, a target near half a turn, a spinning target, a cap of 12 N m holds 9.81 N m and 7 N m does not, all native or through the entry; Wasm through the replay.

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/physics/kernel/Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` | Rust crate `margoengine-physics-kernel`, no dependencies, `cdylib` and `rlib`, the same release profile as section 1.1. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/layout.rs` | The column table. `packages/physics/scripts/build-kernel.mjs` parses it, so JS and Rust read one list. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/world.rs` | The world: header and columns in one block, addressed by offset. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs` | The step: impulses once, then per substep the velocity update and the pose update. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/math.rs` | Scalar, vector and quaternion maths, correctly rounded on both targets. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/mass.rs` | Mass, centre and inertia of a body from its colliders; principal axes by Jacobi rotations. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/broad.rs` | Sweep and prune over fat boxes, the pair rows and their table. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/island.rs` | The awake and active-pair lists, union-find islands, sleep timers and sleeping rings. |
| `packages/physics/kernel/src/joints.rs` | Joint rows, paths of joints solved exactly, motors and limits. |
| `packages/physics/src/wasm.ts` | Generated: raw-deflate blueprint, source hash, column table. |
| `packages/physics/src/kernel.ts` | `KernelWorld`: instantiate, bind views, grow, snapshot, restore. |
| `packages/physics/src/physics.ts`, `body.ts`, `collider.ts`, `joints.ts` | `Physics`, `PhysicsBody`, `PhysicsCollider` and `PhysicsJoint` on the kernel. |
| `packages/physics/src/character.ts`, `vehicle.ts`, `rope.ts`, `debug.ts` | The character controller, the vehicle, the rope and the debug lines, written over the world's queries and impulses. |
| `packages/physics/src/mesh-fit.ts` | Reading a mesh for physics, shared by both entries. |

`npm run build:physics-kernel` rebuilds it (cargo, wasm-opt -O3, deflate); `npm run modern:build` does too. `npm run build:packages` uses the committed blueprint. `npm run test:physics-kernel` runs the native tests.

The 2D kernel (batch 127) is its own crate, `packages/physics2d/kernel`, under the same determinism rule (rotation as a cos and sin pair, no trigonometry on the step path). It holds so far shapes (`shape.rs`: circle, capsule, segment, polygon of up to 8 corners by gift wrapping, each a core and a radius), exact mass of rounded shapes (`mass.rs`) and contact manifolds of up to two points (`manifold.rs`: separating axis and reference face clipping when cores overlap, the exact core distance when apart). It also holds the world (`world.rs`: static, kinematic and dynamic bodies, positions moved in doubles and contacts worked out relative to a pair's first body, so a pile 10 km out steps as one at the origin; islands that wake and sleep as one) and the contact solver (`solver.rs`, over its own compact 32-byte bodies, each half loaded whole and transposed into lanes: the soft step at 4 substeps of one biased and one relaxing pass, the two-point block solve with a row-by-row fall-back, the 3D kernel's chain rule for unloaded dynamic pairs at one pass). Sweep and prune, a dynamic box tree with pairs kept from step to step (`tree.rs`, the 2D default: on the 100-row pyramid 15,133 box tests a step where the sweep made 497,402, the bodies bit for bit the same), islands and sleep timers live in `packages/physics/kernel-common`, a crate generic over the dimension that the 2D kernel uses first; the 3D kernel moves onto it in its own job with a replay bit-equality proof. `check:rust-kernels` runs a kernel when a package its crate reaches by a path dependency changes, so a kernel-common change runs the 2D suite. `npm run test:physics2d-kernel` runs its native tests. Its Wasm build (wasm32 with simd128, no_std, the size-class heap of `kernel-common/src/heap.rs` as its allocator) is built by `check:rust-kernels`, and `kernel/wasm-check` steps the pinned-bits scenes of `tests/bits.rs` (the 100-row pyramid, the joint grid, the mixed scene, 120 steps) inside that build in Node: the four-lane simd128 solve gives the native hashes bit for bit (2026-11-08). `node scripts/physics2d-kernel-browsers.mjs` loads the same module into a page drawing with WebGPU and one drawing with the WebGL2 fallback (Edge 157 both ways, Firefox 157 on WebGL2; Playwright's Firefox has no WebGPU) and gets the native hashes in each, then times the 100-row pyramid against Rapier 2D's Wasm in the page (perf history entry 88), and against Box2D v3's Wasm when `BOX2D_WASM` names a build of it made outside the repository (entry 89); `npm run test:physics2d-kernel-browsers`, a GPU suite check:merge runs, is its bits part in the default browser. Before that the crate built natively only (an f64 square root no_std lacks, no allocator) and no check built it for Wasm. There are no Wasm exports or browser run yet; the other evidence is native: the 20-row pyramid's top drops 28.26 mm and the pile sleeps at 0.73 s, against Box2D v3's 29.11 mm and 1.02 s and Rapier 2D's 29.56 mm and 0.92 s on the same scene (LIM-527). Polylines are chains of segment shapes with ghost vertices (`smooth.rs`, `World::create_chain`): a box and a ball slide across 50 joins at 5 m/s keeping vx within 1e-4, as Box2D v3's chain does and Rapier 2D's polyline does not (LIM-529). Joints (`joint.rs`: revolute, prismatic, fixed, rope, spring, with limits and motors) solve their locks exactly along paths (Baraff 1996, block elimination of the block tridiagonal K) and one joint at a time at branches and rings, and stiffen each body's turning by its taut joints' pull (geometric stiffness, Andrews, Teichmann and Kry 2017): a 50-link chain under a 1000:1 end mass stretches 0.55 percent where Box2D v3 and Rapier 2D fly to 30 and 22 times its length, and the 30 by 30 grid holds within 3.96 mm (LIM-534). The solver visits the contacts colour by colour (`kernel-common/src/colour.rs`, greedy first fit in 16 colours, no two contacts of a colour writing one body), coloured from the top of the scene down along gravity, so a pile rests the same whatever order it was built in (the 20-row pyramid built top down drops 28.35 mm, where it dropped 29.41 mm before). The colours are solved four contacts at a time in SIMD lanes (`kernel-common/src/lanes.rs`, Wasm simd128 and SSE2 with only exact IEEE operations; `solver/wide.rs`), every bit as one at a time (`Settings::contact_lanes` off, native only); two blocks of a colour are visited together so their chains overlap (perf history entry 90), and a step that covers every live lane writes without the selects that keep the others, each point's gap is worked out once after the poses move, and the contacts are read through the colouring's order instead of copied into it (entry 91). Two four-cornered polygons collide down a lane path (`manifold.rs`: placing, both best faces, `closest`'s 32 distances and the incident face four lanes at a time, with `pmin` and `pmax`, defined as the compare and select they replace), every bit as the scalar code kept in `tests/support/manifold_ref.rs` over 11.4 million compared manifolds (`tests/manifold_exact.rs`). In the browser the 100-row pyramid steps in 2.9 to 3.2 ms in Margo's Wasm against Box2D v3's Wasm 1.4 and Rapier 2D's 7.6 to 8.1 (entry 91); in Wasm the solver takes 1.9 ms of it (setup 0.58, passes 1.17) and the narrow phase 0.80 (open in known-bugs). Natively, like for like at four lanes, Box2D v3 steps it in 1.24 ms (its default eight AVX2 lanes 0.98) and Margo in 2.87 (entry 91; physics-refs `native/scripts/native-build-sse2.bat`). Evidence missing: a quiet-machine run of those numbers. Its top drops 684 mm by 10 s against the references' 726 to 735: a pair keeps last step's reference face while the two faces' separations lie within one slop, and a clipped point keeps its end's id, so resting points keep their warm start (before, 1,100 to 1,800 points a step restarted from zero and the top fell 906 mm; `Counts::cold_points` counts them, at most 8 a step after 1 s now). Missing: queries, events and filters, the Wasm layout.

Since 2026-11-24 `@margoengine/physics2d` runs on this kernel and no longer on Rapier 2D. The crate has a C interface (`kernel/src/api.rs`: handles and one shared word buffer, errors as negative returns) built as a committed Wasm blueprint (`packages/physics2d/src/physics2d-kernel.wasm`, 407 kB raw, `node scripts/wasm-blueprints.mjs --rebuild --only=physics2d-kernel`) that `packages/physics2d/scripts/build.js` copies to `dist/physics2d.wasm`; `Physics2D.load()` checks it against the interface version and a hash of its exports and imports before any call reaches it. The world gained collision groups, solver groups, active collision types, sensors, collision and contact force events (`tests/events.rs`), scene queries (`query.rs`, `tests/queries.rs`), removal of shapes, bodies and joints with slot reuse (`tests/lifecycle.rs`), body controls and dominance (`tests/bodies.rs`), continuous collision against fixed and kinematic shapes (`ccd.rs`, `tests/ccd.rs`) and convex decomposition of concave outlines (`decompose.rs`, `tests/decompose.rs`). The character controller is TypeScript over the kernel's shape cast (`packages/physics2d/src/character.ts`). Evidence still missing: physics hooks, locked translation axes, additional mass, CCD between dynamic bodies, triangle, heightfield, halfspace, compound, voxel and one-sided polyline shapes, generic joints, multibody joints, snapshots and debug render data (the rows are in `docs/rapier-parity.md`, T-03 to T-15).

Memory contract: one Wasm instance per world, from `__heap_base`. Every column holds 4-byte rows and starts on 16 bytes; a row keeps its index for life. Growth moves each column up to its larger place, last column first, in the same block, so offsets stay relative, no second copy is needed, and a copy of the block is a whole world. A step can grow the world, as new pairs need rows; `world_layout` counts layouts and JS binds its views again when it moves. Growth changes no later result, since nothing iterates a column by capacity.

Row classes: body, collider, endpoint (two a collider), pair, table, and body list. A body list column is indexed by place in a list, not by body, so freeing a body row leaves it alone; putting a list in the body class zeroed a list slot on every reused row, and the churn test in `tests/sleep.rs` caught it.

Determinism contract: same inputs, same call order and same kernel build give bit-equal state on every machine, browser and Node. Wasm floats round to nearest, ties to even, and only NaN payloads may differ, so the state may hold no NaN. The kernel uses `+ - * /`, `sqrt`, compares and integers; no trigonometry, no fused or relaxed operations.

Step contract: `world_step(dt)` lands impulses once, before the first substep; forces stay in their columns and reach every substep, until the caller clears them. Each substep is semi-implicit Euler (velocity, then pose with the new velocity), so a body's reported velocity is the one that moved it. The gyroscopic term is one implicit-midpoint step in the principal frame, two Newton steps, and may not raise the energy. Rotation uses the exact exponential from a series, with no trigonometry. The contact and joint passes will go between the two halves of a substep.

Broad phase contract: after impulses land and before the first substep, sweep and prune updates the pairs. A pair is two fat boxes that overlap. A fat box holds the shape, what the step can reach from its velocity, acceleration and spin, and a 0.04 m margin. Detection runs once a step and serves every substep. A removed collider stays in the lists until the next step and goes in one pass; new colliders join in one sort, merge and sweep. Nothing that decides an order reads the pair table, so results do not depend on capacity.

Island contract: a step walks the awake list and the active-pair list only, so a sleeper costs nothing. After the broad phase, an awake dynamic body or a moving kinematic one wakes whatever it touches, union-find groups the awake dynamic bodies, and an island whose bodies are all ready becomes a ring. Islands are numbered by their first body on the awake list, a pure function of the calls made; islands are independent, so that order cannot change a result. Fixed and kinematic bodies are insulators. Until P2 touching means fat boxes overlap. A pair that loses its contacts, because the narrow phase found none, the pair became one nothing solves or it left the broad phase, starts both bodies' sleep timers again: a body that cannot sleep keeps its island awake, so what rests on it can be long past its window, and with its support gone it would sleep in mid air at the next look (`kernel/tests/sleep.rs`).

Evidence so far: native tests of layout, growth and hash; Node tests of the views. `packages/physics/kernel/tests/integrate.rs` holds free fall and a projectile against the closed form with the method's own term, a free top against the closed precession rate, a heavy top against the Lagrange rate, energy on a tumbling box and at extreme spin, damping, locks, kinematic targets and an off-origin centre of mass, each bound derived from the method's error term plus f32 rounding. `packages/physics/tests/kernel-step.test.js` repeats the closed forms and the force and impulse contract through the shipped Wasm. `packages/physics/kernel/tests/bodies.rs` checks each solid's mass and moments against a numeric integral of its shape, a dumbbell against the parallel axis theorem, a tilted collider's principal frame, and that freed rows come back last in, first out. `packages/physics/kernel/tests/broad.rs` compares the pairs with brute force on every step of random scenes in which bodies move, teleport, join in batches and leave, and asserts the sorted lists, ranks, pair table and pair lists each time; two runs at different capacities must match, and overlapping balls must always be a pair. `packages/physics/kernel/tests/sleep.rs` compares islands with a plain graph search on random scenes, checks every list and ring through a churn of adds, removals, wakes and sleep requests at two capacities, and proves each rule of the sleep policy. Every row access in the native test build is bounds-checked. `packages/physics/tests/kernel-blueprint.test.js` fails when the committed blueprint's source hash is not the hash of the sources, which closes for this kernel the gap section 1.6 lists for the transform kernel. The gate also rebuilds the blueprint and requires identical bytes.

Replay: `packages/physics/tests/replay-scene.js` runs two 10,000-step scenes, one on `KernelWorld` and one through `Physics`, and hashes the world every 100 steps. `tests/fixtures/replay-hash.json` holds the hashes and the hash of the kernel sources, so a stale file fails. Node (`tests/replay.test.js`), native code (`kernel/tests/replay.rs`, a twin of the kernel scene) and Chromium and Firefox (`npm run test:replay`, in `.github/workflows/browser.yml`) must all give them; `npm run test:browser`, which the full check runs, holds them in that machine's default browser. The scene must reach 8 sleepers, 8 pairs, 8 islands and a growth, and moving one position by 2^-20 must change the hash, so the proof can fail. `tests/step-path.test.js` holds the entry's step path free of `Math`, clocks and `**`, which are the ways TypeScript could part from the kernel.

Missing: everything beyond free motion. Bit equality is proved on one Windows x86-64 PC, in Node, native code, Chromium 156 and Firefox 157 (LIM-366); Safari, ARM and a second machine are not (section 5). Nothing is timed yet: the kernel's speed against Rapier waits for the quiet pass.

## 2. Precise GPU mathematics

WGSL permits large builtin errors and floating-point reassociation. `packages/shared/precise-math.js` provides 19 f32
functions for code that compares CPU and GPU results or results across vendors:

`preciseDiv`, `preciseSqrt`, `preciseSin`, `preciseCos`, `preciseTan`, `preciseAtan`, `preciseAtan2`, `preciseAsin`,
`preciseAcos`, `preciseExp`, `preciseExp2`, `preciseExpm1`, `preciseSinh`, `preciseCosh`, `preciseTanh`, `preciseLog`,
`preciseLog2`, `preciseLog1p`, and `precisePow`.

The implementation uses public numerical methods: integer Payne-Hanek reduction with a 2/pi table, Cody-Waite
reduction for ln 2, Dekker products from 12-bit halves, and minimax coefficients derived by
`scripts/precise-math-coefficients.mjs` at high precision. WGSL is emitted only for requested functions, with shared
helpers emitted once. The derivation solves each Lawson step by Householder QR on unit-scaled columns and stops
reweighting at 2^-44 relative error (f64 noise): the normal equations it used before amplified a 1 ulp difference in the
host's `Math.atan` or `Math.cos` past an f32 rounding midpoint, so macOS arm64 derived other atan constants than Windows,
and tanh's stored set had come from that noise. `tests/precise-math.test.js` re-fits atan and tanh with the host maths
nudged by 1 ulp and needs the same f32 values. The regenerated tanh holds 1.45 ulp (bound 2) on the Apple silicon Mac (Metal)
(`npm run test:browser --workspace packages/compute`, 2026-11-07); other GPUs still need a run with it.

Important primitives:

- `pmSplit` extracts a stable high part by masking mantissa bits.
- `pmProductError` returns the exact product residual for the rounded product.
- `pmFastTwoSum` implements the magnitude-ordered Dekker two-sum. A general Knuth two-sum and FMA emulation are not
  present.
- `preciseDiv` and `preciseSqrt` correct one rounded builtin result using an exact residual.
- `pmHide` reconstructs a float from integer sign, exponent, and mantissa bits through `ldexp`. It preserves the value
  but prevents a compiler from proving and cancelling the expression that produced it.

`pmHide` was required because real compilers legally rewrote error-free transforms: AMD D3D12 folded
`(1 + x) - 1`, and Mesa also regrouped and factored sums. Before the fix a Radeon 680M produced a `preciseLog1p`
result 8,383,741 ulp outside the bound; Mesa had 14 of 17 functions outside bounds. Apple's compiler (M6, Chrome and
Playwright WebKit) lost the last product of `pmProductError` while it was unhidden, so the result was the sum without
it: `precisePow` went 97 ulp out, and `preciseTan` over its bound through `preciseDiv`. Every product there is hidden now.
The same compiler spread an unhidden tail over the large part of `preciseLog2`, regrouped `(0.5 t) t` as `0.5 (t t)` in sinh
and cosh, and lost `f - sd` in pow's log pair. Hides there are named in `tests/precise-math.test.js`. The fixes are guarded by:

- A browser shader rewriter that simulates cancellation and factoring on any GPU.
- A spec-error rewriter that perturbs builtin results by WGSL's allowed error.
- Host text tests that reject self-cancelling and factorable forms.
- Dense host reference tests under fused, unfused, and worst-allowed division/sqrt behavior.
- Browser checks against a step-for-step host mirror and a broad exponent sweep.

The documented bounds are function-specific: most are within 1-2 ulp, tan about 2.5 ulp, and pow 2 ulp while
`|y log2(x)| < 16` and 5 ulp beyond. GPU checks require the bound and no more than 2 ulp from the host mirror; exact
mirror share is reported, not generally required.

At the audited fixes, dense checks and the sweep passed on NVIDIA RTX A6000/D3D12, AMD Radeon 680M/D3D12, and Intel
UHD/Mesa Vulkan. The Intel Arc 140V had not been rerun after the fix. The committed sweep reported 573,720 trig inputs
and 298,646 pow inputs with zero over bound on A6000 and Intel UHD. Bit equality across vendors is not claimed; the
per-function ulp bound is.

`pmLog2Pair` carries `s R` as a pair since 2026-11-05. In one float it left `precisePow` over its bound near the top of the
range on every GPU tried (5.66 ulp on the A6000), and the sweep never drew those inputs. The sweep now has that class,
which fails on the old maths: 318,575 pow inputs, 0 over bound on the A6000 and on an Apple M6 in Chrome 157 and
Playwright WebKit. Worst in a 262,144 input scan of that class: 1.23 ulp on the A6000, 1.03 on the M6. The AMD, Intel UHD
and Arc results above predate this change.

Node 22 and Node 26 once produced different pinned proof digests because V8 implementations of `pow` differed. The
proof inputs now use exact operations, approximated host math is replaced by deterministic stand-ins during the
proof, and the suite runs under both pow modes. NaN payloads are canonicalized only where a proof explicitly defines
that comparison; signed zero otherwise remains significant.

Measured on the RTX A6000 only (`docs/whitepaper/perf-history.md` entry 48): one precise call per element costs 1.0 to
1.8 times the builtin, `tan` 2.3, `pow` 3.0, and the path tracer's panorama and fisheye rays 1% to 7% of a traced sample.
The `pow` figure predates the pair for `s R`, which adds work, and has not been measured again.
`npm run bench` repeats the pairs (`compute-elementwise`, the `tracer` suite; entry 71), diagnostic so far.
Unmeasured: that cost on other GPUs, one kernel rotation-sync call, and cross-machine kernel bit equality.

`@margoengine/compute/subgroups` is opt-in for the same reason: its float sums follow the GPU's subgroup size, so they
do not repeat across GPUs, while integers, orders and sorts equal the default kernels. WGSL promises no subgroup size or
layout, so kernels order work by seats taken with one workgroup atomic, never by `local_invocation_index`. Checked at
sizes 32 (RTX A6000) and 4 (SwiftShader, `BROWSER_ARGS` with `--enable-unsafe-swiftshader` and
`--use-webgpu-adapter=swiftshader`).

Skinning has one optional second path: `@margoengine/animation/dqs` blends dual quaternions in the batched deformation
shader, a pipeline of its own beside the linear one, reading the same 64-byte bone slots (rotation, dual part, symmetric
stretch). The CPU splits each bone matrix by polar decomposition in double precision (Jacobi on the Gram matrix, so a
rank-deficient bone still gives a rotation). Quaternion signs follow the heaviest influence, because glTF fills spare
influences with joint 0 and an idle joint must not choose them. Checked on the RTX A6000 only: 28,512 values against the
double-precision twin, worst 8.8e-7 in position and 2.1e-7 in normal; the narrowest ring of a 170 degree twist stays at
radius 1.000 where the linear path gives 0.087 (`npm run test:gpu:dqs -w @margoengine/animation`). Unmeasured: its frame cost.

A third path, `@margoengine/animation/cor` (2026-11-28, `addPerson`'s default), skins about optimized centres of
rotation (Le and Hodgins 2016): the rotation is the sign-aligned, normalized quaternion sum of the same dual quaternion
slots, applied to the vertex less its centre (after the blended stretch), and the centre moves by the linear blend of
the bones (each bone's slot rebuilt on the centre). The centres are a per-mesh CPU precompute in double precision (the
paper's weight similarity, sigma 0.1, over triangles summed by weights to 1/16; vertex weights exact), carried as one
more vec4 after each vertex's influences, so a mode with per-vertex data has its own influence blocks (the block key now
names the mode: a share-packed or centre-carrying block is never read by another mode's shader). Checked on the RTX
A6000 on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 layer: 49,920 values against Animation's CPU pose, worst 5.4e-7 and 4.8e-7; a 150
degree twist keeps radius 1.000 where linear gives 0.259 (`npm run test:gpu:cor -w @margoengine/animation`). Evidence
on a real asset: the Fauld old man's coat (frames in the rigging lane's `rigging-frames/g9`), whose side panel no
longer balloons at a raised arm. Unmeasured: frame cost, and the precompute's load time in a browser.

`SkinnedCrowd` (`@margoengine/animation/instanced-skin`) skins in the vertex stage from a baked rgba32float bone texture,
drawing through `VATCrowd`'s pipeline code. Its proof runs the stage's own `skinned` function from a compute shader, since a
vertex stage cannot write out. Checked on the RTX A6000 only. Unmeasured: its frame cost.

### Uniform-only inexact operations

A shader result must not depend on how the driver evaluates an expression of uniforms only. On ANGLE D3D11 with
an NVIDIA RTX A6000, core's `normalize(frame.light.xyz)` returned one of two values an ulp apart depending on GPU
load, while per-pixel expressions with the same bytes stayed exact; captures then differed in 24 binary16
components. Core now uploads the unit light direction (float64 normalize, one float32 rounding) and every shader
reads `.light.xyz` without `normalize` or `length`; every package uniform that copies the light is
written through `shared/unit-light.js`, and sun options are normalized on the CPU the same way. `packages/core/tests/unit-light.test.js` checks the upload and scans every package source for
both patterns (a normalized light uniform, a raw `lighting.direction` write); `capture-stability-browser.mjs --compat --gpu-load=3000` reproduces the old failure. Evidence exists
for this one GPU and driver; other vendors, and other uniform-only inexact builtins (division, sqrt, pow on uniforms
alone), have no scan or GPU evidence yet.

### Particle shadow depth and node vectors

`@margoengine/vfx/shadows` draws each live particle as a sphere impostor. WebGPU clips a primitive whose clip z is outside [0, w] (WebGPU specification, primitive clipping) before the fragment stage. The quad's clip z stays inside that interval when the sphere's depth interval meets [0, 1], so a centre past the cascade far plane still draws a front that is in range. The fragment writes the geometric depth, `centerZ - sqrt(max(0, 1 - x^2 - y^2)) * depthRadius`, clamped to [0, 1]. A sphere whose whole depth interval is past the far plane still clips.

`@margoengine/vfx/nodes` normalizes with one scaled length on the CPU and in WGSL, function `nodeNorm`: divide by the largest absolute component, then by the length of that vector (Blue, James L., "A Portable Fortran Program to Find the Euclidean Norm of a Vector", ACM TOMS 4(1), 1978). A zero vector stays zero. WebGL2 translates that same function. Finite values 1e-21 and 1e20 both become a unit vector on the CPU, on WebGPU and on WebGL2. A finite double that is not a finite f32 is rejected for a node literal and for shadow range and intensity (`vfx-float`) before it is stored in a uniform.

### PixelScale, CRT and PaletteQuantize

`@margoengine/pixel/scale` fits a whole-pixel rectangle into each view (contain rounds down the unconstrained side and
centres the result). Nearest selects `floor((2 o + 1) n / (2 w))` by integer arithmetic, so an exact source boundary
selects the texel to its right or below. Sharp-bilinear integrates the last two texels on each axis: at the right edge
