`r = (o + 1) n / w`, it mixes texels `floor(r)-1` and `floor(r)` with weight
`clamp(fract(r) w / n, 0, 1)`, then the two rows the same way. Edge first applies the public Scale2x corner rule
(matching adjacent neighbours and differing opposite neighbours), only when at least 2x fits. Below 1x this two-texel
filter is not full box integration; colours mix in their stored encoding, not linear light.

`@margoengine/pixel/crt` maps the output centre to `c = 2 (o + 0.5) / w - 1`, bends it with
`b = c (1 + curvature * c.yx^2)`, rejects points outside the glass and maps back to source coordinates. Flat glass
avoids that normalized round trip: it uses the same integer nearest quotient as PixelScale. Scanlines multiply by
`1 - scanlines * (1 - sin(pi * fract(t.y))^2)`. The three-column grille passes one RGB channel and multiplies the other
two by `1-mask`. Glow adds a clamped-edge 3x3 binomial `[1,2,1] x [1,2,1] / 16` blur. The beam is multiplied by
brightness, glow alpha is added and clamped, and RGB is capped at alpha before premultiplied compositing. This is a
designed look, not a measured physical tube. All-off must equal rational nearest exactly; it has no excluded samples.

Both screen passes intersect the fitted rectangle with canvas bounds and RenderView.scissor, preserving the original
mapping. Explicit output textures cover their own rectangle, independent of the canvas view. Per-view uniforms
prevent queue writes for a later view overwriting an earlier one. Bind groups retain both source texture and selected
pipeline identity because WebGPU auto layouts belong to their creating pipeline, even when shapes match. Disposal
queries `engine.sceneOf(this)` before unregistering, so equal names in other scenes are untouched; buffers are destroyed
and pipeline/bind-group references released. The same ownership rule holds for PaletteQuantize and LayerCompositor.

`@margoengine/pixel/palette` unpremultiplies nonzero-alpha source texels (unless straight input is requested), adds
`spread * (threshold - 0.5)` in encoded sRGB, clamps to [0,1], then minimizes squared distance in sRGB or Oklab. Oklab
decodes sRGB with its standard piecewise transfer function, applies Ottosson's LMS matrix, cube roots and Lab matrix.
Ties keep the first palette entry. The chosen swap colour is premultiplied by the original alpha. Bayer ranks use
`(rank + 0.5) / side^2`; blue noise is Margo's deterministic 64x64 tile. CPU cycling reduces the finite `rate * seconds`
modulo the run length before subtracting small indices, floors the reduced shift, and optionally interpolates its
fraction in Oklab. Product overflow is rejected with coded `state` and a help link. GPU palette disposal destroys its
palette/dither textures and uniform buffer as well as removing the owning scene's pass.

Evidence: `packages/pixel/tests/screen-pass.test.js` checks auto-layout identity on repeated format changes, scissor
intersection and exactly-once resource destruction; `palette-cycle.test.js` checks huge signed shifts and overflow in
both blend modes. These run in verify, hence check:merge. Both scale/crt GPU harnesses import `screen-regressions.js`
for real-device format round trips, clipped and empty scissors, and same-name plugins in different scenes. The CRT
harness additionally compares 154 source/output size pairs against both rational nearest and PixelScale with exact
bytes and zero exclusions. Existing scale/palette/CRT GPU checks retain CPU maths comparisons and device restore.
Backend evidence and its remaining scope are recorded in section 5.

## 3. Rendering backends and hardware tiers

`@margoengine/vfx` wind (2026-11-17): each particle's horizontal velocity relaxes toward the wind by the exact step of dv/dt = (u - v) / tau, v += (u - v)(1 - exp(-dt / tau)) with tau 0.25 s (Stokes drag on a parcel that moves with the air; Crowe et al., Multiphase Flows with Droplets and Particles, CRC 2011), stable at any frame time. The wind is two half floats in control.w of the 224-byte frame block (0 means no wind), so a steady frame still uploads 224 bytes. Smoke rising at w in a wind U then leans atan(U / w); `packages/vfx/test/features-check.mjs` (checkWind) measures it within 0.07 degrees at U 0.5 to 20 m/s on WebGPU and, with the same numbers, on the WebGL2 route (`shadows-nodes-webgl2.mjs`).

`@margoengine/vfx/shadows` and `@margoengine/vfx/nodes` run on WebGPU and on the WebGL2 compatibility layer from the same shaders. WebGL2 has no compute stage; the particle simulation uses the existing GPU point-draw route in `vfx/src/compat.ts`, and the shadow depth pass is a fragment shader. Every route kernel must plan as a point draw: an invocation never reads back a buffer it stored to (a point draw reads its inputs as they were before the draw). So over-life reads its stored life into locals first (KB-VFX-EMBERCPU1), and `events` keeps a raised event in private memory and stores it once `update` returns, with the slot's generation in a local (KB-VFX-EVENTS-CPU, 2026-11-18; evidence: `packages/vfx/test/route-loading.test.js` counts 0 CPU-tier dispatches a frame for death and collision events, 1 before). Disposal removes the point lights that effect published into its clustered list, and a dispose or device restore during the light read-back settles the cancelled map.

**Area light integrals (2026-11-05).** `@margoengine/clustered/area` returns early from a quad with nothing to clip; the clip's own result, by the same operations. Evidence: `packages/clustered/test/ltc-edge.test.js` (bit for bit in float32) and `examples/package-benchmarks/area-lights-gpu.mjs` as the package's `test:gpu:area` (11 frames byte-equal, RTX A6000 only).

gltf/pbr trims each pipeline to the vertex inputs its finished shader reads (`packages/gltf/src/vertex-inputs.ts`), after
every shader patch. Evidence: `packages/materials/test/vertex-inputs-browser.mjs` (no pixel differs, RTX A6000 only).

A frame is one colour render pass when only a package draws. The main pass with nothing to draw leaves its clear to a next
pass that declares `joins`; that pass opens its render passes through `context.attach`, and the last one resolves. A clear
nobody took runs before the following pass. Core resolves in a pass of its own only when the graph's last pass did not.
Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/last-pass-check.mjs` (pass counts, frames unchanged) and `tests/modern-msaa.test.js`, RTX
A6000 only; the gain on tile-based GPUs is unmeasured.

**Rendering in a worker (2026-11-05).** Core runs on a transferred `OffscreenCanvas` with no change: it reads no DOM it does not
guard. `@margoengine/worker` gives the canvas `clientWidth` and `clientHeight` and copies `devicePixelRatio` and `margoLow`, so
`resize`, `sceneSamples` and `pick` take the same paths as on the page. Evidence: `packages/worker/tests/browser-check.mjs`
(WebGPU and the WebGL2 fallback in a real worker), RTX A6000 on Chromium only.

**Per-device sharing (2026-11-05).** Three caches hold GPU objects by count and free them with their last holder: `Environment`'s BRDF LUT
per device, size and sample count (a failed create drops its count, and nothing joins that LUT again); gltf/pbr's textures per
device, image and format (100 `cloneModel` copies of `p-morph` hold 7 textures, not 700); `@margoengine/shader/raw` buffers per
set of equal bytes, with copy on write. Evidence: `packages/environment/tests/brdf-share.test.js`,
`packages/gltf/test/model-runs.test.js`, `packages/shader/test/raw.test.js`, and the two browser checks they pair with, RTX
A6000 only.

**Textured meshes on the light path (2026-11-06).** `@margoengine/gltf/textured` keeps a mesh a core mesh, claims its batch and draws it
with core's shader plus a UV input and a texture read, in one extra render pass per frame for all textured meshes of a scene.
Native WebGPU and the full WebGL2 compatibility layer share this render path; the preview refuses it. Cut-out shadow masks and draw counts are covered, while core GPU picking remains solid; texturedAlphaMasks provides alpha-aware CPU rays. Evidence: `packages/gltf/test/textured.test.js` and `scripts/test-gltf-browser.mjs` on both backends (batch 200, 2026-11-10): texel RGB [97,27,155], five expected shadow pixels and no errors. No new renderer or GPU maths was added. Meshless scene-data loads allocate no geometry; the loader tests cover scene placement and rollback.

**Lighting in a node graph (2026-11-06).** `Material` gains one internal step, `relight`, that runs after the effects composed; it returns
the code unchanged for every other material. `@margoengine/shader/lighting` reads the sun, its shadow visibility, the clustered
lights, the ambient light and the environment as the attached effects worked them out. Rectangle and disc area lights are not
covered. Evidence: `packages/shader/test/lighting.test.js` and `packages/shader/test/lighting-check.mjs` on a real GPU, a graph
Lambert equal to the Lambert shading.

**TAA history fetched by the motion alone (2026-11-16, KB-TAA-CLAMP1).** Both of TAA's matrices carry the Halton jitter,
so every velocity holds the jitter difference as well as the motion (`taa.velocity.jitter`, kept as the public contract);
the resolve now adds that difference back (`Temporal.offset`, 16 B more uniform) and fetches history at the pixel's
unjittered centre. Before, a still view's history was resampled up to 0.8 px away every frame, blurred, and the
neighbourhood clamp cut it back only in part: 8 px stripes converged 10.5 sRGB levels above their mean. The min/max box
itself was ruled out: a 1D model of the resolve with the history fetched in place converges on the mean with the clamp
on. TAAUpscale already reprojected with unjittered matrices. Evidence: `packages/taa/test/converge-browser.mjs`
(per-frame resolve within 1 level of the settled mean, every rejection mode, RTX A6000) and
`packages/taa/test/converge.test.js`.

**TAA settles a still view (2026-11-16, KB-TAA-STILL1).** With the camera still, a jittered resolve blends one of 8 sample positions a frame into a history clamped to that sample's neighbourhood, so thin wires and highlights changed by up to 189 sRGB levels forever (0.23% to 0.36% of pixels on the Orrery, 2.4% on the bare-TAA fixture). A colour range learned from the jitter cannot tell that from a moving object, but the Halton sequence repeats every 8 frames, so the render pixel's sample in phase k must equal its sample in phase k one cycle ago bit for bit unless the scene changed (the temporal gradient of Schied et al., HPG 2018, with the repeating jitter as the re-shaded sample). A compute pass at render size hashes each sample (pcg4d, Jarzynski and Olano 2020) into 8-bit slots (3 phases a 32-bit word, the count of matching frames in the fourth byte) and copies the word into the phase's layer. A pixel whose 3x3 render footprint has matched for a whole cycle takes the equal-weight running mean of the next cycle's samples (Yang et al. 2009), shows it and keeps it; a mismatch, a camera move, a reset or a reactive pixel hands it back to the clamped history in the same frame. Cost: four textures (slots, word and two means), a 16-byte uniform written every frame, one compute pass and one copy; the resolve gains a second bind group and its uniform 208 to 224 B. The detect hash is 8 bits, so a change is missed only if every pixel of its footprint collides (1 in 256 each). Evidence: `packages/taa/test/still-browser.mjs` (0% of pixels change, largest difference 0), `settle-reactive-browser.mjs` (trail -1.33 against a bound of 3), `converge-browser.mjs`, `rejection-browser.mjs` (settled line 123 every frame, stripes 0 and 0), `packages/taa/test/settle.test.js`; every taa GPU test passes with settle on (13 of 13 native, 5 of 5 on the WebGL2 layer); no visual baseline compares a TAA view. The `--current` call proof `taa-velocity` advanced to `f3ed2ccc73` (docs/whitepaper/claims.md).

**TAA motion coverage on the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-27, KB-TAA-COMPATEDGE1).** GLSL ES 3.00 has no `sampler2DMS`, so the layer reads every sample of a 4x texture from its blit-resolved copy and TAA's motion resolve saw the mean of a pixel's four samples: at a silhouette, object samples mixed with the camera pass's broadcast value and the box's motion came out halved. At 4x on the layer only (`compatTier`), the camera pass now writes the 1x targets itself, object velocity draws write `vec4f(velocity, 0, 1)` into cleared rgba16float 4x targets (4 more bytes a sample), and the resolve writes mean / coverage where coverage is above 0, keeping the camera's value elsewhere. WebGPU keeps rg16float and its nearest-sample pick. Evidence: `packages/taa/test/instance-velocity-browser.mjs --compat` (11,013 of 11,013 moving pixels; 10,787 of 10,812 before) and `far-velocity-browser.mjs` (every box pixel within 0.6 to 1.4 times the median, WebGPU and the layer). Missing: two moving surfaces in one pixel mix by coverage on the layer; no test measures that case.

**Mixed silhouette pixels on the WebGL2 layer (2026-11-27, KB-TAA-COMPATEDGE2).** The coverage route's mean of a pixel whose samples hold two surfaces is a surface between them, and TAA's closest-depth choice handed it to the neighbour; the layer's one-sample depth resolve also gave history the far surface's depth. Object velocity shaders now write log2 of the expected depth in the 4x target's `z`; where log2 of the mean depth exceeds the mean log2 by more than 1/32 (Jensen's inequality: depths 1.6 times apart or more) the pixel takes the motion, expected depth and current depth of the nearest unmixed surface of its 3x3, as WebGPU's nearest sample does, the depth through one fullscreen depth32float pass on that route only. Evidence: `packages/taa/test/stability-browser.mjs --compat`, 2.89 to 0.175 fast and 0.335 to 0.231 slow (WebGPU 0.179 and 0.225), now asserted on both. Missing: surfaces closer than 1.6 times in depth still mix by coverage; measured on ANGLE Direct3D 11 only.

**Scene targets register with the resolved frame (2026-11-27, KB-POST-MRTJITTER1).** TAA draws each frame from a camera moved by one Halton phase and averages the phases back onto the unjittered camera, so anything read after the frame and compared with it (SceneTargets' masks and AOVs, the shot tool's look masks) must be drawn from the unjittered camera. SceneTargets now does so always: it sets `c.camera` to `unjitteredCamera` for its pass and undoes the clip patch in core's shader (`unjitteredClip`, `packages/shared/temporal-camera.js`); a terrain capture from another camera than its prepared rings writes its own per-view uniforms; Scatter and ScatterInstances captures use their own frame's camera; and gltf/pbr capture draws keep a view block of their own per view, since a uniform write is seen by the whole submit. Evidence: `packages/post/test/scene-targets-taa-browser.mjs`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 0 coverage pixels moved for each capture path (without the fix 7 to 210).

**Motion vectors without the resolve (2026-11-05).** TAA's `velocityOnly` leaves out jitter, capture, history and resolve, so `MotionBlur`
no longer pays for them, and the blur runs inside the `PostStack`. It reads the depth and scene target another plugin made, so a
4x MSAA frame with no `PostStack` throws `state`. Evidence: `packages/taa/test/velocity-only-browser.mjs`, RTX A6000 only.
Plain TAA is unchanged.

**Dithered level changes (2026-11-05).** `LODFade` draws both levels for the fade, each pixel from one by a fixed noise threshold, so
depth stays right with no sorting. Core meshes read the value from a buffer by mesh id, one storage read per core-mesh pixel while
attached; models read a lighting effect's uniform. WebGPU only, instant on WebGL2. Evidence: `packages/lod/test/fade-check.mjs`.
Missing: a measured cost.

**Device limits and large scenes (2026-11-10, Scott's approved core exception).** `GPURenderer.create` asks `requestDevice` for the adapter's `maxTextureArrayLayers`, `maxBufferSize` and `maxStorageBufferBindingSize`, at creation and on every restore (a restore runs `create` again), so a desktop adapter's larger buffers reach core and every package that reads `device.limits`; an adapter that offers only WebGPU's defaults gets the same device as before. Evidence: `tests/core-timestamp-feature.test.js` (stub adapters with default and larger limits, and a restore) and `packages/core/tests/scale.browser.mjs` (the real device's limits equal its adapter's, natively and on the WebGL2 layer). Work per steady frame is unchanged (a 300-mesh scene: same draws, bind groups, buffer writes and bytes). Missing: adapters other than the RTX A6000 and the layer on it.

`Geometry` takes up to 11,184,810 vertices (it was 1,000,000), the most 24-byte interleaved vertices one buffer of the default 256 MiB `maxBufferSize` holds; the index buffer keeps its upload-time check against the device's `maxBufferSize`. Evidence: `packages/core/tests/vertex-cap.test.js` (the cap, one past it, and 1,000,001, which failed before) and the `vertices` case of `scale.browser.mjs` (a 1,212,201-vertex plane covers every pixel natively and on the WebGL2 layer). Missing: frame time at the cap (speed phase).

Core's instance buffer (96 B a row, doubling with the meshes of one geometry) is bound by core only through `setVertexBuffer`, for draws and picks, so `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` never applies to it inside core; only `maxBufferSize` does, checked when the buffer is made. The `instances` case of `scale.browser.mjs` draws 1,200,000 boxes of one geometry (2,097,152 rows, 201 MB) with the same pixels as two geometries of 600,000, with no validation error, natively and on the WebGL2 layer, on the code before and after 2026-11-10. The storage-binding limit is a contract for packages that bind `geometryBuffers(g).instance` themselves: bind the rows in use with `offset` and `size` (`CulledMeshes`, c106034b1); `FrontToBack` in `@margoengine/culling` (through `InstanceSorter`) still binds the whole buffer (docs/known-bugs.md).

The backbuffer's per-side cap is the device's `maxTextureDimension2D` (the canvas texture, the MSAA colour target and the depth target all share it), not a fixed 4096; when it applies both sides scale together so the CSS aspect holds. The pixel-ratio cap (at most 2, and at most 4 / samples, so 1 with 4x MSAA) and the quality tier's cap are unchanged, so a desktop canvas draws at most its CSS pixels with 4x MSAA as before: only canvases whose longer side passes 4096 such pixels (5120 ultrawide, 8K) draw more pixels now, as the display asks. A fallback renderer with no WebGPU device keeps 4096. Evidence: `packages/core/tests/backbuffer-cap.test.js` (stub limits 8192 and 16384, the aspect, the fallback) and the `backbuffer` case of `scale.browser.mjs` (5120 x 1440 kept and 10240 x 16 cut to 8192 x 13 on an 8192 device, natively and on the WebGL2 layer; 4096 x 1152 on the code before). Core does not ask for the adapter's `maxTextureDimension2D`, so a device has WebGPU's 8192 unless a package asks for more. Missing: frame time at 5120 x 1440 (speed phase).

### 3.1 Fallback ladder

| Tier | Behavior | Loading and cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native WebGPU | Core `GPURenderer` and all packages | Always attempted first for `backend: 'auto'` or `'webgpu'`. |
| `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview` preview | Core meshes, constant-color PBR, one directional plus ambient light; no textures or effects. `/pick` (which also exports `webglRenderer`, so one `loadFallback` import serves a React Canvas) adds a read-pixels `engine.pick`, the route of `Picking` and React pointer handlers on the preview: evidence `packages/webgl2-compat/test/preview-browser-check.mjs`, `packages/react/scripts/test-scene-browser.js`. The pick uses an R32UI 1x1 target and core's projection narrowing; core's refusal stands without it. `/restore` rebuilds programs and buffers after a lost context and makes `rebootDevice` work, with `onDeviceRestored` in each scene; core's refusal stands without it. Evidence: real-browser `packages/webgl2-compat/test/preview-browser-check.mjs` on Chromium, including a real `WEBGL_lose_context` loss; Firefox and Safari not run. `/auto` chooses between WebGPU, the preview and the layer, moving to the layer when a package refuses the preview during `setup`. | App-provided fallback, normally dynamically imported. Separate chunk; 3,407 bytes gzip in the audited size record. |
| `@margoengine/webgl2-compat` | WebGPU-shaped API over WebGL2 so core and feature packages run unchanged | App installs only when native WebGPU is unavailable. Device, translator, and compute entries are lazy. |
| Unsupported message | Page explains that WebGPU is required and does not download demo code | Used below the supported fallback floor. |

Core requests an adapter without a power preference on Windows and with `high-performance` elsewhere. Requested
features are filtered against adapter support. Desktop scenes default to 4x MSAA; phones, the light tier, and exact
size use 1x. `Engine.create` records the native failure before invoking an app-supplied fallback. `exactSize` fixes the
canvas dimensions, disables resizing, and forces one sample unless `antialias: true` (2026-11-26, GAP-FILM-MSAA:
`engine.fixed` holds "no resize" and `engine.exact` "one sample", so a fixed-size film frame keeps the tier's 4x MSAA;
evidence `packages/core/tests/exact-antialias.browser.mjs` on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). `antialias: false` makes any
engine single-sampled.

**Device destroy (2026-11-06).** A frame on the page is an ImageBitmap of the device's own WebGL2 context, so `destroy()` copies it
into a 2D context of the page before it loses the context. Chrome 157 on macOS crashed the tab otherwise. Evidence:
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/destroy-frame-browser.mjs` in `test:gpu`, run on the Apple M6 in Chrome and WebKit and on the RTX A6000 in Edge.

**No garbage per frame on the layer (2026-11-18, KB-COMPAT-FRAMEALLOC1).** The layer's steady frame allocates no more
JavaScript heap than native WebGPU: its replay of draws, passes, queue writes, copies and compute dispatches allocates
nothing (commands are a pooled tape, `src/device/tape.ts`), and the objects WebGPU returns per call are a browser
wrapper's size or near it (labels default on the prototype, the device is reached through `TapePool.device`, a view
made with no descriptor shares its texture's `ViewRange`). Evidence: `MARGO_COMPAT=1 npm run test:frame-alloc:browser`
holds the layer to the native floors (median frames basic 252, instanced 228, shadowed 800, post 1,464, dynamic 264 B
against 340, 292, 860, 1,528 and 396; Edge 156, RTX A6000), and `packages/webgl2-compat/test/replay-alloc.test.js`
counts bytes per call on Node. Missing: the same browser check on other GPUs and browsers.

**Native compatibility level (2026-11-05).** `allowCompatibilityAdapters` in `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/adapter` adds a
rung between native WebGPU and the layers: `navigator.gpu.requestAdapter` retries with `featureLevel: 'compatibility'`
when the full level finds nothing. Core changes by 0 bytes: it calls `requestAdapter` at creation and in `rebootDevice`,
so answering there covers both. Compatibility devices take the adapter's limits and rewrite `@interpolate(flat)` to
`either`, which core's pick needs. Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/adapter-browser.mjs` on a forced device on the
RTX A6000 (D3D12, Chromium): same pixels as the full level, pick hits and misses, restore keeps the level. Missing: a run
on a real OpenGL ES or Direct3D 11 class device, so forced runs prove the validation, not the older GPU's limits.
Packages on the level (2026-11-06): the adapter's `createShaderModule` turns a depth texture that is only loaded into its
float type with `.x` on each load, and default layouts then bind it `unfilterable-float`, so culling's pyramid and
Shadows' nearest depth run unchanged. `compatibilityLevel` in `packages/shared/compat.js` names the rest: Shadows binds
its map a second time as float for the blocker search (a depth texture takes no plain sampler there), `SceneTarget`
copies 4x depth with one masked draw per sample (no `sample_index`), points' eye-dome lighting does the same and draws its depth in a second pass, as bytes in rgba8unorm (r32float does not multisample at the level, and it has no blend to match the colour target's), the frame equal to the full level's on the forced device, Bloom keeps each level in its own texture (no two
views of one texture in a dispatch) and `PostStack` captures 4x in `rg11b10ufloat`. Evidence in the same check: Shadows
0 bytes apart from the full level with a real shadow on the floor, four depth samples read back as written, the post
frame within 2 of 255. Sky fog, the VolumetricFog composite and water spray also draw once per sample with a constant
sample index and a one-sample mask (`perSample` in `packages/shared/msaa.js`, 2026-11-11), proved by the adapter check's
4x cases and its fogged frame. Surfels at 4x (2026-11-11) pack their front depth into rgba8unorm and add their sums in
two rg16float targets (r, g and b, weight: the full level's half floats), resolved by a masked draw per sample; the
adapter check's surfel frame is within 4 of 255 of the full level's. Since 2026-11-21 (KB2481) native WebGPU at 4x takes
the same masked resolve at the full level, reading the one rgba16float sum target per sample: on the Intel Arc 140V the
one `sample_index` draw over 4x additive sums did not repeat itself (up to 33 of 255 frame to frame over PostStack), a
driver fault. Cost: the resolve is 4 draws in place of 1 (with their 4 pipelines), passes unchanged (3 per frame); the
adapter check's surfel frame on that laptop went from 33 to 4 of 255 apart, and one engine's frame repeats bit for bit
(`surfelRepeat` in packages/points/tests/features-browser.js, which fails on the old route there). Same pixels where the
old route was exact is the arithmetic (each sample shaded from its own sums, blended over its own destination, either
way); it is not measured on another GPU yet (no software WebGPU adapter on that laptop). The WebGL2 layer, which ignores
sample masks, keeps the one draw. On the WebGL2 layer below its full tier surfels pack
the front depth the same way (that tier stores r32float as r16float) and refuse LDR; the tier check's half-float surfel
frame equals the full tier's. Eye-dome lighting packs its depth target the same way below the full tier (tier cases
`points edl` and `points edl 4x`). A lone Bloom at 4x and the float-target test
(`linearHdr`) were fixed the same day (known-bugs.md).

`@margoengine/headless` is outside this ladder: it takes a WebGPU implementation through `installGPU` and a stand-in canvas, so a stage
runs with no page. Stages alive at once share one `gpu`, because `installGPU` changes globals, and `engine.start()` needs
`requestAnimationFrame`, so time moves with `step(delta)`. Evidence: `packages/headless/tests/browser-check.mjs`, on a browser's
WebGPU through the stand-in canvas, and `packages/headless/tests/node-check.mjs`, which runs the README examples in Node on the `webgpu` binding (Dawn), a dev dependency. The stage scene drawn in Node matches the page at changed 0 on the RTX A6000 (D3D12), and the examples run on WARP. Missing: a textured glTF in Node (docs/known-bugs.md); Linux and macOS runs of the binding.

Headless readback (2026-11-24): `packages/headless/tests/readback.test.js` holds the word-wise pixel conversion byte equal to the former byte loop for both formats and alpha modes over every alpha against every channel value, and counts buffers, copies and maps for `readPixels` and the frame reader. The README frame reader example runs on the Node binding in node-check.mjs. Method: several mapped buffers in flight, read oldest first, as in L. Hrabcak and A. Masserann, "Asynchronous Buffer Transfers", OpenGL Insights (CRC Press, 2012), chapter 28, https://openglinsights.com/ , and the ARB_pixel_buffer_object specification (2004), https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/extensions/ARB/ARB_pixel_buffer_object.txt , built from the WebGPU specification, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ .

App-side detection must test both presence of `navigator.gpu` and a non-null adapter. The compatibility layer does not
silently install itself and changes no globals at import time.

### 3.2 WebGL2 compatibility architecture

**Fences need a command after them (2026-11-11).** Chrome on ANGLE's Direct3D 11 back end reported a fence followed
only by `gl.flush()` signaled after about 17 polls (about 270 ms) on a context that showed no frame (raw WebGL2 too),
so `onSubmittedWorkDone()` after work drawn into textures cost that much each time. The device's fence (`fence()` in
`device/tasks.ts`) sends a 4-byte copy between two buffers of its own after the fence; it then signals on the first
poll. Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/idle-fence-browser.mjs` (18 fence checks before, 1 after, a work count)
and the materials owner/lifetime check (WebGL2 leg past its 180 s limit before, both legs 26 s after). Missing: ANGLE
Vulkan, Metal and non-NVIDIA drivers were not probed for the lag; the copy is sent on all of them (one 4-byte copy per
wait).

**3D slices drawn beside depth (2026-11-10, batch 271 job 1).** ANGLE's Direct3D 11 back end drops every draw into a
slice of a 3D texture when the framebuffer also attaches depth or stencil (complete framebuffer, clears land, no GL error;
measured in raw WebGL2 on the RTX A6000: 8 of 30 probe rows fail, all of them 3D with depth). The layer's render pass
draws such a slice in a 2D stand-in of the attached storage's format and level size (`Replayer.standIn` in
`device/render.ts`, kept per storage by `CompatTexture.sliceStandIn`): one blit from the slice when the colour loads,
one blit back when it stores. Passes without depth, 2D and array layers keep attaching directly. Evidence:
`volumeSliceDepth` in `packages/webgl2-compat/test/features.html` (native and layer bytes equal) and
`packages/creative/scripts/test-targets-depth.js --compat` (164 surfaces). Missing: the other ANGLE back ends and
non-NVIDIA drivers were not probed; the stand-in is used on all of them, which costs two blits per such pass.

**XR route (2026-11-06).** `installXR()` in `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/xr` replaces `XRGPUBinding` with a binding on an
`XRWebGLLayer`, so `@margoengine/xr` keeps one renderer: each eye resolves into its own texture and `present` draws it
into the opaque framebuffer after the submit, and the view's projection is remapped to z in [0, 1]. Evidence:
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/xr-browser.mjs` in `test:gpu`, 0 differing pixels in both eyes on the RTX A6000 with stand-in
XR objects. Missing: a real headset.

**XR through the engine (2026-11-07).** An engine made by `createXREngine` (`@margoengine/xr`) asks for its adapter with
`xrCompatible: true`, so `XR.create` shares its device and draws each eye as one view of `engine.render({views})`: every
package pass and post effect runs per eye as it runs per view on the desktop. Each eye renders into a texture, a blit copies
it into the layer's sub-image, and a second blit writes the layer's forward depth24plus depth as 1 minus the scene's reversed
depth (the nearest sample). In AR the alpha is the share of samples that wrote depth, or the eye's own alpha, or the
brightest channel. The eye's alpha is coverage since KB-XR-ARNODEPTH1 (2026-11-27): core clears a view opaque, so right
after the main pass xr's AR alpha pass (order 1e-6, a depth-0 triangle with depthCompare 'equal' and an alpha-only write
mask) sets alpha 0 on every sample nothing drew, and later draws blend their own alpha over it (Porter and Duff 1984). AR
eyes also mark the engine premultiplied (`markPremultiplied` in shared/straight-display.js, as TransparentCanvas does)
for the session, so TAA keeps coverage in its history and display transforms take straight colour. Evidence for the
depthless case: `packages/xr/tests/ar-effects.browser.mjs`, a line with depthWrite false stays opaque two pixels inside
under every effect on WebGPU and the layer at 1x and 4x; without the fix 40 checks failed (Tonemap, DOF, Bloom, SSAO, the
stack). Transparent meshes need nothing more: core's main pass (order 0) draws only core meshes, which have no blending,
and gltf/pbr draws every model at order 1, after the alpha pass; the check's veil round holds a depthless glTF BLEND pane
and a materials pane at alpha 0.6 to their own coverage (153 of 255) under no effect, Tonemap and TAA, on both backends
at 1x and 4x. A package that ever draws blended content inside the main pass would need its own alpha handling there.
Evidence: `tests/modern-xr-passes.ts` in `modern:test:xr:browser`, both eyes byte-equal to a desktop render of the same
camera with a line, a point cloud, terrain and bloom, on the RTX A6000 with a stand-in session. On the WebGL2 layer
(`installXR()`), `packages/webgl2-compat/test/xr-browser.mjs` (in the layer's `test:gpu`) runs the same route with a line
into a stand-in XRWebGLLayer over a real WebGL framebuffer: `xr.route` is 'engine' and both eyes match the native route
with no pixel over 2 (2026-11-07, RTX A6000, Chromium). Missing: a real headset.

**Terrain on the layer (2026-11-08).** The clipmap terrain (`@margoengine/terrain`) and its runtime virtual texture run
on the layer with no route of their own: their passes are draws, which the layer translates unchanged. Evidence:
`packages/terrain/test/compat.browser.mjs` in terrain's `test:gpu` draws rules only, painted weights with a hole, and the
virtual texture natively and on the layer in exact-pixel mode; no pixel differs by more than 1 of 255, and a frame of six
clipmap levels is 6 GL draws and 48 GL calls (Radeon 680M, ANGLE on Direct3D 11, Edge 157). Missing: frame time on the
layer, other GPUs and back ends, and the terrain entries with compute passes (`sculpt`, `deform`, `displace`).

`install()` returns without changes when real WebGPU has an adapter, unless forced. Otherwise it probes WebGL2,
requires highp fragment floats/ints (a HIGH_INT report short of the GLSL ES 3.00 32 bits, as Firefox on macOS gives,
is measured by a one-pixel 32-bit integer draw read back exact) and `EXT_color_buffer_float`, defines a `CompatGPU` at `navigator.gpu`, patches
only `getContext('webgpu')`, and installs missing WebGPU flag constants. `uninstall()` reverses those changes. Lower
half-float and LDR capability tiers are detected but not accepted because the engine depends on HDR and float-data
targets.

Each compatibility device owns a separate WebGL2 context with antialias, depth, and stencil disabled. WebGPU-style
attachments are explicit. Four-sample pipelines use multisample renderbuffers and resolve by blit; exact-pixel mode
stays unsmoothed. The canvas texture is offscreen and is y-flipped only at presentation, which occurs at the end of
each submit so same-task canvas reads see the current frame.

Translation pipeline:

1. Tokenize complete WGSL, including nested comments, Unicode identifiers, numeric forms, and template discovery.
2. Parse the full grammar and its operator restrictions.
3. Resolve and type-check declarations, pointers, abstract numbers, overloads, constants, layouts, stages, and entry
   interfaces; detect declaration cycles.
4. Produce typed IR carrying folded values, spans, and entry-point reachability.
5. Report coded syntax, type, or limit errors with Unicode-aware line/column and help links. Limits include 4 MiB
   source, 255 nesting levels, and 65,536 values in one constant.
6. Emit GLSL ES 3.00 with WebGPU layout semantics, integer operations, conversions, clamped indexes, combined
   samplers, storage reads through data textures, and helpers for missing GLSL builtins.
7. Build resources, render pipelines, a state cache, canvas presentation, and command replay.
8. Analyze compute IR and choose a GPU or CPU execution tier.

Uniformity analysis is intentionally omitted because the recorded corpus already passes the browsers' compilers.

Mapping details:

- `EXT_clip_control` supplies WebGPU depth range. Rendering flips y so textures keep a top-left origin; presentation
  flips back.
- Bind-group entries map to uniform blocks and texture units per pipeline.
- Storage-buffer render reads use RGBA32UI data textures with 16-byte texels and clamped accesses. Bindings in one
  group share a texture, reducing texture-unit pressure. The texture is 2,048 texels wide, or wider when that would
  pass maxTextureDimension2D in height (`rowShift`, 2026-11-11), so a group holds up to maxTextureDimension2D squared
  rows (1 GiB at 8,192); before that a group past 256 MiB in total was refused, a WebGPU rule the layer had added.
  Evidence: `device.test.js` (a 360 MB group on an 8,192 context gets a 4,096 x 5,494 texture) and the 3,000,000-splat
  case of `packages/splats/test/gpu/scale-check.mjs` with MARGO_COMPAT=1.
- Linear HDR targets: a pass's colour target holds linear light when its format is any float format (`linearHdr`,
  `packages/shared/hdr-format.js`), which covers PostStack's `rg11b10ufloat` capture at WebGPU's compatibility level as
  well as `rgba16float`. Packages skip their display encoding and clamp only then; `tests/hdr-format.test.js` fails any
  package source that compares a pass format with `rgba16float` alone (2026-11-11, it found 25).
- Base vertex and base instance use uniforms because measured WebGL2 targets lacked the extension.
- Without indexed draw-buffer state, outputs with matching blend state are grouped; depth/stencil-writing cases that
  cannot be preserved are refused.
- Render shaders that write storage resources are refused.
- The device owns every GL object its context makes (`GLObjects`, `device/gl.ts`) and deletes each one itself: on its
  resource's `destroy()`, at the end of the first submission after the resource was collected (bind groups, samplers
  and pipelines have no `destroy()`), or with `device.destroy()`; a delete asked for during a replay waits for its end.
  Pipelines with the same GLSL, binding table and vertex attributes share one program and VAO (`LinkedProgram`,
  `device/render.ts`; up to 64 idle ones kept, least recently used first out). The binding table is in the key since
  2026-11-11: GLSL names uniforms and samplers by order, so WGSL differing only in `@binding` numbers (terrain with its
  holes texture at 6 or at 8) gave one key, and the later pipeline drew with the earlier one's bindings, in Chromium
  and WebKit alike, whenever the earlier pipeline was still alive (`test/device.test.js`, binding-numbers test). Cause (2026-11-10): the layer had left programs, VAOs and some
  textures and framebuffers for the browser to delete at wrapper collection, possibly mid-replay, and on ANGLE Vulkan
  (NVIDIA 617.42) the voxel tracer's loop programs then wrote fragment output 7 wrong in 13 of 78 renders. Evidence:
  `test/gl-objects.test.js` (created equals deleted after `destroy()`, program reuse, deletes only at a submission);
  the same Vulkan repro after the fix, 64 of 64 renders right; `device.glObjects` counts per kind. Missing: a
  self-contained driver repro (`docs/known-bugs.md`).

### 3.3 Compute tiers

| Tier | Selection | Execution | Important limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fragment | Stores map each invocation to its own renderable texture texel and no buffer is written | Full-target draw, scissored per target/slice | Target must be renderable. |
| Scatter | Bounded stores with no same-invocation read-after-write hazard | Instanced point draw per target; buffer words use R32UI textures of 4,096 x 8,192 words, as many as the buffer needs (one draw each; KB2604d, 2026-11-11) | At most 1,024 stores per invocation per target. A storage binding reaches 16 x maxTextureDimension2D squared bytes (1 GiB at 8,192), the layer's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` and `maxBufferSize` since KB2604d; evidence `compute-browser.mjs` `largeWords` (160 MiB target) and the splats truck in `scale-check.mjs` on the layer. |
| CPU | Atomics, workgroup memory, barriers, unbounded store loops, hazards, unsupported formats, or f16 uniform cases | Typed IR emitted as JavaScript; one invocation at a time, generators across barriers, f32 rounded with `Math.fround` | Under a CSP without `unsafe-eval` the same JavaScript runs on an interpreter (`compute/interpret.ts`), 13 to 41 times slower; cannot read cube, multisampled, or external textures; GPU-written inputs can cause synchronous stalls. |
| Package alternate path | Planned for large atomic, sorting, or GPU-driven workloads | Feature-specific implementation | No recorded shader required it at the snapshot. |

Package routes now cover VFX, scatter (not `ScatterTiles`) and the sky's light projection as well as DOF, splats,
culling and shadows. A CPU-tier kernel that reads a GPU-written resource waits for all GPU work before it, so one small
kernel can cost a whole frame: the sky projection cost 57 ms that way. Evidence: `routes.test.js` and the frame budget of
`visual:compat:budget`; the integrated-GPU budget run is still missing.

A route that reads a resolved multisampled depth must allow for the layer reading it as one sample (WebGL2 cannot
read one sample of a multisampled texture). DOF's route takes the nearest depth of each pixel and its four neighbours
when the capture is multisampled; without it silhouette pixels kept the background's depth under the object's colour
and every far gather drew a faint ring (2026-11-08). Evidence: `packages/dof/tests/gpu/compat-check.mjs`.

Texture read-back left the layer's base on 2026-11-06 (`device/readback.ts`, 70,274 B base): the queue holds a submit
with a `copyTextureToBuffer` until the chunk has loaded, as it does for compute, and the sizes gate measures the chunk in
the split's lazy number. Evidence: `tests/lazy-boundary.test.js` and `readbackOrder` in `compute-browser.mjs`.

The voxel path tracer has a route too (`packages/voxel-pathtracer/src/compat.ts`, 2026-11-10): the path loop of
`trace` runs as a sequence of fragment programs cut from the WebGPU kernel's own text (`src/compat-staged.ts`: start,
then per iteration hit, vertex, surface, and sample, shadow and gather per light kind, then post, and finish), at most
one traversal per program, with the path state in `rgba32uint` pages (about 200 MB for a part of 131,072 paths) and four
`rgba32float` sums a small kernel adds to the image buffers. Every statement runs once in the same order with the same
random numbers; against the single-kernel route 345 of 18,432 values differ by 1 or 2 units in the last place (at
most 2.0e-7 relative, ANGLE Vulkan). Direct3D 11 needed three more changes, each
at its cause: `D3DCompile`'s time grows 3.6 to 5.3 times per doubling of inlined code (the single program never
finished), so the budget is one traversal and one copy of the precise camera maths per program, and the vertex program
is cut in two (`VERTEX_CUT`; offline fxc 62.5 s to 14.4 s plus 25.8 s); fxc rejects the generated one-pass loop with
X3511 at ANGLE's draw-time recompile, which lost the context, so `unloop()` emits guards instead of break and continue;
and ANGLE recompiles every program with more than one fragment output at its first draw, synchronously, so the first
traced frame on Direct3D 11 comes after about 90 s on an RTX A6000. The CPU drives the loop 8 iterations a submission;
after each window a census pass marks the paths that finished an iteration before in a `stencil8` attachment that every
loop program tests, so they are rejected before their fragment runs (early ray masking, Purcell et al. 2002), and an
occlusion query counts the paths still running (Harris and Buck 2005). A readback costs Chromium about 15 ms whatever the
work, so after a tracer's first dispatch each part runs for the iterations the dispatch before needed and every part's
last censuses come back in one read at the end; a part still running there makes the dispatch run again with a read
after every window (no synchronous GPU read, `device.stalls` 0). A viewport batch makes its first submissions inside
the frame that starts it, and the frame that adds a landed batch starts the next (KB-L6b-ti, 2026-11-11; regression
`packages/voxel-pathtracer/tests/route-pace.test.js`): a frame loop that waits for the GPU now counts a sample every 2
frames on ANGLE Vulkan at 96 x 96, against 3 to 4 before (the staging TAA still check, measured 3 runs each at main and
with the change). The compat `queue.submit` ends with `gl.flush()`, so
submitted work starts at once as WebGPU's does; `device.passes` counts
the passes replayed. The layer owns every GL object it creates and keeps one program per GLSL text (up to 64 idle,
`IDLE_PROGRAMS`), so nothing is left for the browser to delete at garbage collection: on ANGLE Vulkan such deletions
mid-render corrupted fragment output 7 of the live staged programs (docs/known-bugs.md). The quick preview kernel is not
compiled on this route (142 to 168 s on Direct3D 11). Evidence: `browser-check.mjs --compat` rows traversal, analytic
and determinism on ANGLE Vulkan and Direct3D 11 (`npm run test:gpu:d3d11`: traversal 92.2 s, longest GPU wait 60 s, analytic 31.6 s (124.1 s before the stencil census),
determinism 0.7 s; 18,432 of 18,432 values identical for one seed; 1,777 passes and 1 census read on a predicted dispatch
against 8,483 passes with every iteration recorded, the same values; 345 of 18,432 values 1 or 2 units in the last place from the single-kernel route);
`analytic` on ANGLE Vulkan right in 64 of 64 renders (13 of 78 wrong before the GL ownership change);
`npm run test:gpu:d3d11-dispose` (tracer then engine disposed one second after submission: engine disposal returns in
25.5 s, bug 45); `tests/compat-staged.test.js`, `packages/webgl2-compat/test/passes.test.js` and
`packages/webgl2-compat/test/gl-objects.test.js` on the CPU; the C2 tracer rows on the
default Direct3D 11 backend; the whole `MARGO_COMPAT=1 test:gpu` check on Direct3D 11 (25 cases, 757 s of case time,
2026-11-11). Missing (KB-L5a-10, docs/known-bugs.md): `MARGO_COMPAT=1` `test:gpu:denoise`, `:denoise-materials`,
`:denoise-caustics`, the resampled lifecycle case and the steps whose first render waits for cold compiles (`:media`,
`:sky`, `:mesh-lights`, `:mesh-pbr`, `:mesh-pbr-lobes`, `:mesh-attributes`, `:denoise-ml`, `:stall`, `:guiding`, and
`:mesh-instances` under load) do not finish inside their limits on Direct3D 11, on main as on the L5a stack (paired
runs, 2026-11-15, each step listed in the entry): a 480 x 300, 16384-sample reference takes about 555 s there against 14 s on WebGPU. Since 2026-11-16 (fewer passes a sample, the same values) `:media`, `:sky`, `:guiding`,
`:mesh-attributes`, `:denoise-ml`, `:mesh-instances` and the resampled lifecycle case pass there (21 of the 29
scripts), and the reference takes about 449 s; the denoise steps, `:stall`, `:mesh-lights`, `:mesh-pbr` and
`:mesh-pbr-lobes` still did not. Since 2026-11-18 (KB-VPT-LOBES-COMPAT) an async render pipeline with more than one
colour target on ANGLE Direct3D resolves only after one rasterizer-discard draw into its own targets: that back end
compiles the pixel shader at link for the first output only and again at the first MRT draw, on the GPU thread, which
had put 206 s of compiles inside the first 8 x 8 image of the staged tracer. Since 2026-11-21 (KB6016e side finding)
a pipeline with one colour target is warmed the same way: on an Intel Arc 140V (ANGLE Direct3D 11, Edge) a 1-output
program reported its link complete after 58 to 74 ms and its first draw then took 194 to 346 ms more, so the compile
came after `ready`. The GPU check there, before the change: no warm draw before a 1-output async pipeline resolved
(it fails); after: one, the same pixels, and its first draw 5.3 ms against 10.7 ms for an unwarmed pipeline of the
same small shader (one loaded run, printed only, not asserted). Later the same day a probe on that laptop (a 256-step
loop, new shader text each run, three runs a kind) showed two more things. First, a program with a fragment stage and
no colour output (a depth-only pass that discards) also compiles at its first draw: link 45 to 53 ms, first draw 128
to 174 ms more (with no fragment stage, 1 to 4 ms). Second, the rasterizer-discard warm draw compiled nothing on that
backend: a warmed 1-output pipeline still took 131 to 152 ms at its first real draw. (The KB-VPT-LOBES-COMPAT probe on
the RTX A6000 had found that a discard draw compiles there.) The warm draw now rasterizes into its 1 x 1 throwaway
targets (scissor test off, viewport 1 x 1, every colour channel written), and every program on ANGLE Direct3D is
warmed, one with no colour target into a 1 x 1 depth-stencil buffer. After the change: link to `ready` 179 to 205 ms
for both kinds, first draw 1.2 to 2.1 ms.
Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-warm.test.js` (CPU, stand-in context: the warm draw rasterizes, and a
depth-only pipeline is warmed) and `packages/webgl2-compat/test/first-draw-browser.mjs` (in `test:gpu`: a count of
rasterizing warm draws before a 1-output and a depth-only pipeline resolve, and the same pixels as an unwarmed
pipeline). Both fail on the code before the change. Missing: the rasterizing warm draw has not been rerun on the
RTX A6000, and no other Direct3D GPU has been measured. `:mesh-pbr-lobes` now passes there in
3 min 53 s (420 s limit); `:mesh-pbr` (376 s) and `:mesh-lights` (383 s) pass their checks but still run past their
300 s step limits on the cold compiles themselves. Since 2026-11-21 (0e11055b5) the warm draw rasterizes and
depth-only pipelines are warmed too; the private-main sync ff88a70e7 (2026-11-24) reverted that, and 508b6c1cc
restored it with its tests on 2026-11-25. Same day (KB-L5a-10, Intel Arc 140V, Chrome 157, ANGLE Direct3D 11), a Chrome
trace of the staged tracer's first compile shows where the time goes: ANGLE compiles each program's pixel shader at
link on its worker threads (D3DCompile on ThreadPoolForegroundWorker) with only `SV_TARGET0` in its output struct, and
the warm draw compiles it again with all seven `SV_TARGET` outputs on the browser's one GPU thread (D3DCompile on
CrGpuMain, 3 to 22 s a program, one after another: 55 s for the denoise tracer). The two HLSL texts differ only in the
output struct (dumped from the trace), so the link-time compile drops the other outputs' code and is no use to the
draw. A probe of 7-output programs showed no WebGL state that changes this: binding the 7-target framebuffer before
`linkProgram`, or one output array, still paid the compile at the first draw (28 ms against 1 ms for the second
draw). While those compiles ran, the layer's synchronous reads of the next program's link status and binding table
held the page's thread (one `getUniformBlockIndex` 18.0 s), so the page stopped answering. Since 2026-11-25 a linked
program reads them only once no other program's warm draw is on the GPU (`LinkedProgram.waiting`, polled through the
warm draws' fences): the same trace's longest page-thread task went from 18.0 s to 0.84 s, and `test:gpu:d3d11`
passes (traversal 105 s, analytic 87 s, determinism 2.9 s). Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-warm.test.js`
("a linked program makes no synchronous query while another program warms", fails on the code before). Still missing:
the serial GPU-thread compile itself, which is ANGLE's design (docs/known-bugs.md, KB-L5a-10), and the 16384-sample
denoise references, which cost the staged route's passes, not compiles. Evidence for the first (2026-11-25): a raw WebGL2 repro
with no Margo code, `packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-mrt-compile-repro.mjs` (run directly, not a gate; Intel Arc
140V, Chrome 157). Three new programs a case, linked together: on ANGLE Direct3D 11 the 7-output programs drawn into 7
targets take 1.8 to 1.9 s each at their first draw, one after another (5.6 s), the 1-output programs and the same
7-output programs drawn into 1 target 1.9 and 2.5 s in all (their compiles run side by side at link); on ANGLE Vulkan
every case takes about 3.1 s in all. Its Chrome trace (`--trace`, category `gpu.angle`) shows every link's D3DCompile
on a worker thread with one `SV_TARGET` and a second one, with seven, on CrGpuMain for the 7-target draws only; most of
each such draw's 1.9 s comes after fxc, in the driver's build of the new shader. ANGLE documents draw-time recompiles on
a change of render targets (The ANGLE Project, "Dynamic Shader Compilation",
https://chromium.googlesource.com/angle/angle/+/main/doc/DynamicShaderCompilation.md). Missing: the same repro on
another Direct3D GPU (the RTX A6000) and an upstream bug for the one-target link layout. No layer-compiled kernel may hold a loop with a constant bound around a traversal: fxc unrolls it, and the
`coverage` kernel's 64-ray loop around `closest()` never finished its first compile in 22 minutes (89.4 s for the whole
`transparent` case with the bound read from the frame uniform, the same image hashes); `tests/compat-staged.test.js`
checks every layer-compiled kernel for it, and since KB-L5a-3 every staged program too, and that no staged program
reaches more than one traversal call: the resampled tracer's proposal loop held `closest()` (directional proposals) and
`shadow()` in its `sample` program, which ANGLE Direct3D 11 linked in 254 s and compiled again for 356 s at its first
draw, so an idle rule ended each `MARGO_COMPAT=1` run of `test:gpu:resampled`. Each proposal is now a pass of light
kind 1 (`const KIND_REPEAT=vec2u(1u,P)` in the kernel; `StagedTrace.steps` repeats kind 1's `sample`, `shadow` and
`gather` draws P times; the reservoir is private state carried in the path pages): 49 s link and 127 s at first draw
for all nine programs, the same image bit for bit on WebGPU (10 scenes, 2 to 64 proposals) and on ANGLE Vulkan but 78
of 768 values 1 unit in the last place apart for 2 proposals (the driver's own contraction). ANGLE Direct3D 11 compiles
every program with two or more colour outputs twice: at link for one active draw buffer, and again at the first draw
for the real ones (probe, 1,500-step program: 3.0 s link and 3.1 to 4.4 s first draw with 2, 4 or 8 outputs, uint or
float; 1 output or only draw buffer 0 active, no second compile). Binding the target framebuffer before
`linkProgram` does not change it. The staged programs write 7 targets, so each costs both compiles. Tracers watch `device.lost` once per device, so a disposed tracer is
collected while its device lives. Speed: a paired A/B of the old and new route builds in one page (per-round minimums,
the same image hash every round) measured a 320 x 240, 4-sample viewport batch 123 to 135 ms against 894 to 979 ms
on ANGLE Vulkan and a 1500 x 1100, 64-sample capture 43.0 s against 299.8 s (busy machine, `docs/limits.md`). Sources:
T. J. Purcell, I. Buck, W. R. Mark, P. Hanrahan, "Ray Tracing on Programmable Graphics Hardware", SIGGRAPH 2002,
https://doi.org/10.1145/566654.566640; M. Harris, I. Buck, "GPU Flow-Control Idioms", GPU Gems 2 ch. 34, 2005,
https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-iv-general-purpose-computation-gpus-primer/chapter-34-gpu-flow-control-idioms;
WebGL 2.0 specification, query and sync objects (results become available only after control returns to the browser),
https://registry.khronos.org/webgl/specs/latest/2.0/. Still missing: a run on ANGLE Metal and on an integrated GPU,
and quiet-machine timings.

**Direct3D 11 path tracer runs (KB6016e, KB6016f, accepted 2026-11-26, Scott).** ANGLE Direct3D 11 compiles each multiple-output program again at its first draw, one after another (`packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-mrt-compile-repro.mjs`), so voxel-pathtracer's `test:gpu:compose-native` and staging's `test:gpu:materials` under `MARGO_COMPAT=1` on that back end are an accepted difference: they need not finish inside their limits. Native WebGPU and the ANGLE Vulkan layer stay gated; no limit changed.

The CPU tier's `new Function` applies only to this opt-in compatibility path, and a strict policy sends it to the
interpreter instead of refusing it. General claims that nothing builds code at run time must stay scoped to the native
engine. Evidence: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/interpret.test.js` compares the two paths over the corpus, and
`compute-browser.mjs` reruns every case under a real policy; there is no quiet speed record of the interpreter yet.
The two paths compare bytes, so a NaN must have one encoding: JavaScript lets an engine write any NaN bits, and V8
wrote different signs on the two paths (2026-11-08). The CPU tier writes every stored, bitcast or packed NaN as
0x7fc00000 (f16 0x7e00), which WGSL 15.7.2 allows; `test/nan-encoding.test.js` holds it on both paths.
Recorded A6000/Edge measurements for CPU clustered binning
over 3,456 clusters were 1.5 ms with 16 lights, 2.8 ms with 64, and 9.4 ms with 256; a 64-wide reduction with seven
barriers reached 4.4 million invocations per second.

`@margoengine/geometry/gpu` has no route through these tiers: `GeometryGenerator` writes core's vertex buffers from a
frame pass at order -1000 and refuses the WebGL2 backend with `unsupported`. Evidence: `npm run test:gpu` in
`packages/geometry` on the RTX A6000, reading vertices back and rebuilding after `rebootDevice`.

`@margoengine/bvh/gpu` has no route through these tiers either: `GPUMeshBVH` takes a `GPUDevice` and refuses anything
else with `unsupported`; WebGL2 keeps the CPU tree. Its ray test is float32 and watertight, with a four-step slack on
each node's exit distance, so rounding never loses a hit. Evidence: `npm run test:browser` in `packages/bvh` on the
RTX A6000 compares 100,000 rays with the float64 CPU tree and fires 123,200 rays at vertices and shared edges from
inside a closed mesh.

`@margoengine/bvh/gpu-build` follows a vertex buffer the GPU writes, on the same WebGPU-only terms. A build is Morton codes, a
bitonic sort and the Karras hierarchy, then bounds climb one level a dispatch: a node's stamp names the dispatch that
finished it, and a parent reads only children stamped by an earlier dispatch, because threads of one dispatch have no
order. Evidence: trees read back and walked node by node, and rays through a pose only the GPU wrote, against a float64
CPU tree, in `packages/bvh/tests/gpu-build-browser.js`.

`CulledMeshes` with `occlusion` runs before core's main pass, so it cannot read core's depth, which has no texture binding
anyway: it redraws last frame's large kept instances depth-only with this frame's camera, at the scene's sample count,
and shares the Hi-Z pyramid of `packages/culling/src/pyramid.ts` with `CulledInstances`. An instance is hidden only
strictly behind the farthest occluder depth in its footprint, so the image is core's. On the WebGL2 layer it stays
frustum and screen size. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/meshes-occlusion-check.mjs`, 0 differing pixels against
core through camera and occluder changes, 9 of 1,509 instances drawn behind a wall, RTX A6000.

`CulledModels` (`@margoengine/culling/models`) runs the same cull on `PBRInstances` rows, world = node matrix x row. gltf/pbr
reads `primitive.redirect` as core reads `Batch.redirect`, so its colour and depth replays draw the kept rows; casters and
picking keep every row. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/models-cull-check.mjs`, 0 differing pixels with and without
shadows, RTX A6000. A primitive without instances gets one 20-byte indirect record from one dispatch and gltf/pbr draws it
through `primitive.culled`, so a culled one still costs its draw call on the CPU (WebGPU has no multi-draw). With
`occlusion` both tests also read the shared pyramid, built each frame from `addOccluder` surfaces drawn with this frame's
camera, as for `CulledInstances`. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/models-plain-check.mjs`, 0 differing pixels on the
real NodePerformanceTest.glb (2,066 of 10,000 primitives drawn close up) and through a wall that moves in, 1 of 146 drawn
behind it, RTX A6000. Still missing: a timed run, skinned and morphed primitives, and members of an instanced batch.

`addOccluder` puts core meshes, models and Terrain into the occluder pass of `CulledInstances`, each with the maths of its
own draw (core's `camera*(model*p)`; Terrain's rings on its own uniforms). An occluder must be a surface the frame shows,
so only front faces draw, by the sign of the matrix, and cut-out, blended, displaced and clipped primitives are left out.
Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/occluders-check.mjs`, 0 differing pixels against core, 0 of 576 parts drawn behind a
core wall, a materials wall and a terrain ridge, RTX A6000.

`bounds: 'box'` on `CulledInstances` adds each geometry's local box after the sphere tests: the box under the part's matrix
is an oriented box, its radius along a plane normal is exact, and its nearest depth is at a corner. It can only drop more than
the sphere, so a part it keeps is unchanged. Hi-Z still compares one nearest depth with the farthest occluder depth in a
screen rectangle, so a long part behind a slanted surface stays in. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/bounds-check.mjs`,
0 differing pixels against core, 0 of 900 rods drawn by box and 900 by sphere under a plate from above, RTX A6000.

`@margoengine/culling/shadows` culls casters per cascade: `prepareShadow` runs one thread per row, tests its sphere against the
six planes of each light matrix (Gribb and Hartmann rows, padded for float32) and appends the row to that cascade's list by
atomic add. List order is free, because a depth-only pass keeps the nearest depth in any order. A caster outside a light box
clips away in that pass, so the map is unchanged. The draw reads rows through an instance-rate u32 vertex buffer, so a batch's
list is a plain vertex buffer offset. Evidence: `packages/culling/test/gpu/shadows-cull-check.mjs`, 0 differing pixels against
every caster drawn in every cascade, RTX A6000. Still missing: a timed run.

Imposters (`@margoengine/lod`) draw 96 bytes an instance: world matrix, colour, emissive. As a shadow source a `LODSystem`
draws, per cascade, a card facing the light per object, reprojecting the ray along the light onto the nearest atlas view with
one parallax step, and stands the depth back by `r*(2/(frames-1)+4/frameSize)` so an imposter does not shadow itself. Evidence:
`packages/lod/test/imposter-full-check.mjs` on the RTX A6000. Missing: other GPUs, and a measure of the cost per cascade.
`@margoengine/selection` asks each engine plugin with `drawSelectionMask` to mark its own pixels; a `LODSystem` redraws the
selected imposters with the same fragment shader at the same depth. A pixel of alpha 0 is discarded whatever `fwidth` says:
it holds no depth, and once landed on the eye, in front of any wall. Evidence: `packages/lod/test/imposter-outline-check.mjs`
on the RTX A6000. Missing: other GPUs.

Shadow outlines have an outside reference: `packages/shadows/test/outside` compares a real glTF model's shadow on a white
ground with Blender Cycles, each side giving the ground's light with the model over its light without it, so no Margo
code decides the answer. Evidence: overlap 0.98 on DiffuseTransmissionPlant and 0.91 on AlphaBlendModeTest's masks, 0.31 with
the masks off. Missing: other GPUs.

`VirtualShadows` takes `drawShadow` sources: a source keeps one uniform per cascade slot and writes it with
`queue.writeBuffer`, which runs before the submit that follows it, so pages go four at a time, each batch in its own
encoder and submit, and the sources need no change. Feedback runs after the pages, because a custom receiver draws there
with slot 0 and the camera's matrix. Voxels read `shadowReach()` where the shadow pass defines it, as `VirtualShadows` does,
since `splits` is a field of the cascades' uniform alone; terrain reads its lighting group's layout from the WGSL the effects declared, since a table of
binding numbers fitted only `Shadows`. Evidence: `packages/shadows/test/virtual-custom-browser.mjs`, overlap 0.97, 0.95 and
0.95 with `Shadows` for culled parts, scatter and voxels; real Mount Rainier elevation against Blender Cycles, overlap 0.86
(`Shadows`) and 0.81 (`VirtualShadows`), 0 with the terrain not casting, RTX A6000. Missing: other GPUs.

Terrain's ambient (2026-11-26, KB-TERRAIN-SKYAMBIENT1) is core's term, albedo x `radiance[3]` x `lighting.ambient` (a
fourth frame row, the floating-origin anchor after it, 192 and 208 bytes). `Sky.add(terrain)` is a terrain lighting
effect whose `finish` runs after every other effect's `shader`: it puts `skyLighting` (nine harmonics, Ramamoorthi and
Hanrahan 2001; split-sum reflections, Karis 2013) at bindings 8, 10 and 11 in place of that term, keeping what earlier
effects multiplied it by (layer occlusion, relief sky visibility) and a hemisphere beside it. Evidence:
`packages/terrain/test/sky-ambient.test.js` (the patch and its bindings) and `sky-ambient.browser.mjs` (coloured
ambient and the sky's blue on flat ground, the same pixels on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, RTX A6000). Missing: other
GPUs; the planet terrain (`@margoengine/terrain/planet`) has no sky ambient.

Terrain layer materials (`@margoengine/terrain/layers-pbr`, 2026-11-07) are a lighting effect in the same group, at
bindings 90 to 92: they patch the layer loop (a height-blend factor on each weight, then the layer's normal and surface
samples) and wrap the fragment so the per-pixel roughness is written into the input before any later lighting code reads
it; the tilted normal is a surface gradient from the three projections' volume gradients (Mikkelsen 2020), so no tangents
exist and shadows and clustered lights see the same `n`. SSR's capture keeps the geometric normal and terrain roughness.
Evidence: `packages/terrain/test/layers-pbr.browser.mjs`, flat maps 0 of 255 from the terrain's own shading with rules,
painted weights and bump; tilts lit from the right side on both axes; real CC0 rock maps 1.6 times the luminance spread of
colour alone; Radeon 680M. Missing: other GPUs, cost timed.

Terrain near displacement (`@margoengine/terrain/displace`, 2026-11-08) sits after the layer materials at bindings 97 and
98: it wraps the materials' fragment so the view ray's hit (parallax occlusion) replaces the shading position, keeps the
surface's own derivatives for every texture read, and multiplies the sun's direct term by the relief's self-shadow. The
shadow ray walks a maximum mipmap (Tevs, Ihrke and Seidel 2008) built from the surface maps' alpha by a compute pass at
attachment, so it cannot step over a ridge; a fixed-count march did (0.08% of the rock shadowed where a CPU trace gives
2.85%). Evidence: `packages/terrain/test/displace.browser.mjs`, shadowed share 2.71% and 30.7% against a CPU trace's
2.76% and 30.85% at 10 and 30 cm of relief; parallax 3.07 of 255 from real geometry, flat 24.5; Radeon 680M. Missing:
other GPUs, cost timed.

Terrain deformation (`@margoengine/terrain/deform`, 2026-11-08) sits at bindings 99 and 100 and wraps the terrain's lit
fragment (whatever effects came before): each near fragment's view ray is marched through a camera-centred relief map
(parallax occlusion, offset limited), the hit's XZ on the undeformed tangent plane replaces the shading position (so
shadow lookups still see the surface the shadow map holds) and the relief's slope bends the normal. The map is written
by compute passes: an atomic maximum over float bits keeps the deepest print a texel, a fixed refill a second fades
them, and a moving window clears the texels it exposes. Evidence: `packages/terrain/test/deform.browser.mjs`, map to
0.06 mm of the CPU profile, picture 6.6 of 255 from real geometry (flat 33.3); Radeon 680M. Missing: other GPUs, cost
timed.

Mesh to terrain blending (`@margoengine/terrain/blend`, 2026-11-08) patches core's standard fragment through the same
mesh-ID varying and per-pixel block as `TerrainColors` (shared in `terrain/src/mesh-patch.ts`, so either runs first
and the shader holds one copy). At the top of the block, where control flow is uniform, it takes the pixel's footprint
from the position's screen derivatives; per blended mesh (a storage row by mesh id) it reads the ground height from the
heightmap, fades the colour toward the virtual texture's, roughness toward the terrain's and the normal toward the
heightmap's over `height`, so core's lighting shades the mesh's foot as the ground. Evidence:
`packages/terrain/test/blend.browser.mjs`, seam 126.6 to 6.8 of 255, nothing off the foot changes; Radeon 680M.
Missing: other GPUs, cost timed, sloped ground in a picture check.

World-space UI panels (`@margoengine/ui/world`, 2026-11-08) share the screen UI's drawing core (`ui/src/painter.ts`,
used by `UiRenderer` too, so one copy of the instanced rectangle and SDF glyph pipeline): each panel's draw list is
painted into an `rgba8unorm-srgb` texture in its own submission only when the list or the glyph atlases changed, then
mipmapped, and a quad pass at order 25 (inside the scene, before post-processing) samples it with depth test against the
scene, one camera uniform per view index so XR eyes never share a buffer written in the same frame. Evidence:
`packages/ui/tests/world-browser.mjs` on a Radeon 680M (colours, occlusion, back face, repaint counts, a real click by
camera ray). Missing: other GPUs, an XR headset, cost timed.

Screen UI on the WebGL2 preview backend (`@margoengine/ui`, 2026-11-08): `ui/src/painter.ts` builds one `UiBatch` of
rectangle and glyph instances (16 floats each) for either backend; `ui/src/gl.ts` draws it with instanced attributes and
two GLSL ES 3.00 programs that compute the same rounded box distance and SDF coverage as `ui/src/shader.ts`. WebGL2 has
no base instance, so each run moves its attribute offsets to its first instance; clip regions are scissors in GL's
bottom-up rows; the atlases are `TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY` (R8 for SDF, RGBA8 for colour glyphs) grown by reallocation and
re-upload. The code is a separate chunk loaded on the first WebGL2 frame. Evidence: `packages/ui/tests/webgl2.test.js`
(a recording WebGL2 context: draws, offsets, scissors, texture units, lost and restored contexts) and the WebGL2 check
in `packages/ui/tests/ui-browser.js` on a Radeon 680M (colours, rounded corner, text ink, clipped list, unchanged
frame). Missing: other GPUs, WebKit and Firefox, world panels on WebGL2.

Planet terrain (`@margoengine/terrain/planet`, 2026-11-08) draws a cube sphere quadtree with its own pass and shader.
Precision: each patch stores float32 vertices relative to its float64 centre; each frame the CPU subtracts the camera
position from each drawn centre in float64 (one instance attribute a patch) and builds a view-projection with no
translation from the camera's position, target, up and projection, so no float32 value holds a world coordinate; depth is
core's reversed z. Evidence: `packages/terrain/test/planet.browser.mjs`, the disc from orbit within 0.2% of a sphere's
projection, the horizon dip within a pixel, no sky through the ground and the same picture with a `FloatingOrigin` at
6,371 km from the world origin; Radeon 680M. Missing: frame cost, other GPUs, shadows and lighting effects on it.

Clipmap terrain far from zero (`TerrainOptions.floatingOrigin`, 2026-11-11, large worlds). The camera is local to a
`FloatingOrigin`; the terrain forms the float64 world eye (local plus `terrain.shift`) and plans in world space: the ring
corners snap to the world lattice and only `corner - shift` is uploaded (`planRings`), the heightmap corner and height
offset go up less the shift, and the virtual texture plans its windows in world texels on the float32 texel the GPU
holds (`planWindows`), bakes each texel at `base + (w - a + 0.5) * e` with `a` the world texel at or below the shift
and `base = a * s - shift` (float64, then float32, under one texel), and reads at `(local + shift mod P) / period`, P the coarsest period, so a rebase keeps every cached page and
bakes nothing. Layer samples that repeat with position add a per-layer `wrap` (the shift from the terrain's anchor less
whole 24 / scale macro repeats) and the macro tone adds `fract(k * 0.302)`, so every texture coordinate equals the
terrain-relative one at any distance. Cache surfaces, overlays and imagery read `local + Frame.anchor.xy`, XZ relative
to the anchor; decal boxes and the deformation window are rewritten local on a rebase; blend reads the heightmap corner
from the cache's frame. Without the option every shader, uniform and rule is unchanged (the uniform work-count digest
pins it). Evidence: `packages/terrain/test/origin.test.js` (planners bit for bit at 0, 100,352 and 10,000,384 m, rules,
rebase uploads, queries) and `origin.browser.mjs` on an RTX A6000, Edge 157, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (identical
pictures at those offsets with the origin there; within 1 of 255 and 99.9 percent equal rebased onto the camera in
place; overlays, layer materials with displacement, footprints and lit-path imagery identical at 1e7), plus a 1e5 case
in `compat.browser.mjs`. The 400 m flight that rebases on the way ends on an origin 2/3 m off the metre grid; it is
checked against two controls with no rebase at that origin: the same flight without a rebase draws the final pose at
rest pixel for pixel, and the flight is within 1 of 255 and 99.996 percent equal to it (99.961 on the WebGL2 layer).
Against the exact picture the flight is 99.836 percent equal (99.828), the rest control 99.832 (99.867): float32
rounding of a frame off the grid, present without any rebase (each local number is the correctly rounded float32 of
the float64 one, IEEE 754-2019; Goldberg, What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic,
1991, https://doi.org/10.1145/103162.103163), so that bar is the control's share less 0.1 percent. Two fixes found on
the way: the ring-move test compared the float32 uniform with the float64 corner, so a cell size not exact in float32
redrew the shadow maps every frame; and the bake placed a texel from its window's corner (`o * s - shift`), so off the
grid a page's colours depended on where the window stood when it baked (36 pixels of a flight differed from the same
pose at rest; `origin.test.js` checks that a texel bakes at one float32 point from any window). The same GPU check
covers blend (a box placed with `FloatingOrigin.place`) and stream: identical pictures at 0 and 1e7, and within 1 of
255 and 99.9 percent after a rebase in place. It found blend's fade noise reading local XZ, so a rebase slid the
noise along the box (82 of 255 on 0.27 percent of pixels); the noise now reads local XZ plus the cache frame's
`anchor` (world less the terrain's anchor), checked in `origin.test.js` across a rebase. Missing: other GPUs, frame cost.

The lit floating-origin terrain draws relative to the eye (2026-11-28, KB-TERRAIN-REBASEROUND1; Cozzi and Ring 2011,
"3D Engine Design for Virtual Globes", chapter 5; Ohlarik 2008, "Precisions, Precisions"). With the 16x anisotropic
layer sampler (KB-TERRAIN-GRAZESMEAR1) a rebase in place changed 0.103 percent of the streamed ground's pixels by one
level on the WebGL2 layer, over the 0.1 percent bar: every float32 number derived from a local position (the clip
position, each layer's texture coordinate and its screen derivatives) rounds differently once the origin moves, and
the texture unit's sub-texel and level steps, taken several times along an anisotropic footprint, turn that into 8-bit
flips. Now `Frame.view` holds each ring's lattice less the eye (float64 on the CPU) and `Frame.column` the camera matrix
times the local eye (float64); the vertex writes `Output.eye` (that lattice plus the ring-relative grid offset, and the
local height less the eye's) and clips at `camera * (eye, 0) + column`. The lit shader's last step (`eyeShader`, after
every entry and effect edits its text, so the text they look for is unchanged) reads each layer sample at the
eye-relative point plus the layer's `eyeWrap` and `eyeTone` (the world eye less the anchor, less whole macro repeats,
rewritten when the eye moves) with that point's derivatives; the virtual texture's bake keeps the local reading (the
same texel, whole repeats apart). Shadow, occluder and local-shadow passes keep the local vertex. What is left after a
rebase in place is the float32 rounding of the camera matrix's own translation inside `column`. Evidence: the stream
rebased in place at 1e7 changes 5 of 76,800 pixels on the WebGL2 layer and 3 natively (79 and 66 before; scratch
builds with one part each: eye-relative texture coordinates alone 45, clip alone 64), `origin.test.js` checks the
lattice less the eye and the layer eye wraps are the same float32 across a rebase in place. Missing: other GPUs.

Both shadow classes take `effects`: objects that declare WGSL at bindings 40 and up (four each), give a factor that
`shadowLit` multiplies the sun by, and update once a frame after the depth passes. With none the shader text is what it was,
which the golden GPU proofs pin. `cloudShadows` runs the sky's cloud remap and erosion along the ray to the sun, with the
sky's noise text, clock and height read from `sky.cloudLayer`, so there is one cloud field, not a copy. `check.mjs` in
`packages/shadows/test/outside` now reads partial light back through Khronos PBR Neutral's toe on a white ground below the
curve's shoulder: until then only full shadow was measured, and partial values on a dim blue ground read too dark. Evidence:
`packages/shadows/test/outside/check.mjs`, a real image as `lightPattern` against a real sheet of it across the sun in Cycles,
overlap 0.996, mean difference 0.0074, 0.71 and 0.26 for the same mask shifted; `packages/shadows/test/light-function-browser.mjs`,
ground and the sky's own render along the sun ray agree on all 256 points, before and after 2,400 m of drift, against 0.64 for
the old ground and the new sky, and core meshes, materials, gltf/pbr, terrain and voxels go dark under a black pattern in both
classes. Missing: other GPUs; a real cloud photograph over real ground is not the claim, the claim is agreement with the sky.

`VolumetricClouds` (`@margoengine/sky/volumetric-clouds`) ray marches a layer between two shells around the planet in one
full-screen fragment pass at order 3, between the sky and its fog. f32 cannot form |o|^2 - (R + h)^2 at planet scale, so the
shell roots use the constant |e|^2 + 2R(e_y - h) - h^2 from the camera's own position and the stable quadratic form, and a
point's height is (|p|^2 + 2R p_y) / (|o| + R). Two tiling noise volumes are generated once by compute on the first frame and
after a device loss; the sky light is reduced from the sky's reflection map by one 64-thread workgroup each frame. Without a
depth texture the pass depth-tests against the cleared sky; with one it reads the first sample of multisampled depth.
Evidence: `packages/sky/test/features-check.mjs` (coverage 0 exact, coverage, depth occlusion in front of and inside the
layer, motion) at 4x and 1x on a Radeon 680M. Missing: other GPUs, a quiet timing, a comparison with a reference renderer.

`volumetricCloudShadows` (`@margoengine/sky/cloud-shadows`) is a shadow effect that renames the clouds' WGSL field with its
binding (`shadowFxCloud...N`) and marches it from each receiver to the light. It keeps its own noise volumes, filled by the
same deterministic generator on its first update, and writes the layer fields with the clouds' own `writeLayer`, so it
shares no GPU object with `VolumetricClouds` and survives either side's device loss alone. Evidence: `features-check.mjs`,
48 ground points against the clouds seen from each point toward the sun, mean 0.0018 before and 0.0021 after 1,500 m of
drift, 0.29 for stale shadows; Radeon 680M. Missing: other GPUs, any timing, a soft edge from the sun's size.
