### Section 5 evidence: Chromium teardown moved to a browser host (2026-11-10)

The process/stdio close recurrence is explained and worked around, not fixed in
Margo: after `TerminateProcess` the browser's exit code is set within 65 ms and every
owned pipe closes within 1 ms of its release, but Windows signals the process object
only once the kernel has torn the process down: 65 ms to 1.2 s beside the batches,
8.7 s beside verify, over 30 s in the failures (docs/known-bugs.md, "Open, outside
Margo"). The suite's event loop was never blocked and Playwright started no helper
program. `scripts/support/browser-host.mjs` now owns Playwright's browser server in
a process of its own; a suite ends the browser through it, is acknowledged in
milliseconds, disconnects and moves on, waiting for the proof of teardown only up to
2,000 ms. Survivors past 120 s are recorded in
`test-results/browser-host-survivors.log`. Evidence: the 40-cycle loop under load in
docs/known-bugs.md, `tests/browser-host.test.js`, `tests/browser-teardown.test.js`.
A close that failed 677 ms after the end (batch 217) was a false survivor: the
native waiter took a pid whose start time it could not read (gone between lookup
and read, or taken by a service this user cannot query) for one of ours. It now
skips such a pid; two regressions in `tests/browser-teardown.test.js` (2026-11-10).
Missing: a run on the laptop and the Apple silicon Mac, and the cause of the kernel's delay.
Close limit (KB-P3h, 2026-11-15): a hosted close still open after `CLOSE_LIMIT_MS`
(20,000 ms) kills the host and browser trees, releases the host and fails with
`SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT` listing `open`, `killed` and `survivors` (docs/limits.md, "Browser
close limit"). Before, the budget threw but left both running and the host referenced,
so a suite that caught the error could not end. Evidence: `tests/browser-teardown.test.js`
(a real stuck host is killed and its suite exits; old code: still running at 45 s).
Missing: the exact path of the one nodes-browser hang that raised it (not reproduced in
12 loaded runs).

#### Batch 197 globe control evidence

Reference ellipsoid rays, geodetic-normal transport, local-horizon tilt and radial
altitude clipping live in the optional controls/globe entry. CPU fixtures cover
WGS84 and triaxial radii and a live floating-origin rebase. The optional-controls
browser gate checks anchor projection, actual foreground rendering and zero
validation errors on WebGPU and WebGL2. It does not establish terrain collision
or full rival navigation parity beyond the batch row. No core/stage code changes.
### Section 5 evidence: optional tile styling (batch 239 job 1)

The streaming renderer now exposes a content decorator without importing its implementation. `tiles/style` evaluates property expressions on the CPU and writes existing optional-package PBR vertex colours, instance tint/matrix rows and point colour/size buffers. Show=false discards mesh surface fragments, degenerates hidden instance transforms and assigns hidden points zero size; alpha uses the native PBR blend path. Bindings retain authored arrays for restoration and declare added GPU buffer bytes to tile eviction accounting. The interpreter never executes supplied JavaScript. Evidence: packages/tiles/tests/style.test.js covers language evaluation, binding updates, invalid styles and restoration; the tiles browser fixture checks two visible red and two hidden features of the real CC0 structural metadata sample. Both rendering backends use the same binding path. No new rendering backend, core maths or speed claim.


#### 5. Batch 273 XR canvas mode persistence

Compatibility presentation preserves a canvas's first output mode across XR
and desktop device configurations. Both transition directions have an owning
unit regression in canvas-present.test.js, which fails on the old code. The
root XR fixtures surface engine/GPU errors while waiting for frames, rather
than waiting forever after XR ends on an error. Simulated stereo sessions are
rendering/lifecycle evidence, not headset evidence; the dedicated compatibility
XR test owns the XRWebGLLayer framebuffer comparison.

### Batch 171 climate input evidence

The optional formats layer reads CDF-1/2 hyperslabs and adapts the existing VTK XML decoder. Numeric data and
intact volume topology feed the existing volume and grid renderers; core/stage, GPU maths and backend shaders
are unchanged. Analytical byte-layout tests plus 200 pinned NOAA samples cover six owner-written files.
The formats-browser leaf exercises both backends and compares identical-source image hashes by renderer kind.
HDF5, oriented-image resampling and general solver rendering remain outside the claim; see docs/limits.md.
No GPU is used for parsing/building or CPU tests.

Batch 171 integration evidence remains incomplete: all 30 root GPU assertions pass, but the shared
Chromium launcher waits past its unchanged 30 s deadline for process/stdio close after native
termination. PID 84700 was absent afterward; exact event/handle cause remains unproved. The owning
shared-launcher repair belongs to batch 160, not sciviz. This is a failing hang and blocks landing
job 4; metadata repairs and pre-rebase GPU acceptance do not supersede it. No failed check is
weakened, retried unchanged, marked busy, or reported as a passing suite. See known-bugs.md.
### 5. Sprite slices and repeat fills (batch 245 job 1)
The optional sprites/slice entry reuses the existing sprite pipeline and frame
hook. Each image occupies up to nine stable instance slots with a common parent
pivot and sort keys. Repeat counts and phase map UVs within each source cell,
using integer loads or explicit-gradient linear sampling. Core and stage have
no changes. CPU layout and real pixel readback fixtures are in sprites/tests/
slice.test.js and slice-check.mjs; both GPU backends are required before landing.
### Section 5 evidence: batch 197 BoxGizmo

The optional controls/box-gizmo reuses controls' OverlayRenderer and tessellate paths for WebGPU and WebGL2. Exact local mesh bounds feed transformed wireframe edges and fixed CSS-size handle triangles; no core or stage change. Its optional-browser fixture checks both backend colors, triangle counts and edited transforms. Original-pose CPU tests cover parent-frame pivot preservation, three rotation axes, snapping and cancellation. Device restoration releases overlay GPU resources through the package plugin. Bounds do not include child meshes, skinning or morph deformation.
### Section 5 evidence: optional FSM views and SCXML (batch 250)
FSM optional entries retain CPU state-machine semantics and add no core/stage or shader dependency. Unit evidence covers payload delivery, final/always macrosteps, task cancellation/generation isolation, DOM view ownership and bounded XML conversion. The package browser gate renders the Inspector-compatible view and checks default DOMParser round trips in normal Chromium and forced compatibility mode. The view has no backend-specific GPU math; these captures establish DOM placement, live trace/history updates and cleanup, rather than renderer numerical accuracy. XML execution, a complete SCXML processor and remote actor inspection are outside these claims. README work is recorded in the build-phase owed list.

### Section 5 evidence: sprite rigging (batch 245 job 2)
The optional skeletal entry owns all new transforms, IK, slots and timeline
math. There are no core/stage changes. The two-bone solver uses the cosine law
where the first bone has uniform magnitude scale; general affine hierarchies
use bounded coordinate descent and report their residual. Bezier time is inverted
before evaluating the channel value. Slot order is independent of bone order.
CPU evidence: rigging.test.js, including skin conversion regressions. GPU evidence:
rigging-check.mjs plus the existing skeletal-check.mjs, on both backends.


### Batch 175 job 5: GPU graphs

The optional graph-gpu entry owns sorted Morton spatial trees, FR/FA2 compute passes, on-device swinging/traction reductions, direct-buffer node/edge draws and GPU force-directed edge bundling. Core and stage are untouched. Graph GPU tests compare both backends with exact CPU equations, track compatibility CPU/GPU routing, check nonuniform-tree error, styled pixels and collision-free labels. The native million-node proof counts every output and records deterministic work and persistent buffers; runtime speed remains unmeasured during build. External GPU state hides after device loss and must be recreated. See docs/limits.md and the batch175 graph GPU result records.

57. Collision for soft bodies (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/probe.rs`, `kernel-common/src/cloth.rs`, tests `tests/soft-probe.test.js`, `kernel/tests/cloth.rs`). Particles meet the rigid world through `KernelWorld.softContacts` (`Physics.softContacts`): a batch of balls, each swept from where it was to where it ended the step (the cast of `cast.rs`, van den Bergen 2004), giving up to 4 contacts a particle as planes (the nearest surface point and the normal out of the collider, the depth or the gap still open within a margin, the surface's velocity there, rigid and deformable, the time of the touch), for every collider shape, honouring per-particle groups and query flags and never meeting sensors; read and written through two fixed buffers (1,024 particles a call). Cloth meets itself through `soft-kernel/src/collide.rs`, which calls `cloth::find_contacts` from kernel-common once a substep and pushes the contacts apart as position constraints (Mueller et al. 2007) with one call site in the soft solver's substep, taking back up to the Coulomb coefficient times the push of the touching points' tangential motion (Bridson et al. 2002, Mueller et al. 2007: a cloth on a slope holds when tan(angle) is under the coefficient and slides above it, tested); The search, `cloth::find_contacts` (a plain Rust function over slices, no allocation, the same bits native and Wasm): sweep and prune over the triangles' swept boxes, point against triangle and edge against edge within a thickness, found by halving the step and dropping the halves a Lipschitz bound shows cannot hold a contact (Wang et al. 2021 inclusion with Mirtich 1996 conservative advancement), grouped by shared vertices (Harmon et al. 2008). Evidence: a dense sampling of 600 random moving triangle pairs finds nothing the search missed, closed forms for the crossing time and weights, the cases of Wang et al. that break earlier methods built from their descriptions (their benchmark files are not in the repository), and a brute-force search of every pair on random soups. Missing: Rapier 0.21 has no soft bodies, so no oracle; the contact response (impulses, friction, impact zones solved) is the soft solver's; with `dt` a particle is swept against a moving collider along the collider's own motion over the step (its linear and angular velocity, first-order rotation of the solver's pose update, halving the step with a Lipschitz bound on the gap), and a particle that starts touching meets the face it came from.

Shape forms, mesh tools and height field cell status (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/mesh.rs`, `kernel/src/mass.rs`, `src/mesh-tools.ts`, tests `tests/next-shape-forms.test.js`, `tests/next-mesh-tools.test.js`, `tests/next-heightfield-cells.test.js`, `kernel/tests/mesh.rs`, `tests/next-trimesh.test.js`). A capsule takes an axis or two end points; a tetrahedron is the convex hull of four points with the mass |det| / 6; colliders resize in place (`setRadius`, `setHalfHeight`, `setHalfExtents`). A closed, outward trimesh has a mass: the kernel sums signed tetrahedra to the mesh's centre (the divergence theorem; Mirtich 1996, Eberly 2002) for volume, first and second moments, then the principal frame, once at creation, and the TypeScript entry refuses an open edge or a negative volume before the build. Connected components (triangles that share a vertex, union-find) and the half-edge topology (a twin for each directed edge, Mantyla 1988) are read on request. `voxelsFromPoints`, `voxelizedMesh` (a triangle-box overlap test for the surface, Akenine-Moeller 2001, and a ray parity fill) and `convertMesh` (hull, box, oriented box by Jacobi eigenvectors of the covariance, Gottschalk, Lin and Manocha 1996) are TypeScript over the existing colliders. `convexDecomposition` takes a `borderRadius` for a rounded decomposition. Height fields keep one status byte a cell in the word rows voxel grids use: a zigzag bit splits the cell along its other diagonal and two bits remove its left or right triangle; `mesh_triangle`, `mesh_across`, the contact route, the ray walk and the sweep skip a removed triangle, and its neighbours see an open edge. Evidence: the kernel meets shapes and rays exactly as the same triangles held as rows do (random statuses, bit for bit), and the statuses survive a snapshot. Missing: Rapier 0.21's JavaScript build has no cell status, tetrahedron, mesh converter, voxel builders or mesh mass, so these have no oracle and the proof is closed forms and the triangle-row equivalence; compound `FIX_INTERNAL_EDGES` and V-HACD's voxel terms are not built.

Combine rules, wide interaction groups, removal events and collider boxes (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/solver.rs`, `kernel/src/events.rs`, `kernel/src/query.rs`, `kernel/src/pair.rs`, tests `kernel/tests/solver.rs`, `kernel/tests/groups.rs`, `kernel/tests/events.rs`, `tests/next-interaction-groups.test.js`, `tests/next-events.test.js`, `tests/next-pair-queries.test.js`). The combine word gains a third bit for each rule (bits 4 and 5, so the old words read the same): clampedSum is min(a + b, 1) and geometricMean is sqrt(a b), 0 when either is 0, and the pair takes the strongest rule by Rapier's documented order. Interaction groups gain upper halves in a second word and wide flags per collider (collision and solver groups), the `or` test used only when both colliders ask for it, and queries carry the upper halves by a flag and one extern; a packed word that is all ones means all 32 groups so the default and every 16-bit user keep their old results (the replay hash moves, because the layout has two new columns). Removing a collider or a body ends what it touched with a stop marked REMOVED, delivered at the end of the next step as Rapier delivers it; the JavaScript side keeps the removed colliders until those events are read. `collider.sweptAabb` puts the body where a collider's next pose needs it for one read of its box and puts it back; `collisionAabb` grows the box, which already holds the contact skin, by the prediction. Evidence: closed forms, the two-way and either-way tests on contacts, solver groups and queries, the packed words against Rapier 0.21 pair by pair, and a stop event per removal. Missing: Rapier 0.21's JavaScript build has no wide groups, test mode, clampedSum or geometricMean (its Rust crate has them), so those have no oracle; sweptAabb merges the boxes at the two poses and does not follow a turn between them.

CCD sensor crossings, debug style and Physics snapshots (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/ccd.rs`, `kernel/src/events.rs`, `src/debug.ts`, `src/physics.ts`, tests `kernel/tests/ccd.rs`, `tests/next-events.test.js`, `tests/next-debug-render.test.js`, `tests/next-physics-snapshot.test.js`, `tests/next-contact-modifier.test.js`). After the CCD pass settles a fast body, each sensor its solid colliders sweep through with the same conservative advancement as solid contacts (van den Bergen 2004; Mirtich 1996), whose pair did not touch before and does not overlap at the end, is told as a start and an end with no pair row; a pair that touches at either end is the step's own events'. Debug lines take a colour style and body axes. `takeSnapshot` copies the kernel bytes with the rows of the bodies, colliders and joints, and `restoreSnapshot` refuses a world whose rows differ. Evidence: a 300 m/s ball through a 2 cm sensor reports exactly one start and one end with CCD and none without; the restore replays bit for bit. 61. Turning shape cast (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/cast.rs`, tests `kernel/tests/cast.rs`, `tests/next-turning-cast.test.js`). A query shape whose centre travels while it turns is cast by conservative advancement (Mirtich 1996, "Impulse-based dynamic simulation of rigid body systems", chapter 2; van den Bergen 2004, "Ray casting against general convex objects with application to continuous collision detection"): the gap to a collider, read through the shape cast's own geometry, allows a jump in time of the gap over |linear| + |angular| r, r the farthest point of the shape from its centre. Evidence: a rod turning about its middle touches a ball at the time acos(0.3 / 1.5) / pi within 1e-3 s, a turn about a far centre keeps the centres 0.5 m apart at its hit, a straight motion equals the straight cast. Missing: Rapier 0.21's JavaScript build has no `cast_shape_nonlinear`, so there is no oracle; the cast takes one convex query shape.
62. Contact pair frames and sub-shapes (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/pair.rs`, `kernel/src/cast.rs`, `kernel/src/api.rs`, tests `tests/next-collider-api.test.js`). The pair query hands the kernel's manifold two more words, the sub-shape of each side: a compound child's index in its chain, or the triangle or cell `each_part` last visited (kept in a cell on the world, not in the arena). TypeScript puts the normal and the points into each collider's frame from its world pose and gives each point the pair's mixed friction and restitution and its surface velocity, which is what the solver reads for it. Evidence: a crate turned a quarter about y reports the floor's normal up in the floor's frame and down in its own, a mesh pair names its triangle, a compound's children are 0 and 1. Missing: a mesh child of a compound names its triangle, not its place in the compound; Rapier 0.21's JavaScript contact manifolds have local normals and points but no friction or restitution per point.
63. Contact modifier per-point edits and pair user data (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/layout.rs`, `src/physics.ts`, tests `tests/next-contact-modifier.test.js`). The modifier may move a contact point's anchors on each body and its distance, and keep a word with the pair. The solver reads each point's gap from the anchors of the two bodies at each substep, never from the stored separation, so the distance setter moves the anchor on the second body along the normal by the difference; the arms and masses are made from the anchors after the modifier, so an edit reaches the solve. The pair's user word is a new column zeroed when a pair or a mesh part is made. Evidence: a crate sinks by exactly the 0.1 m added to its distance, anchors moved off its side tip it over, the word counts the steps a pair lives and starts over for a new one. Missing: friction, restitution and surface velocity stay the pair's; Rapier's solver contacts hold them per point.
64. Debug modes for solver contacts, pseudo normals and soft bodies (2026-11-24, `src/debug.ts`, `src/soft.ts`, tests `tests/next-debug-render.test.js`, `tests/next-soft-debug.test.js`). The solver's contacts are read from the solving list after the step: where each point sits on each body (the anchor turned by the body, from its centre of mass), a line across the gap and a tick along the normal. The pseudo normals of a `fixInternalEdges` mesh or height field (a field's triangles split and thinned by its cell statuses) are the face normal at each triangle's middle, the mean of the two faces' normals at each shared edge's middle and the angle-weighted mean of the faces round each vertex (Baerentzen and Aanaes 2005), which is the normal the ghost rule (Catto 2020) clamps to over a flat or concave edge. Soft bodies draw their edges from the kernel's columns, coloured by strain against the rest length, plus particle crosses and the contact normals the kernel keeps for each particle. Evidence: four points a resting box, a quad's two faces and shared edge, a stretched rope's end edge red. Missing: Rapier 0.21's JavaScript debug render has no such modes.
65. Internal edges of a compound (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/cuts.rs`, tests `kernel/tests/compound.rs`, `tests/next-compound-edges.test.js`). The parts of a convex decomposition meet face to face, but each collides alone, so a shape sliding over a join meets the edge of the part it is on: its contact normal leans towards the cut and a ball is thrown up (0.81 m/s measured, against 2e-6 on one hull). The fix reads the parts' hulls once, at build, after the rule that a normal outside the surface's own cone belongs to the face (Catto 2020, "Ghost Collisions", box2d.org, which the triangle mesh code already follows) and with the plane and polygon tests of Ericson 2005, "Real-Time Collision Detection", 3.8 and 5.4: a face another part holds whole, opposite and in the same plane, is a cut and its contacts are dropped; an edge between an outline face and a cut, with another part's face going on in the outline's plane across it, is flat, and a contact on it takes the outline's normal and is moved onto the outline's plane (the other shape's deepest point along the normal for a single point, or each point of a face contact projected). The marks live in two new hull columns, so a hull must belong to one compound. Evidence: a ball, a box and a capsule cross two and three parts as they cross one hull (vertical speed under 1e-3), a step between parts is untouched bit for bit. Missing: Rapier 0.21's JavaScript build has no compound flags; a face covered by two parts together is not a cut; only hull parts are read.

Collada colliders and work counts (2026-11-24, `src/meshfiles.ts`, `kernel/src/api.rs`, tests `tests/next-meshfiles.test.js`, `tests/next-parameters.test.js`). `parseDAE` reads Collada 1.4 with a small XML reader (elements, attributes, text): the geometries a visual scene's nodes instance, their triangles, polylists and polygons fanned from their first corner, placed by the nodes' matrix, translate, rotate and scale, scaled by the file's unit and turned to Y up from its up axis, welded as the other readers weld. `world_count` hands the world's own bookkeeping to TypeScript (awake bodies, islands, pairs, pairs and contact points solved, joints, impacts, events, steps), which costs no work in the step and is the same for the same inputs. Evidence: a cube as a polylist and as triangles is the same eight welded corners and twelve triangles, in metres, Y up and lifted by its node; a stack of three boxes counts three pairs and twelve contact points. Missing: skins, materials and animations of a Collada file are ignored; 2D has no counts or timing yet.
67. URDF and MJCF robots (2026-11-24, `src/robots.ts`, `src/xml.ts`, tests `tests/next-robots.test.js`). Both formats are read by the small XML reader into links (a pose in the robot's frame, collider options, an optional mass) and the joint to the parent; the poses are composed at the joints' zero, the bodies are made and each joint is a revolute or prismatic joint whose frames on the two bodies line the file's axis up, so the rest pose reads 0 and limits are in the file's own angles. A URDF inertia tensor is diagonalised by Jacobi's method (Golub and Van Loan 2013, 8.5) into the principal moments and a frame the body takes with the inertial's origin. The tree becomes one multibody when its links hang from the root without a floating joint between, else impulse joints. Evidence: a pendulum of a 1 kg point mass reaches sqrt(2 g h) within 0.25 m/s and keeps its centre 1 m from the pivot within 2 mm in both joint modes; a three-link tree has the file's joints and poses; an MJCF arm has its inertial's mass and a plane to rest on. Missing: mimic, planar joints and effort limits (URDF), default classes, actuators and tendons (MJCF); Rapier's own loaders are Rust crates with no JavaScript build to compare with.
68. A scalar build of the kernel (2026-11-24, `kernel/src/math.rs`, `scripts/build-kernel.mjs`, `src/kernel.ts`, tests `kernel/tests/soft_sqrt.rs`, `tests/next-simd-fallback.test.js`). The kernel's only SIMD instructions were the square root through `f32x4_sqrt` (Rust's core has no float square root), so a build without `simd128` needs one of its own: `soft_sqrt` and `soft_sqrt64` take the root of the mantissa as an integer, digit by digit, with the exponent made even, 28 (or 56) more bits than the result needs, and round to nearest even from the remainder (ties to even only when it is exact), which is the correctly rounded result the instruction gives. The scalar blueprint is built with no target feature and no `--enable-simd` in the optimiser, is its own lazy chunk, and carries the same build id as the SIMD one, because the two give the same bits. `loadKernel` probes the engine with a one-instruction SIMD module and loads the scalar build when it fails. Evidence: two million random f32 patterns (normals, subnormals, NaNs) and half a million f64, and the exact squares and their neighbours, equal the hardware bit for bit; the scalar module holds no 128-bit instruction (read with binaryen) where the SIMD one holds thousands; the 10,000-step replay scenes give the committed hashes in both builds; a child process whose engine denies SIMD loads the scalar build and steps. Missing: the 2D kernel has no scalar build yet (its `f32x4` solver lanes already have a scalar path in `four.rs`; its square root does not), and the 3D contact solver does not batch four constraints.

The same integer square root as the 3D kernel (item 68), kept as its own copy in the crate, replaces the SIMD form when the build has no `simd128`; the four-lane polygon clip already had a scalar path. The 3D block solver (2026-11-24, the default since item 81, `packages/physics/kernel/src/solver.rs` `block_normal`, header word `block_solver`, `world_set_solver(25)`, tests `kernel/tests/block_solver.rs`, `tests/next-block-solver.test.js`). Off by default, so a world that does not ask solves as before and the replay hashes of `tests/fixtures/replay-hash.json` are unchanged (the header word fits the padding of its last 16 bytes; only the kernel source hash moved). On, a manifold of two to four points takes the loads that meet its linear complementarity conditions, found by trying the 3^n assignments of its points to free, at zero or at their cap in a fixed order, Cholesky on the free block, the first assignment that meets the conditions within sixteen roundings of the terms it adds taken. Each point's diagonal carries the soft row's own term plus the square root of f32 rounding of its stiffness, which makes four coplanar points (rank three) positive definite and splits their load evenly, as the sweeps' null-space step does. Evidence: a box on four points shares the load within 2 percent and rests where the sweeps leave it to 0.1 mm; a 12-row pyramid settles; of a pile's manifolds fewer than one in a hundred fall to the sweeps. Missing: friction is not in the block, and four-wide batches of this work are not built (B-03).
73. The replay hash covers state, not solve order (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/src/world.rs` `hash` and `arena_hash`, `layout.rs` `SCRATCH`, `tests/fixtures/replay-hash.json`). `World::hash` now takes the header and every column but twelve that only hold the order a step solves in: the pairs and joints it solves (`SOLVE_PAIRS`, `SOLVE_JOINTS`, `SOLVE_LEAD`, `SOLVE_VIA`, `SOLVE_SHARE`), the impacts it found (`IMPACTS`) and the islands it numbered (`ISLAND_*`). `arena_hash` is the old fingerprint of every word. Why: a step that solves independent islands in another order, or on several threads, leaves every body, contact and carried impulse bit for bit where it was and moves those lists, and a replay proof must not see the difference. Before the change the old hash and the new one were taken on the same runs: the arena hashes of the kernel scene, the kernel scene with the block solver on and the `Physics` scene, in Node, equal the committed lists of the old hash word for word (kept in the fixture as `kernelArena`, `kernelBlockArena`, `physicsArena`), and native code gives the same; the state lists (`kernel`, `kernelBlock`, `physics`) are new. A change that only reorders independent work regenerates the arena lists and must leave the state lists as they are. Missing: no multibody or soft-body scratch is excluded yet, because none is reordered. The hash also leaves out the header's layout words (`bytes`, the row capacities and the column offsets): it covers state, not where state lives, so a new column moves no state hash. That second change regenerated the state lists (`kernel`, `kernelBlock`, `physics`) and left the three arena lists as they were, in native code and Node. It leaves out the header's magic number too (it counts the columns) and the header's padding, so a new column moves no state hash; each of these three changes regenerated the state lists and left the arena lists as they were. It also leaves out the multibody walks' call count (`mb_calls`, in the header) and the stamp column it numbers (`MB_STAMP`): a stamp says which walk last reached a root, so it follows how many walks a step made, which an island-by-island solve makes more of; no state is in it. It leaves out the count of layouts (`layout`, in the header beside `mb_calls`) too (2026-11-28, KB-PHYS-LAYOUTHASH1): it tells JS to bind its views again and says where state lives, so a snapshot taken before a step that grew the world (the locks' Newton words, `NEWTON`, or the pairs) and put back after it replayed to another hash with every body to the bit; that regenerated the state lists. The framework's extra state (`RigidSolver.extraState`) leaves out the kernel's workspace columns (`WORKSPACE` in `layout.rs`, `KernelWorld.workspaceColumns()`): scratch a step writes before it reads and carries into no later step, which may grow inside a step (`NEWTON` today), so a snapshot names the same regions on either side of that growth (`tests/world-rigid-solver.test.js`, `kernel/tests/canonical.rs`).
74. The solved pairs are listed by island (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/src/solver.rs` `order_pairs_by_island`, columns `ISLAND_PAIR_START`, `ISLAND_PAIR_COUNT`, `ISLAND_PAIR_CURSOR`, test `kernel/tests/island_order.rs`). The first piece of the island-major solve: `prepare_contacts` puts each island's pairs in one run, in the order they were found (a stable counting sort through the idle `IMPACTS` column), and notes where each run starts and how long it is; pairs with no awake dynamic body in an island come last. The order moves no body: the state lists of the replay fixture (`kernel`, `kernelBlock`, `physics`) are exactly what they were, in native code and Node, and only the arena lists were regenerated. Islands share no body that a solve changes, which is why. The solve still walks the list front to back, so nothing is faster or slower yet; the next pieces give joints and couplings runs of their own and swap the loops to island by island. The joints and the couplings are listed the same way: `order_joints_by_island` sorts the joint paths (a path stays whole, since a path stops at every body that is not awake and dynamic and islands join the bodies of a joint that are, so all its joints share one island; the four lists that go by place in the list move together, through `JOINT_ORDER` and `JOINT_TEMP`), and `order_couplings_by_island` lists the couplings' slots in runs (`COUPLING_ORDER`), each with `ISLAND_JOINT_*` or `ISLAND_COUPLING_*` start, count and cursor columns; tests `each_islands_joints_are_listed_together_with_their_paths_whole` and `each_islands_couplings_are_listed_together_in_slot_order`. A multibody's roots need no list: they are found in an island's run of `ISLAND_BODIES`, which keeps the awake-list order. State lists of the replay fixture unchanged again, arena lists regenerated.
75. Island by island solving (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs` `run_substeps`, `group_window`, `staged_pose`, `integrate_kinematics`, `world.rs` `Window`, `world_set_solver(26)`, tests `kernel/tests/island_major.rs`, `kernel/tests/replay.rs` `island_by_island_gives_the_state_phase_by_phase_gives`, `tests/next-island-major.test.js`). A step's substeps run once for the whole world (phase by phase, as before) or once for each island through all its substeps (the default). Every loop of the solve reads its range from `World::window`: the awake bodies and every listed pair, joint and coupling, or one island's runs (the lists put in runs by island in 74) and the island's run of `ISLAND_BODIES`; the group after the last island holds what no island does. The kinematic bodies are the one shared thing a solve reads at a pose that changes in the step: while the islands solve their columns keep the pose the step began at, and the readers (`pose_rotation`, `pose_center`, `pose_position` in the contact rows, the joint view, the couplings) ask for the pose at the stage of the substep through `staged_pose`, a pure function that repeats `integrate_poses` from the start pose with the same arithmetic and writes nothing; once every island has solved, `integrate_kinematics` moves them through the substeps for real. Joint breaking, continuous collision and the events stay after all islands. Evidence: the state hash is bit-equal to phase by phase after every step of the 10,000-step replay scene (joints of every kind between random bodies, kinematic bodies, sleeping, with and without the block solver), of stacks and a pile, of a platform under two stacks (both kinematic kinds), of joint chains hung from a beam and from a sweeping platform, of gears and distance ranges between islands, and of a multibody arm beside stacks; the whole kernel test suite and the physics package's tests pass with island by island the default; the replay fixture's state lists are unchanged and only the arena lists were regenerated. Sources: D. Baraff, "Dynamic Simulation of Non-Penetrating Rigid Bodies", PhD thesis, Cornell University 1992 (islands of bodies in contact that can be solved apart), and R. Tonge, F. Benevolenski and A. Voroshilov, "Mass Splitting for Jitter-Free Parallel Rigid Body Simulation", ACM Transactions on Graphics 31(4), SIGGRAPH 2012 (independent groups of constraints in parallel). The multibody rows read a kinematic base or parent through the same staged pose as the contact, joint and coupling rows, and the evidence has a multibody arm on a moving kinematic base and one whose link rests on a moving platform. Missing: threads are the next piece, and the audit of the shared state a worker must not touch (`header.impacts`, `mb_calls`) is part of it.
76. The voxel ghost rule drops a graze of a hidden face (2026-11-24, `packages/physics/kernel/src/voxel.rs` `voxel_verdict_of`, tests `kernel/tests/voxel.rs` `a_cube_stopped_by_a_wall_over_the_seam_of_two_grids_is_not_thrown_by_the_cell_under_the_wall` and `the_ghost_rule_drops_a_graze_that_leans_away_from_the_one_open_face_and_keeps_a_body_inside_the_cell`). The rule that turns a cell's contact normal to the nearest open face when the normal leans toward a hidden one turned it, for a cell with one open face on the far side from the normal (the cell under the foot of a wall, open only below), to that face: the cube a wall stopped was pushed along the wrong way and thrown 10 m. Found by taking the voxel package's failing seam test down to the kernel: two coupled grids, a wall on the second's floor, a frictionless cube at 6 m/s, thrown 11 m; the cube's foot grazes the cell under the wall (apart by 0.0994 m along the normal), and in Rapier, run as a black box on the same scene, the throw is 0.004 m. Now a contact whose points are all apart or touching along the normal (`separation >= 0`) and whose normal leans away from the open face it would be turned to is no contact; a shape inside the cell (a point at a negative separation) is still pushed out through the face it leans toward, as the sensor and the body inside terrain need. After this the cube is thrown 0.115 m with the sweeps (0.12 m on a wall inside one grid too: the stop is shared unevenly between the points of two manifolds) and 0.02 m with `blockSolver`; Rapier's 0.004 m. Open: three of the voxel package's seam tests (balls on triangle meshes) fail for another cause, a speculative contact on the edge of a triangle of a neighbouring mesh whose normal, found at the start of the step, has turned by the time the ball reaches the edge; two coplanar `trimesh` colliders reproduce it (a ball at 6 m/s is thrown 1.4 m/s at their seam, none in Rapier, whose contacts reach only 0.002 m ahead).

77. A ghost contact at a seam between two meshes is dropped (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/mesh.rs` `Held`, `on_open_edges`). Two coplanar meshes (the chunks of a terrain, the pieces of a floor) have an open edge where they meet, and the ghost rule needs the triangle across an edge, which a seam has none of. A ball rolling over the seam met the second mesh's edge from the side, a speculative contact with a normal leaning back, and its row cancelled the approach along that normal: a kick of 1.3 m/s up for a ball at 6 m/s, 0.76 for a capsule, where one mesh gives none. Now a new contact of a ball, capsule or box whose points all lie on open edges of a `fixInternalEdges` triangle is dropped when the shape, its half extents or radius held smaller by the depth the solver holds a resting shape at (the slop, to which a rigid speculative row closes every substep, plus the g h^2 one substep of gravity can add before the next solve: 0.37 mm at the defaults; a ball measures 0.217 mm, a box 0.204), stays strictly on one side of the triangle's plane at the start and the end of the step (the centre's travel, and a turn's swing along the normal, off a capsule's axis). The plane is the triangle's, so a triangle of any size is tested exactly; a shape that crosses the plane or sinks deeper than that keeps its contact (an edge struck from the side is a real hit), as does a contact held from the step before. Evidence: `kernel/tests/mesh.rs` (ball, capsule and box cross two plates as one, and the rim of a plate still stops a ball that strikes it from the side), `tests/next-mesh-seam.test.js`, and the voxel package's physics tests (22 of 23 pass; the 23rd is KB-PHYS-WALL1). Still missing: a seam under a hull, cylinder or cone, and a turning cast for the contact that does hit.

78. A buried voxel cell gives nothing to a shape nearer its hidden side (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/voxel.rs` `nearer_hidden_side`). The ghost rule snaps a contact whose normal leans toward a cell's hidden faces to the exposed face it is closest to. For a floor cell under a wall, buried but for its bottom, a cube's foot pressed a slop into its hidden top as the wall stopped the cube was snapped to the open bottom, 1.8 m down; the solver pushed it at its speed cap and the cube sank 2.2 cm (KB-PHYS-WALL1). Now a snap to a face the normal leans away from is dropped when the snapped manifold is deeper than the one before it: the shape is nearer the hidden side it came in by, which is a filled neighbour whose own exposed faces push it out the short way. A shape deeper in the cell from that side than out of it through the exposed face is still pushed out there. Evidence: `kernel/tests/voxel.rs` (the cube sinks no deeper than the solver's resting depth with either solver; it sank 2.2 cm before) and the voxel package's physics tests (23 of 23). Still open: the sweeps throw that cube 0.115 m at 8 substeps and 2 passes (KB-PHYS-SPEC1), which the block solver does not.

79. A height field is edited in place (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/mesh.rs` `refit_grid`, `api.rs` `collider_refit`). The terrain bed (PA-37) changes the ground every step; a deformable mesh would carry a tree and a triangle list for a grid that needs neither. Its heights are written into the field's own vertex rows and `refit_grid` recomputes only the box and radius, marks the motion so contacts reach as far as the farthest height moved for that step, and the collider is looked at again and wakes what rests on it. No rows are added. Evidence: `tests/earth-bed.test.js` (a kernel ray against `Bed.sample` on 1,681 points within 2e-5 m and the same normal; a ball falls into a crater opened over a second, the world's memory and mesh rows unchanged).

80. Faces win ties against a held edge pair (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/sat.rs` `sat_coherent`, test `kernel/tests/sat.rs` `a_face_resting_on_a_parallel_edge_keeps_both_ends_after_an_edge_pair`). The separating axis test keeps last step's face within the 1 mm bias so the reference face stays coherent; it also kept last step's edge pair within that bias, and an edge pair that ties a face lies near parallel along it, so its one point clamped to an end of the edge: a box face resting on a block's edge was held at one end at a time and rocked without end (KB-PHYS-EDGEHOLD1, a voxel debris piece). An edge pair now beats the face by the bias, held or not (Gregorius, GDC 2015). Evidence: on 1,734 poses of a plank on a cube's edge a held edge pair gives what a test with no history gives (1,499 lost an end before); the voxel debris and ragdoll get-up tests pass. The replay fixture's lists moved: every manifold that held an edge pair through a tie now has the face's points.

81. The block solver is the 3D default (2026-11-25, `packages/physics/kernel/src/world.rs` header word `block_solver`, tests `kernel/tests/voxel.rs`, `kernel/tests/stability.rs`, `kernel/tests/replay.rs`). Item 72's exact solve of a manifold's normal rows is now on unless `setSolver({blockSolver: false})`; it waited on KB-PHYS-BLOCK1, closed by the substep levels. It closes KB-PHYS-SPEC1: a frictionless cube a wall stops at 6 m/s no longer rises above its rest height (the sweeps threw it 0.115 m), and that test's bound goes from the 0.2 m it was loosened to back to 0 m. It needed two fixes first: the joint webs' energy ledger (KB-PHYS-LEDGER1), and item 80, without which a voxel debris piece on a block's edge rocked without end with the block solve. The ragdoll get-up test's forward push of 40 sat on the edge between landing face down and face up with the sweeps; with the block solve the edge is at 41 and 40 lands half on its side, so the test takes 36, which lands face down for every push from 32 to 40. The replay fixture's `kernel`, `physics` and `physicsAdaptive` lists are the default world's, and the second kernel list is now `kernelSweeps` (the scene with `blockSolver: false`). Evidence: the whole kernel suite with the new default, the 20- and 30-row piles at 9.81 and 9.80665 under 1 mm/s from 30 to 90 s, all 60 joint webs with no gain over the kinematic work with either solver, native and Wasm bit for bit. Missing: friction is still solved a point at a time against the block's loads (item 72).

82. The rigid kernel lives in a world memory (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/memory.rs`, `api.rs` `io_bind`, `packages/physics/src/kernel.ts` `KernelWorld`, `scripts/physics-modules.mjs` `KERNEL_SLOTS`, tests `tests/kernel-arena.test.js`, `tests/world-rigid-solver.test.js`). The kernel is linked as a module of the world's memory: it imports the memory, its statics sit in slot 15's window (14.9 KB of 64 KiB: the face and particle batch records, 720 KiB, moved out of statics into a region the host binds), and it links no stack (KernelWorld gives it a 1 MiB stack region). Its world's block is a region of an `Arena` (item K05 of the framework): `Arena::ensure` asks the host's `region_resize`, which allocates or resizes the block, moving it with one copy when it cannot grow in place; the kernel already re-reads its base after every growth, as growth re-lays its columns. KernelWorld's views rebind whenever the memory's buffer changes, so another region growing the memory between steps leaves them reading the world. `new Physics(null, {arena: world.arena})` puts the rigid solver's state in the physics world's memory, and its regions then name no memory of their own. Evidence: the replay fixture's state and arena hashes are unchanged (only the kernel source hash moved), a block forced to move steps on to the bits of one that grew in place, and a Physics on the world's arena steps and restores to the bits of one alone. Missing: the shared-memory (threaded) build of the kernel, so a shared world memory is refused with `unsupported`; the soft and 2D kernels still keep memories of their own.

83. Islands share no solve state (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/solver.rs` `normal_rows`/`solve_impacts`, `world.rs` `Window`, `claim_stamps`, `multibody.rs` `unite_multibodies`, test `tests/next-multibody.test.js`). Groundwork for solving islands on threads: the strikes a substep finds are listed in the window's own run of `IMPACTS` (from its first pair times the manifold size) with the count in the window, not the header; multibody walk stamps come from per-window ranges claimed when the window is set up; and the moving links of a multibody under a fixed or kinematic root are one island (KB-PHYS-MBISLAND1). Evidence: the replay scenes' state hashes are unchanged (only the arena lists moved, as the header's walk count moves), the physics (1,219) and kernel suites pass. Missing: the solve window itself still lives in the one `World` the kernel's static holds; a thread needs a view of its own.

84. Islands solve on threads (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/integrate.rs` `step_begin`/`plan_islands`/`solve_island`/`step_end`, `world.rs` `thread_view`, `api.rs` `world_step_begin`/`world_solve_islands`/`world_step_end`, `packages/physics/src/kernel.ts` `useThreads`/`stepAsync`, `src/kernel-thread.ts`, tests `kernel/tests/threads.rs`, `tests/kernel-threads.test.js`). A step is begun on the main thread (broad and narrow phases, islands, rows) and every island's substep level and first multibody stamp are planned there in island order (ISLAND_LEVEL, ISLAND_STAMP, scratch); then any thread solves any island on a view of the world of its own (`thread_view`: the same block, a window, clock readings and counts of its own), and the main thread ends the step. Planning the levels before any island solves gives the same bits as before (an island's level reads only its own state). The kernel has a third build, threaded (Wasm SIMD and atomics, importing a shared memory, built as the cdylib alone so fat LTO compiles `core` with atomics), loaded only by `loadKernel({threads: true})`; each worker is its own instance of it over the world's memory with its own stack region. Evidence: the state hash after every step equals one thread's at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads, with native threads (300 steps, up to 43 islands a step) and with Wasm workers in Node (240 steps); the replay state hashes are unchanged. Missing: the broad and narrow phases are serial; the engine plugin's `Physics.step` steps on one thread; no browser run of the workers yet (Node only).

85. A step's order is the world's own (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/island.rs` `canonical_lists`, `sort_list`, test `kernel/tests/canonical.rs`). At the start of every step and again after the island build's wake-ups the awake list is put in body order and the active pairs in the order of their colliders and parts, by a stable bottom-up merge sort through scratch columns (ISLAND_BODIES and IMPACTS are free at those points), O(n log n) a step. Islands are numbered by their lowest body, and finding pairs, numbering islands, solving and reporting events follow rows and colliders, not the order bodies woke or pairs were found (KB-PHYS-ORDER1). Evidence: worlds woken in three shuffled orders, reshuffled every 50 steps, and one restored from a snapshot at step 300 step to the same bits for 600 steps; the replay fixture's lists were regenerated, as the solve order is new. Missing: the state hash still covers pair rows, which come from a free list, so two worlds whose pairs were found in different orders can move alike and hash apart; the broad phase and islands are still the 3D kernel's own, not kernel-common's (framework section 6).

86. A multibody's projection stays a projection at any length (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/multibody.rs` `mass6`, `symmetric`, test `kernel/tests/multibody_chain.rs`). The articulated-body pass from the last link to the first keeps a symmetric inertia symmetric, but it grows the asymmetry rounding leaves, about 3.5 times a link in a chain of slender links. Each link's inertia is now built in doubles from its principal axes and mirrored, and D, the articulated inertia and its transport to the parent are made symmetric at every link (KB-PHYS-MBSYM1). Evidence: a chain of 24 and of 64 capsules released level keeps every link under the speed its fall can give it for 600 steps, where it ran past 10^5 m/s or out of range before. Missing: the projection is checked by energy on chains only, not on wide trees.

87. A multibody solves springs, pins and drag directly (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/multibody.rs` `tree_springs`, `spring_tree`, `add_pins`, `add_drag`, `hold_multibodies`, columns JOINT_ELASTIC, MB_HELD, FLOW_X, DRAG_ACROSS; facade `Multibody.setImplicitMotors`, `pinJoint`; tests `kernel/tests/multibody_chain.rs`, `packages/physics/tests/multibody-springs.test.js`, `rod.test.js`).
    - A link's motor springs marked JOINT_ELASTIC, its pins and its drag toward a flow are taken into the articulated-body pass as backward Euler terms. The springs are terms on the joint coordinate (h d + h^2 k on D). The pins are stiff springs between anchors (h^2 k = 10^6 m). The drag is h J^T C J on the link's own mass matrix.
    - The pass runs after the pushing passes and before the poses move. It adds only what it changes, the projection with these terms less the projection without, so the joint rows' push to close their gaps stays. Projecting the speeds outright took that push out, and a cantilever crept 5 % in 40 s.
    - The joint passes leave a held tree's elastic motors alone. A pin's other body takes its pull back after the pass.
    - Evidence: a cantilever of 8 to 64 links at 4 and 16 substeps lands within 0.0002 % of where its springs balance. Motors in the joint passes ran away from 16 links on. A taut cable between two pins rings within 0.07 % of its closed form.
    - Missing: a loop inside one tree (a pin between two links of the same tree) is not held. A pin's reaction on its other body is applied after the pass, not solved with it.

88. Friction anchors follow a turning body, and kinematic bodies can move on smooth paths (2026-11-26, `packages/physics/kernel/src/solver.rs` `tally_drift`, `integrate.rs` `kinematic_pose`, `smooth_velocity`; facade `PhysicsBody.setNextVelocity`; tests `kernel/tests/solver.rs` `a_plate_rides_a_deck_turning_about_an_axis_far_away`, `a_plate_rides_a_deck_on_a_smooth_path_for_minutes_at_any_substeps`, `packages/physics/tests/deck-props.test.js`).
    - A friction anchor's slide is its material points' move over the substep: the centres' steps and the arms' turns at the arms the bodies have now, as a series in the substep's spin, so a turning body's centripetal carry is counted (KB-PHYS-ANCHORLEVER1).
    - A kinematicPosition body given a target velocity moves along the cubic Hermite path of its pose, target and end speeds, at its chord each substep, and every kinematicPosition body's substep pose is taken along its path from the step's start (KB-PHYS-KINJUMP1). Its spin each substep is the turn its poses make, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series of the path's rotation vectors to third order, so a deck that rolls and pitches at once carries its props where its surface goes (KB-PHYS-SPINBCH1).
    - Evidence: a plate 60 m from a pitching deck's axis holds within 0.7 mm over 36 s (1.8 cm before), and on a smooth path within 0.09 mm for six minutes at 8 and 16 substeps (21 cm before). On the storm deck (demand 0.56 g) a plate at 1.3 times the demand holds within 1.84 mm over 36 s (2 cm before), plates and chairs below it slide, cups tip by w/h, and every pile hold-still test is unchanged.
    - Missing: f32 poses far from the origin round each move the same way, so a body 1 km out at 17 m/s falls behind its speed (KB-PHYS-POSEROUND1, a floating origin planned); from 32 substeps a prop on a moving deck still slips (KB-PHYS-FINECONE1). A body touching through several colliders (a chair on four legs) holds as one collider does since KB-PHYS-MULTIPAIRCREEP1 (2026-11-28).

89. A multibody's pin to a free body is solved as a spring between two bodies (2026-11-27, `packages/physics/kernel/src/multibody.rs` `pin_terms`; test `packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js` "a weight on a rope's end hangs still").
    - The pin's implicit spring eliminates the free body's velocity within the step: C and pull are taken through (I + C W)^-1, W the body's mobility at its anchor (inverse mass and inverse inertia through the arm). A fixed or kinematic body has W = 0 and keeps them.
    - Evidence: a 2 kg and a 50 g weight on a rope's end hang within 1e-3 m of the rope's length and stand still (thrown 19 m up, and blown up, before). Multibody, joint, rod and replay suites unchanged.
    - Missing: several pins on one free body each eliminate it alone (one Gauss-Seidel sweep over them); a light rope's links held against a surface under high tension (3 g links at 100 N) are still unstable in the contact solve.
90. A taut tree holds its tension's stiffness across its links in its solve (2026-11-27, `packages/physics/kernel/src/multibody.rs` `add_tension_stiffness`, `pin_tension` in `add_pins`; test `packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js` "a cable whose tension dwarfs its bending stiffness").
    - A joint whose spring along the links carries a tension T gives each of its links h^2 T (l / 2)(I - t t^T) on its turn in the backward Euler solve, and a pin that gives its end link the same from its spring's pull (the geometric stiffness of Tournier et al. 2015, per link: a taut string's energy is (T / 2) sum l theta^2). It is taken in by the share rho / (1 + rho) of the link's turning stiffness the tension is (rho = T (l / 2) over the joint's bending spring), so a rod its bending holds is unchanged and a cable its tension holds is stable at any step.
    - Evidence: a 7.9 m cable of bending stiffness 1 N m^2 at 48 kN, which swung to hundreds of metres at 30 and 60 steps a second, rings within the pluck's 0.76 mm at 30, 60 and 600; ordinary rods damp as before within a part in 1,000 a period (0.23 % against 0.12 % at 60 steps a second); the measured vortex-induced vibration cases and the multibody chain tests are unchanged.
    - Cost: a cable its tension holds is damped by backward Euler, about 4 % of critical at 30 to 60 steps a second and 0.7 % at 600.
    - A pin that gives (`pin_spring`) holds across at PIN_GIVE = 1,000 times its give's stiffness rather than at h^2 k = 10^6 m, which grew as 1 / h^2: at 2,400 steps a second a rounding gap of 3e-8 m was a pull of 10^6 N, whose turn with the link the solve held explicitly, and a rod stretched 3 % at its pins was stopped by the kernel. Evidence: the same cable rings within the pluck's swing at 2,400 steps a second; an inextensible rod pinned at both ends (no give, still 10^6 m) holds at 60, 600 and 2,400; the multibody, rod and measured vortex-induced vibration tests are unchanged.
    - Missing: a tension's stiffness under compression (left out: pushed, a chain buckles by its own springs).

## Batch 252 navmesh worker evidence (section 5 supplement)

The optional navmesh/wasm entry loads one feature-local Rust SIMD raster asset and an owned CPU worker. Exact output evidence is in packages/navmesh/test/wasm.test.js and the crate's tests: byte-identical ordinary/tiled polygon files, equal reference clipping counts, cancellation/error/timeout teardown and source/artifact hash enforcement. The SIMD work proof keeps coverage, triangle order, span merging, classification and polygonization unchanged. Native rasterization uses fixed stack clip buffers, not allocations per cell. Evidence still owed: quiet-machine end-to-end speed measurements and browser/CSP hosting matrix. No core/stage or GPU backend change.
Batch 215 scroll pin evidence (section 5 supplement): packages/tween/test/scroll-pin-browser.mjs checks actual window/element layout and scroll destinations under native and compatibility browser runs. CPU fixtures use deterministic RAF clocks. Dependency VFX compatibility replay equality remains separately blocked as recorded in docs/known-bugs.md; no rendering-backend change is made by the pin entry.

## Section 5 evidence: batch 262 standalone bindings

Inspector's optional tweak entry has native DOM interaction checks alongside
rendering WebGPU and WebGL2 preview engines (test/parity-browser.mjs), plus
a forced --compat run of the same WebGPU path through WebGL2 compatibility. The browser script
is discoverable as inspector/test:browser for check:gpu-packages. CPU tests
exercise gesture boundaries, shared undo, enum identity and abort/disposal. No
core, stage, GPU mathematics or rendering pass is added.

## Section 5 evidence: inspector gizmo ownership and arbitration

The selection bridge uses existing controls rendering, including its WebGL2
compatibility path; it adds no GPU math or core API. Real pointer tests prove
rendered handles, selection retention, camera suspension and whole-drag undo.
The owner-scene regression now prevents inspector cleanup from removing a
same-named plugin in the default scene. Every gizmo plugin is attached in the
inspector's scene and is removed on abort, engine disposal or inspector removal.


### Batch 171 geographic atmosphere evidence

The optional sky/planet owner reuses AtmosphereTables and Hillaire transport for a supplied world-to-planet transform and observer. The sciviz facade inverts Figure.model, supplies ECEF solar direction from sky/astro, and shares an optional fragment appearance with geo tiles, scalar/point meshes and GPU flow. A type-only interface keeps sky out of existing root/feature imports. Each data fragment gets its own aerial segment rather than sampling an opaque globe depth at the wrong elevation. Earth polar stretch, chordal ground lighting and camera domain are explicit in limits.md.

### Section 5 evidence: float32 GGX D at low roughness (KB6016c)
Every GGX D now writes its denominator as |n x h|^2 + a2 nh^2 instead of nh^2 (a2 - 1) + 1 (equal for unit vectors), because in float32 1 - nh^2 cancels near the peak of a narrow lobe: core's D was 28 % high at roughness 0.03 on an RTX A6000 (WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer alike). packages/core/tests/ggx-precision.browser.mjs cuts core's D statements into a compute shader and compares 576 float32 cases at roughness 0.03, 0.05 and 0.1 with an f64 D: worst 6e-5 after the fix (bound 0.2 %). The term is max(|n x h|^2, step(nh, 0)): where the half vector faces away and nh is clamped to 0, |n x h|^2 alone fell below 1 and made D unbounded on back-facing shading normals, so D stays a2 / pi there (back-facing cases in the GPU test; CPU in packages/core/tests/smith.test.js and tests/smith-shaders.test.js). The shared ggxD/ggxDOf text carries the same form to every package that imports it. Evidence still missing: the scalar ggxDenominator callers (environment, water, voxel-pathtracer) and materials' ggxNamed lobes (KB6016d).
### Section 5 evidence: WGSL return paths on every browser (KB-FF1b)
Firefox's WGSL front end rejects a value-returning function that does not end in a return on every path, a stricter rule than the spec's behavior analysis that Chromium and the WebGL2 layer follow (KB-FF1: water's coastal `root` ended in a `loop` left only by `return`). The rule is a quality gate in three layers: `npm run hygiene` reads every `.wgsl` file and every WGSL function written out whole in the package sources (scripts/support/wgsl-returns.mjs, fatal); `npm run check:wgsl` runs the same token-level analyzer on every shader builder output, fragments included; the WGSL guard every browser check installs reports a gap in any module a page creates as a `[wgsl] error`, so assembled shaders are checked as the GPU gets them. A function must end in `return`, an `if`/`else` returning on both sides, or a `switch` whose clauses all return; `loop`, `for` and `while` never end one. Regression: tests/wgsl-returns.test.js. Evidence still missing: a full Firefox GPU run of every package suite (only the biomes suite has run there).
### Section 5 evidence: tracked conflict-marker hygiene (Job 0)
`npm run hygiene` also rejects a `process.exit(` call in tracked JavaScript or TypeScript (KB-OWN-EXIT2, scripts/support/process-exit.mjs, fatal). `process.exit` shuts V8's platform down while the isolate lives, so a background task waiting on a main-thread collection can hold the exit for ever (KB-OWN-EXIT1, nodejs/node#54918); a script sets `process.exitCode` and lets its event loop end. A line may keep the call only with `// process.exit: <reason>` (a watchdog ending a hung run, an interrupt). The files still owed are listed, exactly, in scripts/support/exit-owed.json, which shrinks to empty: the check fails on a new file and on a listed file that no longer calls it. Regression: tests/process-exit-check.test.js (also runs the fixed gate scripts through tests/support/end-recorder.js). Evidence still missing: the files on the owed list.

`npm run hygiene` rejects retained conflict lines before its scored gates, including warn and quick modes. It scans all tracked docs and md/ts/js/json/mjs/wgsl/glsl working files, excludes LFS and binary content, and reports path plus line. `tests/hygiene-conflict-markers.test.js` covers all extensions, docs text, CRLF, unchanged tracked inputs, binary attributes/bytes, LFS, untracked content and safe near-matches. This also protects check:merge through its existing hygiene step; semantic conflicts still require package tests.

## Batch 173 transfer classification (section 5 supplement)
Existing scalar volumes accept owned classifier LUTs through sciviz alone; core/stage are unchanged. Shader classification uses physical anisotropic central/one-sided gradients, half-texel-correct LUT coordinates and ordered front/back lookups. Classification metadata and LUT bytes survive CPU-backed device restoration; slice bindings follow live LUT replacements. CPU tests cover analytic gradients, tent/Gaussian geometry, ordered optical integrals, cancellation and editor lifetime. The GPU regression uses an analytic linear field spanning outside the colour range: a gradient-1 classifier draws while a disjoint gradient classifier is empty. This prevents the former pre-classification scalar clamp from destroying boundary gradients. Both WebGPU and WebGL2 also render the attributed TCIA field, edit it live, replace slice LUTs and reject edits after disposal. Constant-field preintegration agrees with the ordinary march to one display byte on the checked centre ray. No benchmark is run during build phase.

PNG export now awaits figure/drawable restoration, encodes a COPY_SRC canvas-to-buffer copy during the frame, then maps the owned buffer. This closes stale captures when compatibility compute/culling is loading lazily. The transfer browser regression holds submissions and verifies a new blue frame over the previous red frame on each backend; glyph restoration retains its exact pixel assertion.



### 5. Batch 243 trace extension-lobe ownership
Optional mesh-pbr expands its private material packet; the common Mat carries only a PBR marker. A WGSL invocation-private PBRLayer is prepared once per current surface, with cached view Fresnel. The sampled-emitter reader is pure and cannot overwrite receiver layer state; a regression interleaves distinct receiver/emitter materials. The engine facade and core remain unchanged. Evaluation and sampling use the same full mixture density; perfectly smooth components have delta mass and zero continuous density. Geometric hemisphere rejection retains its null probability. Shared thin-film text is byte-preserved from gltf/pbr and its existing random-input Khronos-reference tests still run. Six new CPU/WGSL cases verify channels, independent GGX/Fresnel, spectral reference, emission layering, hemisphere energy and glTF snapshots; mesh-pbr-lobes-browser.mjs checks both backends and logs create/ready/image phases.

KB5451 (2026-11-11): `pbrMaterial` reads its texture slots through one `pbrTexture` call in a loop bounded by the record's slot count (word 3), so fxc, which inlines every HLSL call, keeps one filter body: 42 to 20 inlined copies over the tracer's entries, the same Direct3D 11 image hash; other staged programs still compile for minutes cold (docs/known-bugs.md).

KB5451 (2026-11-28): the staged WebGL2 route runs mesh PBR's shading normal and material in programs of their own (`shading`, `material`) between `vertex` and `surface`, each computed under a guard that holds wherever its call runs and kept in the path state; the surface program's paired offline fxc went from 94.2 s to 14.1 s (shading 3.7 s, material 9.6 s), and the cold Direct3D 11 first image of mesh-pbr-lobes from 272 s to 200 and 193 s on the busy workstation, readbacks the same on WebGPU and the layer. Still missing: the 120 s bar (sample 83 s, hit 45 s, shadow 28 s cold) and a quiet-machine timing (docs/known-bugs.md).

KB5451 (2026-11-28, emit): the staged WebGL2 route evaluates a mesh emitter's radiance in an `emit` program between `sample` and `shadow` (light kind 5 only), the record and its draws passed through the kind's own `radiance` words so the path state keeps its 280 words, and fetches mesh PBR texels in one tap loop (one `pbrPixel` per `pbrTexture` instead of five); paired offline fxc over the staged programs 89.6 s to 68.0 s, cold Direct3D 11 first image of mesh-pbr-lobes 94 and 91 s to 80 and 77 s on the quiet workstation (bar 120 s), 1,576 readbacks the same on WebGPU and the layer, WebGPU's shader untouched. Still missing: a busy-machine first image under 120 s (167 to 205 s measured) and the `post` and `shadow` programs (about 16 to 18 s each offline; docs/known-bugs.md).

Batch 243 final evidence: mesh, instances, attributes, mesh-pbr, mesh-pbr-lobes and mesh-lights GPU fixtures all pass native WebGPU and WebGL2/Vulkan after the final Wasm build. The lobe suite keeps its 120000 ms image signal and 1e-5 bound. Emitter-only reading evaluates four texture slots instead of fourteen, and continuous BSDF sampling reuses view Fresnel (two evaluations instead of three); independent CPU/WGSL output assertions remain unchanged. Light-family count resides in scene data, preserving proposal order, PDFs and RNG draws. The tagged padded-BLAS input distinguishes actual geometry limits from acceleration bounds: validation recovers only the known one-ULP padding, and TLAS construction still transforms the full conservative box. Ten Rust tests and the exact +/-1e8 emissive-triangle regression pass. The extra cache-disabled compiler defect is tracked, not waived as machine slowness. Receipt: whitepaper/results/batch243-mesh-lobes-20261110.json.


mesh-pbr BLEND (2026-11-25): glTF alphaMode BLEND is stochastic transparency inside the existing any-hit candidate test (`pbrVisible` in `src/mesh-pbr-shader.ts`), so camera, bounce and shadow rays share one rule. The uniform is `hash(rng ^ hash(round13(bits(t))))`: it reads the ray's current rng state without advancing it, so OPAQUE and MASK scenes keep their exact random sequence (the GPU suite's coverage-1 BLEND scene equals OPAQUE bit for bit), and keying on the rounded hit distance gives edge-sharing triangles one decision. A first build keyed on the triangle address measured 0.269 instead of 0.25 on an unjittered 8 x 8 image (exact diagonal pixels decided twice); keyed on t it measures 0.25008 on native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Vulkan (Intel Arc 140V, `npm run test:gpu:mesh-pbr`). Sampled light points on BLEND emitters emit coverage times emission, the expectation path hits reach, so MIS weights are unchanged. Evidence missing: no ANGLE Direct3D 11 run (KB-L5a-10 still blocks it) and no layered-BLEND reference image against an outside renderer.

## Lens post-pass evidence (section 5 supplement, batch 236 job 3)
weather/lens uses the existing PostStack stage protocol and shared fullscreen, display and viewport helpers. Seeded stationary drops and downward streaks distort captured HDR scene colour before display encoding; no changes to core, stage or post are needed. Native and compatibility GPU tests compare 4,400 pure field cases against JavaScript below 0.0001, require wet drops, motion, streak removal and seed changes to alter the image, and require exact identity for dry/disabled and repeated-time frames. Native counts: wet 4,469, motion 6,836, streaks 985, seed 6,630 pixels; both backends report zero shader/validation errors. CPU lifecycle tests cover one-time stack ownership, resource recreation and idempotent disposal. weather/cover (batch 236 job 2) reuses the WeatherFX top-down depth map at graph order -3 and patches core (group 0) and gltf/pbr (group 2) weather calls with one depth test that takes the highest occluder of the four texels around the receiver. GPU evidence on both backends (parity-browser.mjs cover): map probes [0,1,1,1,0,0,0], 0 of 11,564 sheltered pixels change while 11,443 exposed pixels change, rain occlusion 656 pixels, no validation errors. The earlier red gate had two causes: the fixture shelter lay outside the camera-centred map (radius 8 map spanned z 0 to 16), and a single-texel lookup left a half-texel band inside shelter edges exposed (167 pixels). Still missing: MSAA edge pixels are shaded at the pixel centre (see docs/limits.md).

### Section 5 evidence: retarget rest alignment of fingerless mocap hands (KB-RIG-FLATHAND1)

Retarget maths is unchanged: a mapped target bone's world rotation is the source's world delta from rest times the target's aligned rest. Rest alignment now treats a source hand with no finger bones (a BVH End Site, an ASF or Xsens hand segment) as one rigid segment and lays the target hand and long fingers along it; the unmapped bones it turns are held at the aligned rest by `Retarget` (`hold`). Evidence: `packages/loaders/tests/mocap-fk.test.js` checks `parseBVH` against an independent matrix forward-kinematics reader in all six Euler orders (under 1e-9 m); `packages/rigging/tests/retarget.test.js` checks arm, hand and finger directions against the source to 1e-6 degrees. On the 100STYLE Aeroplane excerpt the loader matches the independent reader to 9e-16 m and Elias's upper arm, forearm and hand follow the source to 0.0 degrees. No core, stage, backend or shader change.

Second report (KB-RIG-ARMS2): `tests/mocap-theatre-arms.test.js` drives both theatre takes through the demo's own capture path every frame and checks each arm against the capture's direction (0.5 degrees) and human ranges (carrying angle up to 20, forearm roll 30, pronation 90, wrist 70, in the hinge plane read from Elias's bent bind elbows), and that skinned arm vertices stay on their bones. An upper arm twisted 180 degrees at rest fails it.

Third report (KB-RIG-ARMS2, 2026-11-28): the second report's evidence was Margo's own forward kinematics, and its elbow floor of -10 degrees let the Aeroplane take through. Evidence that is not Margo now exists: Blender 5.3 beta's BVH importer reads the excerpt to the same joint positions as `parseBVH` + `Skeleton` (worst joint 0.062 mm over 64 frames, fixture `tests/fixtures/mocap-theatre/aeroplane-referee.json`, checked by the test within 0.2 mm for the loader and for the skeleton the stage draws). The reversed product, each negated axis, the other handedness, child-frame offsets and radians each miss the referee by 0.27 m or more and move the stance toe 1.7 to 400 times further per frame. So the reading is right and the recording itself holds both forearms 10 to 14 degrees off the upper arm's line, up and back, on every frame. The take is held off the stage (`recordings.brisk.held`), and the test now fails when a listed take passes straight by more than 2 degrees or a held take is on the page. Still missing: target joint limits in the retarget, and an arms-out capture with sane elbows; both wait for Scott (docs/known-bugs.md). No core, stage, backend, shader or package change.

## Batch 173 fusion (section 5 supplement)
The optional sciviz/labels entry owns its textures, CPU snapshots, one uniform packet and one renderer drawable. Its single march traverses the transformed-box union and samples each inverse-registered source at the same data-space point. Ray-projected voxel distance controls both sample spacing and optical correction; partial final segments use their actual length. Integer r32uint category textures use textureLoad with nearest indices, and lossless uint32-to-dense remapping prevents float32 aliasing above 2^24. Eight screen-footprint neighbours detect per-category pixel outlines; ray derivatives are computed before divergent control flow. Component and RGB/RGBA textures are binary16, sampled linearly before classification. Device restoration rebuilds from owned packed snapshots; palette replacement validates before publishing.
CPU checks cover exact/unknown category IDs, transformed-corner bounds, immutable restoration snapshots, palette edit rollback, invalid input before resource publication, escaped legend text and cleanup after a rejected figure attachment. Native WebGPU and WebGL2 GPU checks compare a constant optical field to a closed-form reference, interleaved components to independently transformed sources, rotated scalar ramps to aligned analytical ramps, all three mixing modes, integer categories with an absent adjacent ID, pixel-width outlines, palette restoration, source ray ordering and attributed real MRI rendering. The checked analytical, component/fusion, rotated-ramp and restored-image errors are zero display bytes on both backends. No core/stage changes or timing measurements.

### 5. Condition-based browser check readiness (2026-11-10)

The fixed-wait gate follows lexically scoped frame helpers with explicit simulation deltas (a helper that renders with its own parameter as the delta steps time when the call passes a number above 0, KB-GLTF-FIXEDWAIT1), bounded condition polls and process-kill deadlines. Playwright Promise-valued predicates are valid. Regression coverage is in `tests/check-fixed-waits.test.js`, including zero-delta waits, misleading callback names, unbounded polls and lexical shadowing. The baseline only decreases. Scientific volume checks accumulate to their public sample counters with a hard deadline; progressive-rendering checks await full refinement and cinematic accumulation; voxel model and inspector shader checks await pipeline and submitted-work completion. Inspector relay checks await delivered state, React checks await the requested dimensions/factor and compiled pipelines, and Stats awaits populated CPU/GPU/memory/pass histories. The CPU-load diagnostic samples real browser setup work.

Clean-room sources compared: W3C GPU for the Web Working Group, *WebGPU*, 2026, https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/ (queue completion does not replace asynchronous pipeline completion); Microsoft Playwright contributors, *Page.waitForFunction*, 2026, https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-wait-for-function (Promise predicates are awaited); Node.js contributors, *Child process*, 2026, https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html (exit events versus kill deadlines). These standards and API contracts determine readiness; no external implementation was read or used. No rendering feature, API or timing claim changes.
